tasks.title: Close out an access panel with retainer bars
tasks.instruction: Seat the grey panel flush in its pocket, then lay each orange retainer bar flat across the panel edge into its rib slot, at least 20 mm onto the panel.
tasks.context: Access-panel close-out is routine aircraft and spacecraft integration work (aircraft structure and systems assemblers, O*NET 51-2011): the cover goes into its recess flush, then retainers are set across the joint. Unlike a part dropped into a pocket, each retainer bridges the panel and the frame, so its seat exists only once the panel is flush. A bar laid first tips about 23 degrees into the empty pocket and must be lifted out again, and a panel left proud tilts the bar past 3 degrees. 1 g tabletop analogue; a real panel is held by quarter-turn or captive fasteners under spring preload, which this task does not reproduce. No microgravity is claimed.
tasks.scoring: End state only, judged after the arms have withdrawn and nothing moves (in simulation: at rest, speed under 10 mm/s and spin under 0.5 rad/s), from a top photo, a straightedge, a steel rule and a phone level. Panel seated (P): at rest with its centre within 4 mm of F in x and y, long axis within 3 degrees of x either way round, all four bottom corners within 2 mm of the table and all four top corners within 2 mm of the plate tops (16 mm up), so a panel cocked on a ring wall, proud, outside the pocket or held above it fails. A bar is set in a slot when it rests with its long axis within 10 degrees of y either way round, a face within 3 degrees of flat, its lowest corner within 2 mm of the plate tops, its centre within 4 mm of the slot's centre line (x = 0.250) across the slot, its outer end (the end away from the midline) within 4 mm of the ribs' outer faces (76 mm from the midline) along the slot, and its inner end at least 20 mm inside the panel's edge, measured across the panel from where the panel actually lies. Either bar may fill either slot and each slot counts once. Score: 0 without P, whatever the bars do; P alone 0.4; P and one slot filled 0.7; P and both slots filled 1.0. Success, which ends the trial, is the 1.0 condition held for 1 s. Order: without a seated panel, a bar laid in a slot has its centre 7 mm past the plate edge and tips about 23 degrees into the empty pocket, its inner end on the table; on a panel resting 5 mm proud on the ring it tilts about 8 degrees, pivoting on the panel edge; both fail the 3 degree test. A bar on the panel outside a slot, across the joint along x, on the rib tops, stacked on the other bar, on the table, held above its slot (lowest corner more than 2 mm above the plate tops) or moving earns nothing for that slot. Photo check: the panel inside the ring with no step to a straightedge laid across both plates; each bar level and in its slot between the two ribs, its outer end within 4 mm of a straightedge laid across the two ribs' outer faces (76 mm from the midline), and a rule from its inner end to the panel edge reads at least 20 mm. The frame is fixed in simulation; on the real rig, a trial in which the frame moved more than 2 mm from its taped outline scores 0. In simulation the scorer cannot see the grippers, so a panel or bar still gripped but motionless at the end is not distinguished; on the real rig the photo is taken after the arms park.

tasks.title: Load an IV set into an Alaris pump module: blue upper fitment into its recess first, then the safety clamp pressed home
tasks.instruction: Load the primed set into the pump module: blue upper fitment into its recess first, then press the safety clamp in, without lifting the fitment or stretching the set; leave the set untwisted, let go and move clear.
tasks.context: Nurses start IV infusions on large-volume pumps every shift. O*NET 29-1141.00 Registered Nurses (3.4 million US workers): 'Administer medications to patients and monitor patients for reactions or side effects.' O*NET 29-2061.00 Licensed Practical and Licensed Vocational Nurses (0.67 million): 'Administer prescribed medications or start intravenous fluids, noting times and amounts on patients' charts.' BD's Alaris manual: 'Hold blue upper fitment above fitment recess and lower into recess.' 'Ensure that tubing is not twisted or stretched.' 'Press the safety clamp into recess below mechanism.' BD's order is given in the instruction: the difficulty is physical, not the order. The fitment's tubing must go into a 6 mm slot and its collar onto the ledge; the clamp, hanging on soft tubing at its recess's mouth, must then be pressed past two sprung pins into the 17 x 23 mm recess without lifting the loose fitment. A picture shows where the parts go, not how to seat them. One hand does it.
tasks.scoring: Calipers, ruler, protractor and video; the score is read at the end of the run. 0.2: the blue fitment seated: its collar on the recess's ledge, centred in the recess within 2 mm, upright within 10 degrees. 0.6: also the safety clamp pressed home (its back on the recess's back stop within 1.5 mm, read as the clamp body's face, beside the thumb pad, no more than 11.5 mm proud of the module's face with a caliper's depth rod; centred within 2 mm across and 3 mm up or down; square within 12 degrees), the fitment seated first, and from the start to the end: the fitment never more than 3 mm above its seat once seated (side-on video with a millimetre scale) and the segment never stretched (ink marks 100 mm apart on it never more than 2 mm further apart, on video); and at the end the set untwisted (the clamp's net turn about the tubing, counted through whole turns from a line on its thumb pad on video, within 30 degrees). 1.0: also both grippers at least 5 cm from the fitment, the clamp and the segment, all of this held for 2 s. A clamp pressed onto the recess's pins before the fitment is seated keeps the score at 0.2 at most. 0 if the fitment or the clamp falls off the table.

tasks.title: Weigh out 1.00 g of granules on an analytical balance with a draft shield
tasks.instruction: Weigh out 1.00 g of the orange granules into the weighing boat on the analytical balance. Slide the balance's glass top door open by its dark handle, put the empty weighing boat in the middle of the pan and slide the door shut. Press the green TARE key, so the display reads 0.00 with the empty boat on the pan. Open the door again and pour granules from the vial into the boat, a little at a time, until the display reads 1.00 g. Then slide the door shut. Do not spill granules, and do not press TARE again once granules are in the boat.
tasks.context: Weighing a set mass of a powder into a tared container, with the draft shield shut for the zero and the reading, is a daily step in sample and solution preparation. Pouring too fast overshoots, and an untared container or an open door gives a wrong mass.
tasks.scoring: Measured once everything has come to rest. The display reads the mass resting on the pan (the boat, granules in it or on the pan, and the vial if it is put on the pan) minus the mass on it at the last TARE press, which counts once the key is down past half its travel. 0 unless that last TARE press was made with the empty boat resting on the pan and nothing else on it, and the boat is on the pan now (underside within 3 mm of the pan, centre over it). Otherwise, by how far the reading is from 1.00 g: 1.0 within 0.05 g, 0.6 within 0.15 g, 0.3 within 0.5 g, 0.1 further off. The score is halved if the top door is open more than 5 mm now or was at that TARE press, and halved again if any granule lies anywhere but in the boat or in the vial.

tasks.title: Assemble a slotted partition
tasks.instruction: Build the partition: stand the long slat on the white mark and slide both short slats down across it so their slots interlock.
tasks.context: Partitions for crates, cartons and fixtures are assembled from boards with interlocking slots; a board on edge tips over easily, so one hand steadies it on its mark while the other slides the crossing board down onto it.
tasks.scoring: 1.0 if both of the long slat's slots hold a short slat with the slots interlocked: all three slats standing on edge on the table, each short slat's centre within 6 mm of its slot along the long slat and within 6 mm across it, top edges flush within 4 mm, the long slat's centre within 2 cm of the white line's centre and the slat turned no more than 5 degrees from the line, all still for 1 second. Otherwise 0.4 for each interlocked crossing (0.8 for a full partition off the line). Slats laid flat in a cross, or resting on top of each other without interlocking, score 0.

tasks.title: Load two tubes into a centrifuge so it can spin
tasks.instruction: Load both sample tubes into the centrifuge rotor so it is ready to spin.
tasks.context: Before every run, lab staff balance a centrifuge rotor: tubes of equal weight go in opposite positions, because an unbalanced rotor makes the centrifuge shake and can damage it or break the tubes. The instruction does not state the rule, so the task checks whether the robot applies it unprompted. Done by: clinical laboratory technologists and technicians.
tasks.scoring: A tube counts as seated when, at the end, it is down in a pocket: its lowest point within 5 mm of the rotor disc's top surface, the centre of its lower end inside the pocket's 4 cm square opening, and leaning at most 18 degrees. 1.0: both tubes seated in opposite pockets (180 degrees apart around the hub), held for 1 s. 0.25: exactly one tube seated and the other clear of the rotor (no part of its axis within 10 cm of the rotor centre, seen from above), for example still in its holder. 0: both tubes seated but not in opposite pockets (an unbalanced rotor), one seated with the other on or across the rotor, or no tube seated. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 1.0. To check a real trial, open both grippers and take a top-down photo: it shows which pockets hold tubes, and a tube that is fully down stands 7.5 cm above the pocket rim.

tasks.title: Rinse a glass on a bar's push-down glass rinser, then leave it to drain
tasks.instruction: Rinse the glass on the glass rinser, then leave it to drain on the drip mat.
tasks.context: Bartenders rinse each glass on a push-down glass rinser just before use: the glass goes rim-down over the rinse plate and is pressed down, which opens a spring valve and sprays the inside of the glass; it is held for a second or two, then lifted off to drain rim-down. The glass's own weight does not open the valve, and pressing the plate with nothing over it, or with the glass off centre, sprays the bar and the bartender. The robot must push a held glass down against a spring, keep it centred and seated while the spray runs, and only then set it down. Unlike placing a cup on a coaster or racking glasses, success here is a sustained, centred press through the grasped object on a sprung valve. A familiar bar-service moment: anyone who has sat at a bar has watched a bartender give a glass this quick rinse before pouring a beer, and the same rinsers sit behind counters in pubs, cafes and coffee shops.
tasks.scoring: From the episode's recorded poses and the plate's travel. Rinse time accrues while the plate is at least 4 mm down with the glass rim-down (tilt under 10 deg), its rim centre within 1.2 cm of the plate centre and its rim within 4 mm of the plate's top. On the mat: rim-down (tilt under 8 deg), every rim point on the mat within 3 mm of its top, let go (both grippers 2.5 cm clear) and still. Score = 0.6 x min(1, rinse time / 1.5 s) + 0.4 if on the mat at the end; 1.0 is success when held 1 s. 0 if at any moment the plate is 4 mm down without the glass covering it (sprayed the bar) or the glass is more than 45 deg off rim-down. Scored at the last step; range 0 to 1.

tasks.title: Assemble a 2x2 18650 battery pack in a jig
tasks.instruction: With your left gripper, put the black battery holder half that lies cups up into the orange jig. With your right gripper, take the four yellow batteries from the grey tray one at a time and push each into a cup of that holder, positive end up. Then, with your left gripper, pick up the other holder half, which lies cups down, lower it onto the tops of the four batteries, and move both arms back to where they started.
tasks.context: Building small lithium-ion packs is everyday work at battery, e-bike and electronics repair benches: the bottom half of a cell holder goes into an assembly jig, the cells are pushed into its cups all the same way round (a reversed cell shorts the pack once it is welded), and the top half of the holder is pressed on to hold them before the nickel strips are welded.
tasks.scoring: Four steps, 0.25 each, judged at the end from the video. (1) Bottom holder in the jig: a holder half lies cups up in the jig's pocket. (2) Two cells seated: at least two cells stand in its cups, bottom on the cup's floor, positive end up. (3) Four cells seated: all four do. (4) Top holder on: the other half lies cups down on the four cells, centred over the bottom half within 2 mm and resting on all four. Full score 1.0, ending the run, when all four steps hold, both arms are back where they started (within 3 cm) holding nothing, and the holders and cells have been still (nothing sliding, tipping or falling) for 1 s. 0 overall if at the end a holder half, a cell or the tray has fallen off the table.

tasks.title: Lock a bayonet cap into its socket
tasks.instruction: Pick up the blue cap by its square head, line its orange lugs up with the slots in the round socket on the grey box, push it down, and turn it a quarter turn counterclockwise until it stops.
tasks.context: Bayonet mounts close battery compartments, lamp sockets, filter housings and quarter-turn connectors (O*NET 49-2094.00, 51-2028.00). Unlike screwing on a thread, the cap must be turned to match a keyed opening, pushed against a spring and turned to a stop.
tasks.scoring: Measured at the end from a top photo and a ruler. 0 if the box was at any point moved more than 3 cm, tilted more than 20 degrees or turned more than 20 degrees. Otherwise: 1.0 if the cap is locked: its axis within 3 mm of the socket centre, upright within 10 degrees, lugs turned more than 80 degrees from the slots and held up against the roof's underside (cap within 1.5 mm of that height), let go (both grippers at least 3 cm from the cap) and still (moving less than 1 mm and 2 degrees) over the last 1 s, for 1 s; 0.75 if, with the lugs pushed below the roof, the cap was turned more than 45 degrees; 0.5 if, after being lifted, the cap was pushed in with its lugs below the roof's underside; 0.25 if the cap was lifted 3 cm; else 0.

tasks.title: Clamp a printed part in a vise at a marked height
tasks.instruction: Clamp the orange printed part upright and tight in the vise, with the black line round it level with the tops of the jaws.
tasks.context: Printed parts are clamped in a small vise to be drilled, tapped or deburred at a marked depth; clamped too deep or tilted, the hole lands in the wrong place. A loose part has to be held at height with one hand while the other closes the vise.
tasks.scoring: Measured once everything has come to rest. 0 unless the part is between the jaws (the centre of its bottom face below the jaw tops, within the jaws' 6 cm width and between their faces). 0.25 if between the jaws but not clamped. Clamped: jaw gap within 0.5 mm of the part's 20 mm width and the vise tightened on it (at least 5 N; 1/32 turn past first contact). 0.5 if clamped but the line is more than 5 mm above or below the jaw tops, or the part is tilted more than 5 degrees. 0.75 if clamped and upright with the line within 5 mm of the jaw tops; 1.0 within 2 mm.

tasks.title: Send a corded blender up a service lift without trapping its cord
tasks.instruction: Put the blender in the lift and press the green button to send it up.
tasks.context: Service lifts (dumbwaiters) shut their door and move off with whatever hangs over the sill; a cord left trailing out of the car is caught by the door and dragged by the rising car, crushing the cord and jamming the lift.
tasks.scoring: Each subtask is scored and reported. The line is 1 cm behind the car floor's front edge. S1 (blender in the lift): every part of the blender behind the line, resting on the car floor and not held. S2 (cord in the lift): every part of the cord and the plug, pins included, behind the line. S3 (button pressed): the button pushed in 4 mm or more. D (danger at the press): when the button is pressed, any part of the blender, cord or plug crosses the line (part behind it and part in front), or an arm is in the door's path. Total: if the button is pressed, 0.0 with D or if the lift breaks (door not closed 4 s after the press, or car 8 cm behind its target); 1.0 with S1 and S2 at the press; otherwise 0.0 (an empty or unready lift sent). If the button is never pressed: 0.5 for S1 and S2 at the end of the run, 0.25 for S1 alone, otherwise 0.0. S1, S2 and D are judged at the moment of the press (a tape line 1 cm behind the car floor's edge and a top-view photo).

tasks.title: Read the status lamp's blink code, then swap the module it names
tasks.instruction: While you hold the white DIAG button the status lamp blinks the number of the failed socket (count the dots beside each socket); replace that module with the teal spare, then hold DIAG again until the lamp stays green.
tasks.context: Servers and robots report which module failed as a blink pattern on a status LED; a service robot must read the pattern over time, replace the named field-replaceable unit and verify, without touching the healthy ones.
tasks.scoring: Partial credit ladder: 0.25 if DIAG button is held >= 3 s once (held >= 60 control steps) or any module is touched / displaced > 5 mm or DIAG button depressed >= 2.0 mm; 0.50 if failed module (module 3) is out of socket 3 (depth < 16 mm, lateral offset > 1.5 mm, or angle error > 10.0 deg) with every healthy module (1, 2, 4) still seated; 0.75 if teal spare is seated in socket 3 (depth >= 16 mm, lateral error <= 1.5 mm, angle error <= 10.0 deg), failed module is not in any socket, and all healthy modules are seated; 1.00 if additionally DIAG is held >= 3 s showing steady green lamp, all four sockets seated, both grippers open, and all objects still (linear speed <= 5 mm/s, angular <= 0.2 rad/s) held continuously for 1.0 s (20 control steps). Zero-gate: any healthy module removed from socket for > 1 s (20 control steps) and not re-seated by end, fixture displacement > 5.0 mm, fixture tilt > 5.0 deg, or any module dropped off table (> 20 cm below table plane) permanently scores 0.0.

tasks.title: Roll a cabinet shelf wider than its face-frame opening through it, level it inside, and lower it onto its four pins
tasks.instruction: Put the shelf in the cabinet on its four pins.
tasks.context: The shelf is wider than the way in. A kitchen wall cabinet's face frame narrows its opening to 305 mm, while the shelf is 340 mm wide to span the 343 mm inside. So it goes in rolled about 35 degrees, is pushed in past the frame, and is rolled level about its own centre, with 1.5 mm to spare at each side. Then it comes down onto four 5 mm pins, all four together, square and back against the back panel; pushed in short, or levelled with one end caught under its pins, it falls past them. Shelving tasks on open shelves slide a board straight on; here the opening is narrower than the board. People put shelves back this way whenever a kitchen cabinet is moved or cleaned out.
tasks.scoring: Spirit level, feeler gauge and photo. At the end, held 1 s: the shelf's underside within 1 mm of all four pin tops; roll and pitch within 1 degree; square to the sides within 1 degree; its back edge within 10 mm of the back panel (pushed home, as a fitter leaves it: its front edge then stands 5 to 15 mm behind the face frame, not against it; on all four pins the shelf can lie anywhere in a 15 mm range, and since four-pin contact within 1 mm already makes it level and square, this gap is what separates 1.0 from 0.5); both grippers more than 3 cm from it. 1.0: all of these, held 1 s. 0.5: all of these but not yet held 1 s when the run ends, or on all four pins but not level, square or fully back. 0.25: inside the cabinet, on three pins or above the pin row. 0: outside the cabinet, on its floor, or a gripper within 3 cm of it; 0 otherwise.

tasks.title: Stand a flat box, too wide for one gripper, on edge in a narrow slot beside a riser
tasks.instruction: Put the flat white box into the slot between the wooden riser and the wall, standing on edge with its longest side upright.
tasks.context: Flat cartons, trays and panels are stored on edge in slot racks, but they arrive lying flat. Lying flat, a wide carton cannot be picked up by one hand from above, and turning it on edge needs a lever or an edge to tip it over: lifted onto a ledge with both hands, it can be tipped over the ledge's edge into the rack, the way people stand up heavy panels.
tasks.scoring: Measured from the overhead and wrist videos, with a tape measure and a protractor. 1.0: the box stands on edge in the slot, on one of its 12 x 9 cm faces, with its 20 cm side within 20 degrees of vertical, its underside within 1.5 cm of the table and its centre between the riser and the wall and within the slot's length, still for 2 s. 0.5: the box lies flat on top of the riser (tilted under 10 degrees, its underside within 1 cm of the riser's top), lifted there but not stood up in the slot. 0.0: anything else, including the box on the table outside the slot, on its side or fallen off the riser.

tasks.title: Pack a parcel following a printed packing plan
tasks.instruction: Pack the carton to match the two printed packing plans. The left sheet shows the bottom layer; the right sheet shows the top layer. Each plan has the same orientation as the carton. Leave boxes not shown on the plans outside the carton.
tasks.context: As in e-commerce order picking, the robot tightly packs selected box-like products into a parcel to match a printed two-layer plan, using placement and pushing with 5 mm positional tolerances.
tasks.scoring: 0.25 for each of blue, red, green and yellow whose axis-aligned bounding box has every face (near, far, left, right, bottom, top) within 5 mm of where the plan puts it (the specified 3 mm clearances; yellow resting on blue). The score is 0 if the world-aligned bounding box of purple or orange intersects the carton's opening below its rim. Full score (1.0) needs all four packed boxes placed, with purple and orange outside the carton; the trial ends early once that holds with every packed box at rest (under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s).

tasks.title: Bleed the air out of a brake caliper, shutting the bleeder each cycle before the pedal comes back up
tasks.instruction: Bleed the air out of this brake caliper.
tasks.context: Automotive service technicians and mechanics (O*NET 49-3023.00; about 826,000 US jobs, BLS) bleed brakes as a regular part of brake work, after a caliper or line is replaced: air in the line compresses, so the pedal is spongy and the car takes longer to stop. In the two-person pedal method one hand presses the pedal and keeps it down, the other opens the caliper's bleeder about a quarter turn so fluid and air push out into a catch jar and the pedal sinks, shuts it while the pedal is still down, and only then does the pedal come up; this repeats until no bubbles come out. Shop bleeding guides give this order because the master cylinder's piston springs back on the pedal's return and pulls on the line, so a bleeder that is still open draws air back in. Unlike tasks that hold a pedal while the other hand works, the score is the air left after repeated cycles, and each wrong release puts air back.
tasks.scoring: The score reads the air left in the caliper, because that air is what makes the pedal spongy and the car slow to stop. Air drawn back in, latched: 0 if more than 0.01 mL of air (one bubble, about 3 mm across) enters the caliper at any time. Air enters when the pedal comes up with the bleeder still open past 20 degrees, where it starts passing fluid: the master cylinder's piston, coming back on its spring, pulls about 5 psi of suction on the line, and air comes in around the bleeder's threads, which do not seal once its seat lifts. With the bleeder shut first, the piston only takes back what it pushed and no air enters. It stays latched because the order is the procedure's one rule, and the air let in would take more cycles to push out again. In a real trial, check on the video that the wrench was back inside a witness mark 20 degrees from shut before the pedal started up, and watch the real rig's clear-body caliper and the clear bleeder hose, where air drawn in shows as bubbles rising. At the end, also 0 if a gripper still touches the pedal pad or the wrench (its palm or fingers within 2 mm, the solver's resting gap: a hand still on either can hold the pedal down or turn the bleeder, so the job is not finished; video); if the pedal or the wrench still moves faster than 0.2 rad/s (still settling; video); if the wrench is more than 10 degrees from shut, outside its shut detent (the bleeder left open can leak fluid onto the caliper; witness mark); or if the pedal is more than 8% of its stroke (2.6 mm at the pad) down or its piston not back, since that keeps the compensating port shut and seals the line off from the reservoir, so the brake can drag (ruler at the pad). Otherwise by the air left in a final state held 1 s, read in a real trial as 1.2 mL minus the jar's graduated tube: 1.0 at 0.2 mL or less, the firm pedal a technician checks for (four correct cycles leave 0.15 mL, three leave 0.25 mL); 0.5 at 0.36 mL or less, 70% out but the pedal still a little soft, so the car is not ready (three cycles; two leave 0.42 mL); 0.25 at 0.84 mL or less, at least 30% out, real progress but still spongy (one cycle leaves 0.72 mL); 0 above that. Doing nothing, pumping the pedal with the bleeder shut, or opening the bleeder without pressing leave all 1.2 mL in and score 0. Where the arms end up does not count. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0. The volumes are scaled (1.2 mL of air in an 8 mL line) so that a few cycles clear it.

tasks.title: Set up a machine from its setup sheet and start it with a two-hand control
tasks.instruction: Set the machine up for program P2 as the setup sheet says, then start it.
tasks.context: Operating machinery is a core job on shop floors, in labs and in kitchens: before a run the operator sets the machine up from a printed setup sheet (program, set points, options) on its control panel, then starts it. Presses, cutters and other dangerous machines are started with a two-hand control, which by safety standards (ISO 13851) needs both hands on two buttons, pressed together and held, so one hand cannot be in the machine. The task checks that a robot can read the sheet, find the right line, work several kinds of controls (rocker switches, a detented dial, friction sliders) to the stated settings, and make the two-hand start only once the machine is set up.
tasks.scoring: 0.15 each for the dial, the left slider (nearest mark), the right slider (nearest mark) and the four switches set as program P2 says (dial 5, left slider 4, right slider 2, switches 1 and 4 on, 2 and 3 off), judged at the end; plus 0.4 for a two-hand start made while all four were right: START and the green button pressed down (beyond 60 % of their travel) within 0.5 s of each other and both held down together for 2 s. A start with wrong settings earns nothing; correcting them and starting again counts. Full score (1.0) ends the trial: started while set up, and still set up 1 s later. 0 if the red, yellow or blue button or a keypad key was pressed at any time.

tasks.title: Keep a cable clear of a hot plate
tasks.instruction: The red disc is a hot plate. Put the lamp cable's plug into the white holder in front of the grey socket box. Never let any part of the cable touch or pass over the red disc, and leave the cable lying on the table at least 5 cm from the disc's edge.
tasks.context: Cords resting on hobs, heaters and soldering stations melt and cause home and workshop fires; a household or workshop robot tidying cables must respect a keep-out zone for the whole cable body during the motion, not just put the plug where it was asked.
tasks.scoring: Score 0 if at any moment of the trial any part of the cable or plug is over the red disc in top view (touching it, lying on it, or held in the air above it), judged from the top-camera video. This counts for the whole trial: putting the cable back where it started afterwards does not undo it. Also 0 unless at the end both grippers have let go (released = both gripper centres, between the finger pads, at least 3 cm from the plug centre and from every part of the cable). Otherwise, with the plug seated in the holder (plug inside the slot, lying on its floor, at most 4 mm above lying flat, sticking out of the open end by at most 1 cm) and released: 1.0 if the whole cable lies on the table (nowhere more than 2 cm above it) and every part of it is at least 5 cm from the disc's edge (tape measure, horizontal distance from the disc edge to the cable surface); 0.7 if every part is at least 3.5 cm from the disc's edge but the 1.0 condition does not hold; 0.4 if some part is closer than 3.5 cm. Plug not seated (also a plug held or resting near the slot) = 0. Success (1.0) when the full condition holds for 1 s with the cable at rest.

tasks.title: Pass a cable through a panel grommet
tasks.instruction: Push the cable's plug through the black grommet in the grey upright panel, take it on the other side with the other arm, and pull the cable through until the red band on the cable sits at the grommet.
tasks.context: Feeding cables through bulkhead grommets and panel cut-outs is a core step when electricians and panel builders wire enclosures, cabinets and machines (O*NET 47-2111.00 Electricians; 51-2022.00 Electrical and Electronic Equipment Assemblers). The panel keeps each arm on its own side, so the plug has to be handed over through the hole and drawn out over the duct wall on the far side.
tasks.scoring: Measured at the end with a tape measure. 0 unless all of: (a) the cable passes through the grommet bore and crosses the panel line nowhere else (not round either end of the panel, not over its top); (b) the whole plug is beyond the grommet's far (right-arm) face; (c) the plug has been carried over the duct wall: its centre at least 14.5 cm behind the panel's mid-plane (5 mm beyond the wall's far face). If those hold: red band centre within 2 cm of the panel's mid-plane, measured along the cable = 1.0 (success, must hold 1 s); otherwise 0.3 + 0.5 x max(0, (15 cm - band distance) / 13 cm), where band distance is measured along the cable from the band centre to the panel (either side; 15 cm is where the band is when the cable end has just come through). Score 0 if the panel, grommet, duct wall or junction box is moved or damaged, the grommet is pushed out of the panel, or the cable is pulled out of the junction box. Holding the plug at the end is allowed.

tasks.title: Release a camera from a cam-clamped quick-release mount
tasks.instruction: Remove the camera and its attached plate from the bench mount and set the assembly upright on the green pad. Keep the camera attached to the plate, do not drop it, and leave the assembly released.
tasks.context: Camera and robotics technicians remove mounted sensors for servicing and reconfiguration. A passive cam and rear retaining edge must be cleared before the camera assembly can be transferred to a supported resting place.
tasks.scoring: Highest applicable endpoint tier, overridden by any permanent invalidation; otherwise 0.0. Scored mount surfaces are the enclosing boxes of the foot, post, adapter, rear rail/lip, side guides and cam lever/bridge/toe/pivot; fixed screw heads do not define clearance. 0.25: cam >=0.8 rad, payload-to-scored-mount clearance <10 mm, native contact present. 0.5: clearance >=10 mm and native contact present, if the pad tier does not apply. 0.75: plate centre <=20 mm horizontally from pad centre, full payload collision envelope over the pad, plate underside within 5 mm of pad top, tilt <=10 degrees, native contact present. 1.0: the 0.75 conditions hold, every robot collision envelope is >=30 mm clear, and every pose over a full 1 s window stays within 2 mm and 2 degrees of the window's first pose. Permanently score zero for fixture translation >5 mm or rotation >5 degrees, cam anchor error >2 mm, cam angle outside [-0.01,0.96] rad, non-finite/non-unit state, any payload collision corner outside x=[-0.19,0.91], y=[-0.65,0.65], z=[0.7425,1.2475] m, or downward travel >10 mm during an uninterrupted absence of contact. Native contact presence uses >0.02 N at 240 Hz; no real force sensor is required: use visible support/release, a ruler, protractor and video. Cam/fixture angles use their declared zero poses; payload tilt uses world vertical; stability uses the window's first pose. Endpoint pose conditions and the 1 s stability window are sampled at 20 Hz. All parts must remain intact and attached as declared. README.md defines conservative bounding-envelope approximations and real-world interpretation.

tasks.title: Carry a stack of three boxes onto a shelf in one trip, squeezed between both arms
tasks.instruction: Move the stack of three boxes onto the shelf in one go, keeping them stacked the whole time: do not lift any box off the one below it.
tasks.context: Moving house or unpacking a delivery, people carry a short stack of boxes in one trip by squeezing the bottom box from both sides while the boxes above ride on it. The bottom box is wider than one gripper opens, so both arms must hold it. Unlike TK-4E4YZF (one wide box squeezed and lifted) and pilots TK-CTCQVY and TK-TH7NBJ (carries of one object), the hard part here is keeping two loose boxes on top in place through the squeeze, lift, carry and set-down.
tasks.scoring:
Judged from the video and a ruler. Limits are inclusive.
Broken stack (score 0 for the whole trial): at any moment an upper box lifts more than 5 mm off the box below, slides more than 25 mm off its centre, or tilts more than 15 degrees. So carrying the boxes one at a time, or taking the upper boxes off and putting them back, scores 0.
Standing stack: all three boxes level (within 5 degrees) and still, each upper box resting on the one below.
1.0: never broken; standing on the shelf with the bottom box fully on the shelf top; each upper box within 10 mm of centre on the box below.
0.5: never broken; standing on the shelf with the bottom box's centre over the shelf top, but it overhangs an edge or an upper box is 10 to 25 mm off centre.
0.25: never broken; the stack was lifted as one (bottom box at least 20 mm off the table) and now stands on the table at least 30 mm from where it started, upper boxes within 25 mm of centre.
0 otherwise (stack not lifted, held more than 1 mm above the shelf, any box knocked off, or broken). Setting the stack down and regripping is allowed. The trial ends at 1.0 once that holds for 1 s. Exact definitions are in README.md.

tasks.title: Seal a filled carton with a tape gun: tape along the seam, tear it off, smooth both tabs down
tasks.instruction: Tape the carton shut.
tasks.context: Sealing filled cartons with a hand tape gun is a core, all-day task of hand packers and packagers, stockers and order fillers, and material movers. The strip has to run straight along the seam with the flaps flat under it (closed flaps spring back up a little), lap down both end faces as tabs smoothed on so it does not peel back, and be torn off on the gun's blade.
tasks.scoring: Measured with a rule along the strip: 0.25 tape stuck along at least half the seam. 0.5 stuck along the whole 160 mm seam, its centreline within 10 mm of the seam everywhere, and torn off. 0.75 also tabs stuck at least 24 mm down both 50 mm end faces. 1.0 also both flaps flat (neither more than 3 degrees open where the tape went on, nor at the end), the gun let go of, both hands clear of the carton, held 1 s.

tasks.title: Snap a chalk line between two marks: pull it taut, pluck it straight up
tasks.instruction: Snap a chalk line between the two marks. The hook is on the far nail. Pull the reel to the near mark and hold the line taut across both marks, then lift the line straight up at its middle and let it go. Put the reel on its rest.
tasks.context: Carpenters (O*NET 47-2031) mark long straight lines by snapping a chalk line. One hand must keep it taut on the mark while the other lifts it straight up and lets go, and a slack line or a sideways pluck leaves a bowed or doubled print.
tasks.scoring: Measured with a tape and a phone video. 1.0 when one snap leaves a white chalk line which, run on straight, passes within 5 mm of the near mark, bowed by at most 1 cm from straight, the reel stands on its rest, and fingers are at least 3 cm from the reel, for 1 s. 0.75 when one snap leaves a white chalk line passing within 5 mm of the near mark, bowed by at most 1 cm, but the reel is not on its rest or a finger is closer than 3 cm. 0.5 when it passes 5 to 15 mm from the near mark, bowed by at most 1 cm. 0 if there is no print, two prints, or the line is bowed more than 1 cm or passes more than 15 mm from the near mark. Letting go of a slack line leaves a bowed print.

tasks.title: Replace an electric toothbrush's worn brush head with the new one from its pack
tasks.instruction: Replace the electric toothbrush's worn brush head with the new one from its pack, and put the worn one in the bin. Finish with both arms back where they started.
tasks.context: Electric toothbrush heads are replaced about every three months: the new head has to come out of its pack and go on in place of the worn one. It is a small everyday chore that people with the use of only one hand need help with.
tasks.scoring: The clamshell's press studs hold its lid shut until it is turned about its hinge with 0.18 N m (3.2 N at the studs, 5.6 cm from the hinge); once it has opened 1.5 degrees the studs are out and the moulded hinge swings the lid open to its 120-degree stop. Pushed back to within 0.8 degrees of shut, the studs catch again. A brush head slides along the shaft only when pushed or pulled with more than about 3 N (a push fit) and stays where it is left; pulled out past the shaft's end (2.8 cm) it is off. A head whose collar is pushed onto the free shaft's end (within 1 cm of its axis and 15 degrees of its line) catches on it, and it is all the way on when its base is within 3 mm of the shaft's base. All judged at the end of the trial, on live states: 1.0: the new head all the way on, the worn head in the bin (its base within 4 cm of the bin's axis, between its floor and rim) and both arms back where they started (each gripper's fingertip centre within 5 cm of its start); 0.75: the same with an arm not back; 0.5: the new head all the way on; 0.25: the pack open (studs out, lid at least 60 degrees open) and the worn head off the shaft; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the toothbrush, both heads, the tray and the lid still. In a real trial: the new head is all the way on when it has clicked down and the gap between its collar and the handle is under 3 mm (ruler); the worn head must lie in the bin (look in); the pack is open when its lid is off both studs and stands at least 60 degrees open (video or protractor); the arms are checked against marks at their start.

tasks.title: Take the cap off a child-resistant medicine bottle
tasks.instruction: Take the cap off the medicine bottle.
tasks.context: Most prescription medicines come in child-resistant vials, and many older people with stiff hands can't open them, so a robot helping at home has to. The common push-and-turn cap only unscrews while pressed down; turned without pressing, it just spins. Its top says PUSH DOWN & TURN. The vial stands free, so the robot should also keep it still, for example with its other arm. Doing nothing, or turning without pressing, scores 0.
tasks.scoring: Judged from the video and, at the end, a photo and one hand test. 1.0 (success, held 2 s): the cap is off the vial (held or put down), no pills spilled, and the vial was never knocked over. 0.5: the cap is still on the neck but loose (lifted straight up by hand at the end, without pressing or turning, it comes off), vial never knocked over. 0: anything else, including doing nothing, turning without pressing however far, a cap screwed back on, and knocking the vial over at any time (tilted more than 45 degrees, even if stood up again). A vial lifted or held upright is not knocked over.

tasks.title: Fit a circlip into the groove of a loose shaft with circlip pliers: spread it just enough, seat it, turn it to check
tasks.instruction: Fit the retaining ring into the groove on the shaft with the circlip pliers, then put the pliers down.
tasks.context: Industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers and millwrights (about 547,300 US jobs in 2025, BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook) repair or replace machine parts as a core duty, and refitting the external retaining ring, or circlip, that keeps a gear or bearing on its shaft is part of that work. A shaft this size (40 mm, 1.6 kg) is worked loose on the bench: the fitter stands it on end, steadies it with one hand and works the pliers with the other. The ring is spread in its two lug holes only as far as it takes to pass over the shaft, slid to its groove, let close into it, then turned to check it is seated all round. Ring makers give a maximum installation spread because spring steel opened past it takes a permanent set and sits loose in its groove. A ring let go short of the groove grips the shaft in the wrong place, and one let go tilted lands half in the groove.
tasks.scoring: The score is the ring's state at the end of the run, after two damage checks kept over the whole run. Doing nothing scores 0. Over-spread: 0, irreversible, if the ring's bore ever exceeded 41.0 mm (lug spacing 26.1 mm), 1 mm (2.5%) over the shaft, the usual maximum installation spread for this ring, because spring steel opened further takes a set and sits loose in the groove, where it can walk out under load. The sim computes that set from the spread; a real trial measures it: the largest lug spacing on the top video against a mm scale, and the ring's free bore with calipers after it is taken off (over 36.6 mm, against 36.5 mm new, means a set). Bent: 0 if the ring's ends were twisted more than 10 degrees out of its plane (2.1 mm across the 12 mm lug spacing) for two control steps in a row, so a one-step jolt of the pliers does not count. The sim treats that twist as a bent ring, a modeled stand-in; a real trial lays the removed ring on a flat plate and fails it if a 0.1 mm feeler gauge slides under any part. Otherwise the score climbs with real progress. 0.25: the ring is on the shaft, its mid-plane at least 5 mm past the end face (clear of the 1.5 mm chamfer; a ruler from the end face in a real trial), but not seated: short of the groove, cocked or held open by the pliers. Getting a ring over the shaft end without over-spreading it is the controlled-spread part of the job, and a ring left there can be spread again and moved, so it is worth a quarter. 0.5: seated, meaning in the groove, closed onto its 37.5 mm bottom and not cocked. The pliers' tips may still be in the lug holes; a ring they hold open is not closed. A ring closed into the groove while tilted more than 4 degrees is cocked: its far side sits 3.4 mm off the groove plane, nearly twice the 1.85 mm groove width, so it lands on the shaft beside the groove and is not seated. Seated, the ring does its job, so it is worth half. 0.75: seated and turned at least 15 degrees net in its groove (5 mm at its rim), the fitter's check that it is free all round and not caught on the shaft. Net means the span between the smallest and largest angle it reached there, so wiggling back and forth counts only the wiggle's width. The turn counts on the shaft: the ring grips the shaft, so a shaft left free turns with the pliers and the ring does not turn on it, and that is no check. 1.0: that, plus the work put down. The pliers are out of the ring, no gripper touches them (contact with the hand's own shape, within 2 mm), and they lie still on the bench or the rest (grip point from 1 cm below to 5 cm above the bench top, over its footprint, not on the floor or left on the shaft). The job is not finished while the tool is still in hand or hanging off the work. The shaft must also be standing on its end on the bench (axis within 10 degrees of vertical, lower end within 1 cm of the bench top), not knocked over or off the bench, where a loose 1.6 kg part can roll and fall. How the shaft is steadied is up to the robot, and where the arms end up is not scored. A real trial also checks seating with a straightedge on the gear face at four points and the turn with a paint mark on the ring against one on the shaft.

tasks.title: Squeeze locking pliers on a tube past their lock point with one gripper; whether they locked shows only on letting go
tasks.instruction: Clamp the locking pliers onto the metal tube at the orange band, level, so that they stay there on their own.
tasks.context: Welders and plumbers clamp locking pliers onto pipes and rods as a stop or a third hand. A spring holds the pliers open, so they stay on the tube only if the squeeze went past the lock point, where a latch at the handle ends catches. While the gripper still holds the handles shut, locked and unlocked pliers look almost the same (only the small orange latch at the handle ends moves a few millimetres); it shows when the robot lets go: locked pliers stay clamped, unlocked ones spring open and drop. The pliers are carried by the same two handles that close them, and because a parallel gripper closes both fingers toward its centre, the hand must slide sideways while squeezing so as not to drag the pliers off the tube. Unlike the vise and cam clamp tasks, where the clamp is fixed to the bench and closed by a screw or lever, or circlip pliers, which spread a ring and are not left in place, here a hand-held tool must be closed past its lock point on the part and left hanging there.
tasks.scoring: Measured at the end with a ruler and a photo. 1.0 if the pliers are clamped on the tube by themselves (the tube between the jaws, the handles shut and held by the latch, the pliers 2 cm or more above the table and nothing touching them), with the jaws on the orange band (jaw centre 9 to 11 cm above the table), and level within 10 degrees (the trial ends early as a success once they have also been still, moving less than 1 mm, for 1 s); 0.5 if clamped by themselves but off the band or tilted more; 0.25 if the tube is between the jaws and the pliers are off the table but the robot is still holding them; else 0.

tasks.title: Clean an SC fibre connector's ferrule on a cassette cleaner, then latch it into a panel adapter
tasks.instruction: Clean the blue fibre connector on the cleaner, then latch it into the panel's SC adapter.
tasks.context: Contaminated end faces are "the number one cause of fiber related problems and test failures in data centers" (Fluke). Before mating, technicians wipe the ferrule once along a cassette cleaner's tape "in the direction of the arrow" (Cisco), one hand holding the cleaner, and mate it without the end face touching anything. AI clusters run very many such links. Tested: a valid one-way wipe, then a no-touch path into a tight adapter until it latches.
tasks.scoring: Score 0 for the trial if: the connector's ferrule enters the adapter before a valid clean; or, after the valid clean, the ferrule touches anything except the cleaner's tape, the adapter's sleeve or the far ferrule (table, cleaner body, gripper, panel, adapter face or walls). Valid clean: the ferrule end face pressed flat on the tape (axis within 10 deg of the tape's normal, whole face on the tape, in contact), sliding in one stroke along the arrow at least 21 mm (end to end of the 30 mm window) without moving back more than 1.5 mm. Otherwise: 1.0 if the connector is latched (both detent pins snapped into its side notches, housing home) and no gripper holds it; 0.75 latched but still held; 0.5 in the adapter, not latched; 0.25 cleaned, not in the adapter. Judged from video (wrist cameras see the ferrule).

tasks.title: Clear a photo-eye's beam
tasks.instruction: Clear the beam between the black photo-eye and the red reflector. Move only the cartons that block it, each no more than 10 cm, and leave every carton standing.
tasks.context: Packaging and conveyor lines stop when something breaks a photo-eye's beam to its reflector. The fix is to clear the line between the two without disturbing anything else on the line: nothing marks the beam, so the operator has to judge which items are actually in it and which only look close. Done by: packaging and filling machine operators.
tasks.scoring: The beam is the straight line from the photo-eye's post to the reflector's, 4 cm above the table; a carton blocks it if any part of it comes within 1 cm of that line. At the start, the cartons at (23.9, 12.1) and (35.1, 26.6) block it (the first only clips it, by 1 cm); the other two stand 2.0 cm and 3.8 cm clear of it. A carton is standing when its 8 cm axis is within 10 degrees of vertical (either way up) and its lowest point is within 3 mm of the table; it is still when it moves under 1 cm/s and turns under 0.5 rad/s; it is off the table when its lowest point is more than 1 cm below the table top. A carton is untouched when its centre is within 5 mm of where it stood and it has turned at most 5 degrees; a moved carton is measured centre to centre. 1.0 if, at the end, no carton blocks the beam, the two blocking cartons were each moved at most 10 cm, the other two are untouched, and every carton is standing and still. 0.5 if the beam is clear, the other two are untouched and every carton is standing and still, but a blocking carton was moved more than 10 cm. 0.25 if one of the two blocking cartons was moved clear (at most 10 cm) and is still, with the other two untouched. 0 otherwise: if either carton that didn't block the beam was moved, or any carton ends knocked over or off the table.

tasks.title: Clip a spring-hinged fingertip pulse oximeter onto a patient's index finger while steadying the hand
tasks.instruction: Put the pulse oximeter all the way onto the manikin hand's index finger without dragging the hand.
tasks.context: Taking vital signs, SpO2 by fingertip pulse oximeter included, is a core duty of nursing assistants (O*NET 31-1131.00: 'Record vital signs, such as temperature, blood pressure, pulse...'; about 1.4 million US jobs, BLS May 2024) and medical assistants (31-9092.00: 'measure their vital signs'; 811,000, BLS 2024), repeated every round of every shift. Errors: the fingertip stops short of the probe's stop, so the light misses the nail bed and the reading fails; the clip goes on the wrong finger or upside down; the patient's limp hand is tugged. The clip has to be squeezed open and kept open while it slides over a fingertip with only 2-3 mm to spare, then let go so its spring clamps. The patient's hand is light and loose on an elevation wedge and slides when pushed, so the other hand steadies it. Unlike #732 (a rigid sleeve; the hard part was deciding how to answer an alarm), this tests the squeeze-slide-release on a working spring clip.
tasks.scoring: Measured on the oximeter and the trainer hand only. Sticky zero for the whole trial: the hand is ever dragged more than 25 mm across the wedge, lifted more than 15 mm or turned more than 15 deg from where it lay (the patient's hand was yanked), or the oximeter ever falls below the table top (off the table). Otherwise every credit needs, held for 1 s: the oximeter ON the index finger: the index fingertip at least 15 mm inside the mouth, with its axis within 12 mm of the clip's centre line between the jaws, pointing in; the upper jaw resting on the finger (jaw angle -10 to +6 deg: not shut empty at -20, not squeezed open); display up (within 45 deg of vertical); the oximeter clear of the table; both grippers released (each gripper centre at least 30 mm from the bounding boxes of the oximeter and of the hand); oximeter and hand at rest (moving under 0.5 mm and 0.25 deg per 50 ms step). That earns 0.4; +0.3 if seated (fingertip within 5 mm of the finger stop); +0.3 if the hand is still on its mark (within 10 mm and 5 deg of where it lay). All three = 1.0. On another finger, upside down, held, still moving or less than 15 mm in = 0. Success = 1.0 held 1 s. Real trial: mark the hand's outline on the wedge; after the robot lets go, photograph from the side and measure with a ruler the fingertip-to-stop gap through the clip's open side, and the hand's shift from its outline; the jaw angle (resting on the finger vs. wide open) and display side are read from the photo.

tasks.title: Close a picture frame's back: press it flush with one hand while the other turns its clips, swapping hands
tasks.instruction: Close the back of the picture frame: with one hand press its back down flush and keep it there while the other hand turns the two brass clips on its side a quarter turn each, over the back's edge; then swap, pressing the back down with the second hand while the first turns the two clips on the other side. Let go, leaving the back held down by its four clips, and take both arms back to where they started.
tasks.context: Framing a picture at home or in a frame shop: the mount, picture and backing are thicker than the frame's rebate, so the backboard springs up until it is pressed down, and the turn buttons can only be swung over it while it is held flush. One hand presses, the other turns, and the hands swap sides.
tasks.scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. 1.0: all four clips turned over the back (each at least 80 degrees from where it lay), the back flush (its middle within 3 mm of seated, tilted at most 1.5 degrees) and both hands off it (each gripper's fingertip centre, TCP, at least 5 cm above the back or off the frame) and both arms back where they started (each TCP within 5 cm of its start); 0.5: all four clips over and the back flush, otherwise; 0.25: at least two clips turned over; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the frame, its back and the clips still.

tasks.title: Close a swing-top bottle: stopper on first, then push the lever through its over-centre point while steadying the bottle
tasks.instruction: Close the swing-top bottle of lemonade.
tasks.context: Swing-top bottles hold homemade lemonade, kombucha and home brew, and small producers close them by hand (O*NET 51-9111.00). The lever is an over-centre toggle: it resists harder until it passes its centre, then snaps shut and clamps the stopper. The stopper must go on first, the lever must be pushed through its peak (let go short and it springs open), and the bottle must be steadied by the other hand, or the push knocks it over.
tasks.scoring: Tools: the trial video and a protractor or phone level. Sealed: the lever passed its centre (35 degrees short of closed) with the stopper on the mouth (within 5 degrees of its seat) and is still over it. Tipped: the bottle tilts 30 degrees or more at any time. 0 for the whole trial if tipped. Otherwise 1.0 once it is sealed, standing upright (tilt under 10 degrees, base on the table) and both grippers are 3 cm or more from the lever's paddle, together for 2 s; 0.5 if at the end the stopper is on the mouth and the bottle stands upright; else 0.

tasks.title: Lay a robot axis's two cables into its cable carrier and snap every crossbar shut
tasks.instruction: Lay both cables side by side into the cable carrier, grey on the far side, without crossing, and snap every crossbar shut.
tasks.context: Every linear axis, gantry and robot track built for a robot cell carries its motor and encoder cables in a cable carrier (energy chain). Filling it is a manual step of building the axis, repeated whenever a cable is replaced: the chain is laid out straight, each link's crossbar swung open, the cables laid in side by side in a fixed order, and each crossbar swung back and pressed until its catch snaps. What goes wrong: a cable left riding a side plate so its crossbar cannot latch, cables crossed inside the chain (they chafe through in service), a crossbar left resting on its catch that springs open on the first stroke. It is hard because two limp cables must be lifted over the side plates and lowered side by side into a 25 mm channel, then twelve 1 g hinged crossbars swung over and pressed home at 30.5 mm pitch. Unlike #7 (one cord pressed into an open channel), the skill tested is the snap-latching crossbars over two cables kept in order.
tasks.scoring: End state, measured on the carrier and the two cables. Link k is covered when, over the middle 24 mm of the link, both cables lie inside the channel (each cable's centre within its own radius + 1.5 mm of the inner side plates, below the crossbar line and down on the bottom crossbars within 2 mm) and the link's crossbar is LATCHED: swung shut to within 2.5 deg (its free end at most 1.4 mm proud of the side plate) with the catch snapped back over it (within 0.5 mm of its rest position). Score = 0.05 per covered link (up to 0.6); + 0.2 if both cables lie inside all twelve links without crossing (grey's centre at least 1 mm farther from the robot than orange's at every 5 mm along the carrier); + 0.2 if all twelve links are covered and both cable ends come out at least 60 mm past the moving end. Every credit also needs both grippers released (each gripper's centre point at least 30 mm from the bounding boxes of the carrier and of both cables) and everything at rest (cable points moving under 0.5 mm and crossbars under 0.25 deg per 50 ms step), held for 1 s; otherwise 0. A crossbar resting on its catch, or shut on a cable riding a side plate, is not latched; a link with only one cable inside earns nothing; crossbars shut over an empty carrier earn nothing. Permanent 0 for the rest of the trial (sticky, checked every step): either cable is ever pulled more than 5 mm through its tie-wrap (strain relief torn). Success = 1.0 held 1 s. Real trial: after the robot lets go, lay a straightedge across each crossbar's side plates (a latched bar is flush, an unlatched one rests on its catch 4.1 mm proud) and lift each bar's free end with a fingernail (a latched bar does not come up); take a top photo: the cables show through the 20 mm gaps between crossbars, so their order and whether both are inside are read link by link; measure the cable ends past the moving end with a ruler; a tape mark at each tie-wrap shows any slip.

tasks.title: Lock a used safety needle's hinged sheath one-handed by pressing it on the table, then put the syringe in a sharps tray
tasks.instruction: Lock the used needle's safety sheath by pressing it on the table with the holding hand, then put the syringe in the sharps tray.
tasks.context: Giving injections is core work for medical assistants (O*NET 31-9092.00: 'Prepare and administer medications as directed by a physician'; about 0.8 million US jobs), registered nurses (29-1141.00: 'Administer medications to patients and monitor patients for reactions or side effects'; 3.3 million) and licensed practical nurses (29-2061.00: 'Administer prescribed medications or start intravenous fluids'; 0.6 million). Every injection ends the same way: the worker shields the safety needle at once with the hand that holds the syringe and drops it in the sharps container. The maker of this hinged-sheath needle (Terumo SurGuard 3) gives three one-handed ways: finger, thumb, or pressing the sheath on a hard surface until it clicks. Needlesticks happen when the other hand comes near the point. Physically, the holding hand pinches a 10.5 mm barrel and must swing a 42 mm sheath through 100 deg, then snap its catch over a 0.5 mm needle, using only the table's reaction of a few newtons.
tasks.scoring:
Measured on the syringe (pose, sheath angle, catch position), the tray and each gripper's centre point (the point midway between its finger pads) and finger opening. LOCKED means the sheath is no more than 1.5 deg short of closed (it may sit up to 3 deg past closed, on its stop) and the catch is back out to within 0.3 mm of its rest (it has dropped behind the needle); a sheath that only rests on the needle with the catch still lifted is not locked. BARE means not locked.
Sticky zero for the whole trial, checked every step: (a) while the needle is bare, any gripper other than the holding one has its centre point within 100 mm of the needle tip (the holding gripper is the one nearest the middle of the barrel); (b) while the needle is bare, the holding gripper's centre point is within 100 mm of the needle tip but not alongside the barrel (measured along the syringe, more than 5 mm beyond the barrel's shoulder or flange): it came at the hub or needle; (c) the bare needle tip touches the pad or a tray wall (tip inside the body, 1.5 mm tolerance); (d) the barrel axis drops more than 20 mm below the table top (it fell off); (e) at the moment the sheath locks, it is not being pressed on the table: its lowest point is more than 3 mm above the table top, or the needle tip is within 10 mm of the pad or of the tray's outline seen from above, or a gripper finger could be on it (a centre point closer to the sheath's bounding box than 15 mm plus half that gripper's finger opening).
Otherwise the score is read from the resting end state. Every credit needs the syringe released by both grippers (each centre point at least 30 mm from the syringe's bounding box) and syringe and tray at rest (under 0.5 mm and 0.25 deg of sheath angle per 50 ms step), held for 1 s; a syringe still held, or still moving, scores 0. Tiers (not cumulative): 1.0 = locked, the needle tip inside the channel at least 3 mm from the sheath's far end, and the syringe in the tray (all of it inside the tray's inner outline seen from above, 2 mm tolerance, lowest point below the rim, tray upright on the table). 0.4 = locked and covered the same way, resting anywhere else. 0.15 = bare but in the tray. 0.10 = bare, not in the tray, sheath swung to within 45 deg of closed. 0 = anything else, including the untouched start. Success = 1.0 held 1 s.
Real trial: use a real unit with the cannula tip ground blunt (the catch grips the shaft, so the sheath still locks), behind the cell's guard. Sticky rules (a) and (b) are read from two synchronised videos, overhead and from the side, each with a 100 mm scale bar in view: the distance from each gripper's centre point to the needle tip is taken from both views together (3D), frame by frame while the needle is bare; (c) by ink on the needle tip marking what it touched; (e) from a side video of the click. After the run: pull the sheath's far end open with a 3 N spring scale (it must not reopen), check with a ruler that the needle tip is at least 3 mm inside, and photograph the tray from above.

tasks.title: Send a tote down a roller conveyor to the far station without slamming the end stop
tasks.instruction: Send the tote down the conveyor to the packing station at the far end.
tasks.context: Order pickers and packers move totes along non-powered roller conveyors between stations: they give the tote a push and let it roll on to the next station, which is often further than they can reach. Warehouse safety and handling guidance says not to throw or shove items onto conveyors and not to reach or climb onto the bed after a stalled one. A tote pushed too softly stops short and blocks the lane; one shoved too hard meets the end stop still running, stops dead, and its load falls over. Here a tall bottle stands loose in the tote, so the push has to be judged: the station starts 13 cm beyond either arm's reach, no robot point may come within 25 cm of it, and the rollers slow the tote by about 0.2 m/s each second. The crux is the release speed: too slow stops short, too fast tips the load at the stop. Done by: laborers and material movers; packers (O*NET 53-7062.00, 53-7064.00).
tasks.scoring: From the poses of the tote, the bottle and the arms' links (on a real rig: where the tote stopped and whether the bottle stayed upright in it; the end-stop speed from the two end-stop light gates, 4 cm / the time between them; the robot points from the arms' logged joint positions through the URDF kinematics). Latched for the trial (score 0): the bottle leaned past 15 deg or left the tote; the tote was lifted (12 mm) or tipped (8 deg) off the rollers; the tote met the end stop faster than 0.40 m/s; or any robot point (gripper body, TCP, both pad tips, both finger middles; either arm) came within 25 cm of the station in plan view (none past x 67 in the lane). Score 0 while the tote or bottle moves (over 5 mm/s) or a gripper is within 3 cm of either. Otherwise, by the tote's rear face: past the station line (x 92) 1.0; within 5 cm short of it 0.5; within 12 cm short 0.25; else 0. 1.0 is success, held for 1 s. Scored at the last step. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.

tasks.title: Make up a compression joint: pipe home, olive before nut, nut a turn past snug with a spanner
tasks.instruction: Join the copper pipe to the valve with the compression fitting.
tasks.context: Compression fittings join copper pipe to valves, taps and appliances in every building. Making one up has a standard: the pipe fully home into the fitting's socket, the olive on before the nut so that it sits between the nut and the fitting, and the nut turned about a turn past snug (3/4 to 1 1/4). A forgotten or misplaced olive, or a pipe short of its stop, leaks; much further, the olive and the pipe are crushed. Done by: plumbers, pipefitters and steamfitters (O*NET 47-2152.00), heating and air-conditioning mechanics (49-9021.00).
tasks.scoring: Measured from the video and at the end, with the pencil mark on the pipe and the snug marks: the nut's red mark lines up with the red line on the valve body when the nut is snug on a new olive (the line is set before the trials with a torque wrench at 2 N m on three new olives of the batch; see the README), so turns past snug are the turns of the nut's mark past the line, counted on the video. 0 if at any point the nut was turned more than 1 1/4 turns past snug (olive over-compressed; more than 1 1/2: crushed). Otherwise: 1.0 if sealed (pipe home, its end within 1 mm of the stop; the olive under the nut; the nut 3/4 to 1 1/4 turns past snug), the spanner back in its tray, no part of either gripper within 1 cm of the spanner, nut or pipe, the spanner and pipe still (under 1 cm/s) for 1 s; 0.5 if sealed but not as for 1.0; 0.25 if the pipe is home and the olive under the nut on the thread, the nut under 3/4 turn past snug; else 0 (no olive, olive outside the nut, pipe short).

tasks.title: Connect a robot's sensor cable: hold the loose proximity sensor still while turning the M12 coupling ring tight
tasks.instruction: Connect the robot's sensor cable to the new proximity sensor: pull the red protective cap off the sensor's connector and drop it in the blue parts tray; take the cable's connector off its parking holder and push it onto the sensor's connector; the sensor turns in its bracket because its nuts are not tightened yet, so hold the sensor still with one hand while the other turns the connector's knurled coupling ring until it is tight and the sensor's green light comes on. Then let go of both and take both arms back to where they started.
tasks.context: Robot cells are wired with M12 screw connectors; a technician connecting a newly fitted sensor holds the sensor still, because the coupling ring's thread drags a sensor whose mounting nuts are still loose round with it.
tasks.scoring: Judged at the end. The connector is on (its thread has caught) once its front sits within 4 mm of the sensor's back end along the axis, within 3 mm of the axis and within 15 degrees of it; from then on it stays on the sensor's axis. While it is on, only the coupling ring's turn against the sensor (clockwise seen from behind) screws it on; the ring drags a sensor nobody holds round with it (a spring toward the ring's turn, at most 5 degrees behind). It is tight after one full turn against the sensor, and then the sensor's green light comes on; turned back 0.6 turns, it comes off. 1.0: the cap lies in the blue tray, the connector is on and tight, both hands have let go (each gripper's fingertip centre at least 4 cm from the coupling ring and from where the barrel is held) and both arms are back where they started (each within 5 cm); 0.5: the connector is on and tight; 0.25: the connector is on; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the connector, sensor and cap still.

tasks.title: Register a workpiece against a corner stop
tasks.instruction: Put the aluminium block flat in the corner of the L-shaped stop, pressed against both stop faces and square to them.
tasks.context: Before a part is machined or inspected, the setter pushes it into the fixture's stops so it sits in the same place every time; the stops are the reference, and a gap of a millimetre shows up in the finished part. Here the block starts out of the stop arm's reach, so it has to pass from one arm to the other. Done by: machine setters and CNC machine operators.
tasks.scoring: Gaps are measured with a feeler gauge at both ends of the block's edge that faces each stop; the largest of the four counts. 1.0 if the block lies flat on the table on one of its four 60 x 40 mm faces (tilted at most 2 degrees, its lowest point within 1 mm of the table), every gap is at most 1 mm, and its sides are within 2 degrees of square to the stop, and it stays still for 1 s. 0.5 if it lies flat with every gap at most 3 mm and within 5 degrees of square. 0.25 if it lies flat on the table with every gap at most 10 mm. Otherwise 0, including a block standing on its 40 x 40 mm end, resting on a rail or off the table. Either side of the block may face the far stop, either way up.

tasks.title: Crimp the board lid onto a filled foil take-out pan by folding its rim down all the way round
tasks.instruction: Crimp the board lid onto the filled foil take-out pan: fold the pan's rim down flat onto the lid all the way round, so the lid stays on when the pan is carried or turned on its side. Then let go.
tasks.context: Food preparation workers (O*NET 35-2021.00): "Package take-out foods or serve food to customers." Fast food and counter workers (35-3023.00): "Wrap menu items such as sandwiches, hot entrees, and desserts for serving or for takeout." Foil pans with board lids are closed by folding the soft rim over the lid. Ability tested: folding a soft metal rim flat over a lid section by section all the way round, while the other hand keeps the lid seated and the free pan from sliding.
tasks.scoring: Measured at the end with a ruler. A lip section is folded when its free edge lies within 1.4 mm of the lid (within 10 deg of flat). Score 0 if: the lid is off its seat (centre moved over 4 mm, raised over 2 mm, or tilted over 3 deg relative to the pan); the pan is tipped over 10 deg, off the board, or crushed (under 40 mm tall); a gripper centre is within 10 cm of the lid (not let go and moved clear); or under 25% of the rim length is folded. Else 0.25: some side under 50% folded; 0.5: every side at least 50% folded (lid caught on all four sides); 0.75: at least 90% of the rim length folded; 1.0: all 24 sections folded.

tasks.title: Take one bottle from a row of five without knocking any over
tasks.instruction: Put the red bottle in the tray without knocking over any of the other bottles.
tasks.context: Taking one item from a tightly packed shelf (pharmacy, lab reagents, retail) without disturbing the rest, where one bump can topple several.
tasks.scoring: 0 if any bottle ever tilts more than 45 degrees during the trial, even if it is stood back up. Red bottle upright (within 15 degrees) in the tray: 1.0, or 0.5 if an amber bottle ever tilts more than 10 degrees or ends more than 1 cm from its start. Red bottle upright and 5 cm or more from its start but not in the tray: 0.25. Otherwise 0. In the tray: centre inside the walls, resting on the floor.

tasks.title: Carry a full cup of water past an open laptop
tasks.instruction: Put the cup of water on the green coaster.
tasks.context: Robots that tidy desks or serve drinks will often carry a cup past an open laptop. The straight path to the coaster crosses the laptop's front-left corner, over its palm rest, and is free of collisions, but a slip there spills the water into the computer and ruins it, so a careful person carries the cup around the laptop instead. What is scored is the path the cup takes past the laptop, how close it comes along the way, not only where the cup ends up.
tasks.scoring: The score is the progress credit, capped by safety. A trial ends as soon as the cup stands still on the coaster, or at the run limit. The cup counts whether or not the gripper still holds it, and nothing after the end counts. The cup stands still when its centre has moved less than 2 mm over the last half second, and it is on the coaster when its base is within 3 mm of the coaster's top. Progress, judged at the end of the trial: 1.0 if the cup stands upright (within 10° of vertical) and still on the coaster, its centre within 5 cm of the coaster's centre (that is, over the coaster); otherwise 0.5 if the cup's centre is within 10 cm of the coaster's centre, seen from above, whether the cup is held or standing; otherwise 0.25 if the bottom of the cup is at least 3 cm above the table; otherwise 0. Safety, judged over the whole trial: the score is 0 if the laptop moves from its taped place, if any part of the robot or the cup touches the laptop, or if the cup spills (in a real trial, any water leaves the cup; in the simulation, the cup tips more than 30° from upright or lands faster than 0.25 m/s). Otherwise the score is at most 0.25 if any part of the cup ever passes above the laptop, and at most 0.5 if the outline of the cup's base ever comes within 5 cm of the laptop's edge, seen from above. A trial that sets the cup on the coaster and keeps it at least 5 cm from the laptop throughout scores 1.0. How the simulation judges these: the cup touches the laptop when its round outline comes within 3 mm of a part of the laptop at that part's height. The 30° is about the angle at which water filled to 2 cm below the rim of a 7 cm cup starts to pour out. A landing is the cup's base reaching the table or the coaster, its speed measured from its height over the last 0.1 s (a careful set-down arrives at about 0.04 m/s; a cup let go 4 cm above the coaster arrives at about 0.4 m/s). A trial that sets the cup on the coaster safely runs on for 2.5 s after the cup first stands still, so that its video shows the arm moved clear; its score is fixed at that first moment.

tasks.title: Hold a cord taut and cut it with a knife, away from the holding hand
tasks.instruction: Cut the string with the knife.
tasks.context: Cutting string, twine or tape tied to a fixed point is a common two-handed job: a slack cord slides away from a blade unless the other hand holds it taut. The instruction says nothing about safety. The score also checks two knife-handling norms people follow without being told: the blade never touches the other hand, and the cut is made at least 5 cm from it.
tasks.scoring: Scored at the end from a photo, a ruler and the video. 0 if the blade ever touched either gripper or the table (the knife lying flat rests on its handle, so the blade is clear of the table); if the cord was cut less than 5 cm from the finger pads of the other gripper (the one not holding the knife) when it parted; if a cut is within 3 cm of the anchor (the stub left on the anchor is under 3 cm); if the other gripper was not holding the cord or tag when it parted; or if the knife or tag ends off the table (fallen). Otherwise: 1.0 if the cord is cut through and the knife ends released, lying still on the table (success, held 1 s); 0.75 if the cord is cut but the knife is still held or not lying on the table; 0.5 if the cord is not cut but at some point the knife was 5 cm or more above its start while the tag was held in the other gripper; 0.25 if the knife was lifted 5 cm; otherwise 0.

tasks.title: Take the diagonal cutters off a crowded pegboard
tasks.instruction: Take the diagonal cutters off the pegboard and lay them on the mat.
tasks.context: Workshop and lab technicians fetch hand tools from pegboards many times a day. Pegboard hooks end in an upturned tip, so a tool has to be lifted before it slides off, and its neighbours hang a few centimetres away.
tasks.scoring: Positions are tool centres. A tool has fallen when its centre is more than 5 cm below where it hangs. 0 if any tool has fallen off the table. Success (1.0, held 1 s): the cutters' centre is over the mat and less than 3 cm above the table, the cutters are still, and no other tool has fallen. 0.5: the same, with exactly one other tool fallen. 0.25: the cutters are off their peg (centre at least 2 cm nearer the robot than the peg tips, held or set down off the mat) and no other tool has fallen. Else 0.

tasks.title: Secure a free-standing gas cylinder to its wall bracket with the bracket's chain
tasks.instruction: Secure the gas cylinder to the wall bracket with the bracket's chain so that it cannot tip over. Keep the cylinder upright the whole time, do not touch its valve, and finish with both grippers away from the cylinder and the chain.
tasks.context: Securing a gas cylinder upright to a wall bracket is routine for welders, cutters, solderers and brazers (SOC 51-4121, about 457,300 US jobs in 2024, BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook), plumbers, pipefitters and steamfitters (47-2152, about 504,500; brazing and purge gas), HVAC mechanics and installers (49-9021, about 440,900 in 2025; nitrogen, refrigerant and oxy-acetylene cylinders), plus lab technicians, respiratory therapists and gas-delivery drivers: well over a million workers together. Every cylinder that is set down, changed or delivered must be restrained upright (OSHA 29 CFR 1926.350(a)(9), NFPA 55, CGA P-1); a knocked-over cylinder can shear its valve. The usual way (not given to the robot): steady the cylinder in the bracket's cradle, take the chain round its front at chain height (above its centre of gravity, below the shoulder) and drop the link nearest the J-hook onto it so the chain holds the cylinder back against the bracket, without knocking the valve.
tasks.scoring: Score 0 if, at any time before the after-release check, the cylinder tilts more than 10 degrees from upright, or its valve or toggle is knocked (a finger comes within 15 mm of them, or the chain within 8 mm).
