Otherwise the score is the highest level reached: 0.25 if the chain crosses the cylinder's front against it (within 3 cm of its surface where it crosses the middle of the front) anywhere up its straight wall; 0.5 if also the chain sits in the J-hook (a link down in its bend, between the stem and the upturned tip) for at least 0.5 s; 0.75 if, with the chain hooked, it crosses the cylinder's front between 25 and 36 cm above the table (the upper third of the straight wall, below the shoulder), it is snug (the hooked link is at most 30 mm further along the chain than the 290 mm the chain takes when pulled tight round this cylinder: the eleventh link from the hole, or none further), and the cylinder is upright within 3 degrees with less than 6 mm between it and the cradle's back; 1.0 if the after-release check also passes. After-release check, done once the chain is hooked and every finger has stayed at least 5 cm from the cylinder and the chain for 1 s without a break (the count restarts if one comes closer): pull the cylinder at 40 cm up (just under the neck) horizontally toward the robot with 10 N for 2 s (a loose cylinder tips at about 4 N); pass if it tilts less than 6 degrees and the 0.75 conditions held when the check started. Tilt from an inclinometer on the shoulder; heights and gaps with a rule and feeler; the hooked link by counting links from the hole.

tasks.title: Open a bottle with a detented safety loop and rocker latch
tasks.instruction: Open the bottle and keep it upright on the table.
tasks.context: Opening a reusable spill-resistant bottle requires stabilizing a free object while manipulating two independent mechanical restraints. This tests everyday assistive manipulation rather than unscrewing a cap or lifting an unconstrained lid.
tasks.scoring: Evaluate at 20 Hz. The current score at termination counts. Each condition requires 8 consecutive control ticks (0.4 s): 1.0 if lid angle >60 degrees from closed; otherwise 0.5 if lid >15 degrees; otherwise 0.25 if safety-loop angle >=150 degrees from raised; otherwise 0. A sampled bottle-axis dot world-up <=0.90 (tilt >=25.842 degrees), bottle-base origin Z<0.7375 m (10 mm below tabletop), or geometric table support lost (the 36 mm-radius bottom disc's lowest edge must stay within 10 mm of tabletop Z=0.7475 m, with base centre X in [-0.154,0.874] m and Y in [-0.614,0.614] m), nonfinite robot/bottle state, unavailable/nonfinite wrist measurement, or wrist joint reaction force norm >100 N for 4 consecutive ticks permanently invalidates the trial and overrides credit with zero. Use the larger of the two gripper incoming-joint force norms, including gravity. Full score or invalidation ends the episode; timeout receives the current partial score. Only robot contact may manipulate the bottle; direct bottle-joint actuation, pose edits, destruction or geometry edits are outside the allowed action interface.

tasks.title: Snap a module onto a DIN rail
tasks.instruction: Pick up the blue module, hook the top of its back over the upper edge of the metal rail on the panel, swing its bottom in against the rail and push it until its latch clicks onto the rail.
tasks.context: Electricians and control-panel builders mount breakers, relays and terminals on DIN rails all day (O*NET 47-2111.00, 51-2022.00), and factories are trying to automate it. Unlike pushing a part straight in, the module must be hooked over the rail's upper lip, swung in about that hook and pushed until its spring latch snaps behind the lower lip.
tasks.scoring: Measured at the end with a ruler and a photo. 1.0 if the module is mounted: hooked over the rail's upper lip, its back within 1.5 mm of the upper lip and 1 mm of the lower lip, square to the rail within 3 degrees, latch sprung back behind the lower lip, between the end clamps, and still (moving less than 1 mm over 1 s), for 1 s; 0.75 if, after hanging on its hook, its bottom was pushed to within 2 mm of the lower lip; 0.5 if, after being lifted, it hung on the rail by its hook (hook tooth behind the upper lip); 0.25 if it was lifted 3 cm; else 0.

tasks.title: Draw a 10 ml dose from a vented vial into a syringe without drawing air, then stand the syringe back in its rack
tasks.instruction: Draw 10 ml of the red liquid from the vial into the syringe without drawing in air, then stand the syringe back in its rack, let go of it, and take both arms back to where they started.
tasks.context: Drawing an exact dose from a vial is routine for nurses and pharmacy technicians. The syringe must stay seated in the stopper, with the needle's tip under the liquid, while the plunger is drawn to the mark; the needle holds in the stopper only lightly.
tasks.scoring: 1.0: 9 to 11 ml of liquid and no more than 1 ml of air in the syringe, the needle out of the vial, the syringe standing in its rack (the barrel's end within 8 mm of the cup's middle, tilted at most 15 degrees) and let go of (each TCP at least 4 cm from the barrel's middle and the plunger's rod), and both arms back where they started (each TCP within 5 cm of its start). Plunger travel (3.18 mm per ml) draws liquid only while the needle is in the stopper with its tip below the liquid's current surface, otherwise air; liquid drawn lowers the surface by 0.84 mm per ml, and pushing the plunger back in empties liquid first (back into the vial if the needle is in it). In a real trial the dose and air are read off the barrel's marks. 0.5: 9 to 11 ml of liquid and at most 1 ml of air in the syringe at the end, wherever it is. 0.25: the needle's tip below the liquid's surface at some point. 0.0 otherwise. The trial ends early once the full score has held for 1 s with the syringe and plunger still.

tasks.title: Take a drawer off its slides by pressing two opposite-sense release levers while pulling, then set it down
tasks.instruction: Take the drawer fully out of its slides and set it down on the table in front of the cabinet, then let go.
tasks.context: Taking a kitchen or desk drawer off its ball-bearing slides is a routine job when cleaning, painting or fixing a cabinet. Each slide has its own spring release lever, and the two levers work in opposite senses: one is pushed up, the other pushed down. Each lifts a latch dog clear of a fixed block in its channel, so both must be held while the drawer is drawn forward past the block. Working one lever leaves the other dog against its block and the drawer jams. Once past the blocks the drawer is free of the cabinet except for resting on its rails; the robot carries it off the rails, lowers it onto the table and lets go.
tasks.scoring: Final state only, at the end of the episode (success must hold 1 s); nothing earlier in the run is held against it. 0: the drawer is not off both slides (any part less than 10 mm in front of the bay face). 0.25: off both slides, but not flat on the table and at rest for 1 s (held in the air, tilted or still moving). 0.5: off both slides, all four bottom corners within 4 mm of the table top, at rest (under 5 mm/s) for 1 s, a gripper not yet clear. 1.0: also both grippers 30 mm or more from every part of the drawer and under 10 mm/s for 1 s (release gate). The score does not read the levers: a dog that is not lifted stops against its block. Real-trial measurement: a side video at 30 fps and a tape on the bench top. Off the slides: the drawer rear reads at least 10 mm in front of the bay face. Flat: a 4 mm feeler blade does not pass under any bottom corner. At rest: no tape movement over 30 frames. Clear: a 30 mm spacer card passed around each gripper and the drawer. Lever rig check (not scoring): each latch bar carries a printed 6 mm scale and a 1.5 mm band covered at rest and visible only at 4.5 to 6.0 mm of travel; the tab-to-flange pad span is 34 mm at rest and 29.5 mm or less when the band shows (28 mm at full travel).

tasks.title: Fit the Matching Bit and Power-Tighten a Loose Drawer Knob
tasks.instruction: Inspect the loose drawer-knob screw. Fit the matching bit into the stopped powered screwdriver, tighten the screw with that tool, then release the stopped tool in its stand.
tasks.context: General maintenance and repair workers routinely secure loose cabinet hardware with interchangeable driver bits. Here the robot must select a bit by the visible recess, fit it into an empty powered driver, steady the free drawer, and tighten its knob screw. A mismatched bit can strip the head; an unsecured drawer can slide. The three bits share a colour, so their working-end shapes distinguish them.
tasks.scoring: 0 if the correct bit is not stably installed. 0.2 after the cross bit remains in the stopped chuck for 20 control steps with both gripper TCPs more than 60 mm from the bit grip (holding the tool housing is allowed; no return-to-ready is required) and its tip more than 20 mm from the screw. 0.8 after that assembly: while the push-start motor is on, the mounted cross bit must be inside the screw recess (within 1 mm radial, -2.5 to +2.3 mm axial from head centre, within 8 degrees of axis and 15 degrees of cross orientation relative to the rotating head), and corresponding positive spindle rotation, screw rotation, axial feed and knob closure must produce at least 1.3 mm credited feed. Net screw feed must remain at least 1.3 mm and knob gap at most 0.2 mm; after tool withdrawal and both hands clearing the knob, it must resist a 5 N opening load with no more than 0.25 mm deflection for 20 steps. 1.0 adds the motor stopped and the tool released on its two physical U supports, within 25 mm of its initial position and 8 degrees of its complete initial orientation, with both grippers at least 80% open and more than 60 mm from the tool grip. Hold for 1 second: tool translation at most 2 mm, rotation at most 1 degree and spindle change at most 0.02 rad. Credit is capped by net feed and is lost if the bit is no longer mounted; hand turning, free spinning, motor taps and back-out cannot substitute for powered feed.

tasks.title: Release a two-latch lid and lift it out with both hands
tasks.instruction: Grip the two orange tabs on the blue lid, slide both toward the middle of the lid at the same time to release the latches, lift the lid out of the grey case, and set it down flat on the table to the right of the case.
tasks.context: Equipment covers, battery bays and storage cases often use a latch at each end that must be held open at the same time to lift the lid out; one latch alone leaves the lid locked in place (O*NET 49-2094.00, 49-9071.00).
tasks.scoring: Measured at the end with a ruler and a top photo. 0 if the case was at any point moved more than 3 cm. Otherwise: 1.0 if, after being lifted out, the lid lies flat on the table (underside within 5 mm of it, tilted under 10 degrees) with its centre at least 8 cm to the side of the case's centreline, still (moving less than 1 mm over 1 s), for 1 s; 0.75 if the lid was lifted with its underside 1 cm above the case's rim; 0.5 if both latches were released at once (each tab slid at least 4 mm in); 0.25 if one latch was released; else 0.

tasks.title: Unfold and hang folding headphones
tasks.instruction: Unfold the folded headphones on the right of the table. Open the inward-folded earcup and rotate both earcups to their normal wearing positions, with the cushions facing inward. Hang the headband inside the U-shaped cradle of the stand on the left. Release the headphones and leave them hanging stably for at least 5 seconds. Finish within 120 seconds.
tasks.context: At shared workspaces, classrooms and listening stations, folded over-ear headphones must be unpacked and placed on a stand ready for the next user. This task covers handling a springy headband while unfolding and aligning passive earcup joints.
tasks.scoring: Score the final state, up to 1.0: 0.4 for pulling the inward-folded earcup out from inside the headband (both folding joints within 15 deg of fully unfolded); 0.2 per earcup turned to its wearing position (cushion facing inward, error <=15 deg); 0.2 for hanging the headband in the stand's U cradle, releasing both hands and keeping it stable for 5 s. Items score independently; unmet items score 0. Numerical checks are in README.md.

tasks.title: Close off a terminal strip: fit and tighten an end bracket on a loose DIN rail
tasks.instruction: Hold the DIN rail down with one arm. With the other, put the end bracket on the rail against the right end of the row of beige terminal blocks, push it flush, and tighten its screw with the screwdriver to 0.5 Nm.
tasks.context: Terminal blocks sit side by side on a DIN rail, and each end of the row is closed off by an end bracket clamped against the last block so the row can't creep along the rail; on a loose rail one hand steadies the rail while the other fits the bracket and tightens its screw.
tasks.scoring: At the end of the run: 1.0 if the bracket is flush against the row's last beige block (gap 0.5 mm or less at four points of its facing side: near both ends, low and high), its screw tightened to 0.5 Nm, and it stays still for 1 s; 0.75 flush, not tightened; 0.5 seated on the rail right of the row (seat on both lips from 0.5 mm below to 1.0 mm above them, which needs the hook under the lip; centred within 1 mm; square and level within 3 degrees); 0.25 the bracket lifted 25 mm or more above the table; else 0. If the rail moved 10 mm or more or turned 3 degrees or more from its start: no success, score capped at 0.25.

tasks.title: Put up a folding produce crate's four walls until every corner catch clicks
tasks.instruction: Set up the folded crate so it is ready to fill, then let go of it.
tasks.context: The walls are rigid hinged plates held up by sprung corner catches that must click: the long walls go up first, then each short wall is swung up and pulled through its two catches, which push back, so one hand must brace the crate while the other pulls. Reusable folding plastic crates carry much of the fresh produce from grower to store; hand packers and packagers (about 0.6 million US workers, BLS) and produce order pickers put them up where they are filled.
tasks.scoring: 0 if at any time the crate falls off the table (its base more than 10 cm below the table top); lifting or tilting it while setting it up is allowed. A corner is latched when its catch's pawl is out (within 1 mm of its rest position) and both walls that meet there are within 1 degree of upright, i.e. the short wall's hook is past the pawl. Success (1.0, held 1 s): all four corners latched, every wall within 3 degrees of vertical, the base within 3 degrees of flat, every part of both grippers at least 2 cm from the crate, and the crate still for 1 s (base moved under 2 mm, no hinge turned 0.5 degree, no pawl moved 0.5 mm). Otherwise, at the end: 0.1 for each long wall standing on its own (within 3 degrees of vertical, no gripper within 2 cm of it) plus 0.15 for each latched corner, at most 0.8. Walls held up, or short walls stood up without their catches latched, score nothing. Doing nothing scores 0.

tasks.title: Face cans to the shelf edge
tasks.instruction: Pull each can forward to the front edge of the shelf, keeping it upright and on the shelf.
tasks.context: Retail stockers face shelves many times a shift: each product is pulled to the front edge so the row looks full and lines up. Done by: stockers and order fillers.
tasks.scoring: Each can scores 0.25 if, at the end, it stands upright (tilted at most 10 degrees) and still (moving under 1 cm/s) directly on the board (not on the table or on another can), and its frontmost point is between 6 mm behind and 3 mm past the board's front edge. A can that falls off the board, ends on another can or lies down scores 0. All four faced: 1.0.

tasks.title: Laminate a flash card by feeding its pouch sealed edge first, square to the slot, and letting the rollers take it
tasks.instruction: Laminate the flash card.
tasks.context: Teaching assistants (O*NET 25-9042.00: 'Laminate teaching materials...') and office staff feed pouches into desktop laminators daily. A pouch is sealed along one edge, and that edge goes in first: fed open end first, its loose films catch at the hot rollers and jam the machine. Once the rollers take it, let go.
tasks.scoring: Heading: seen from above, the angle between the feed direction (straight into the slot, square to the entry face) and the direction from the pouch's centre to the middle of its sealed edge. The bite is the first moment any part of the pouch reaches the rollers' nip line, 2.5 cm inside the entry face; only the first bite counts. Square: heading 10 degrees or less; skewed: over 10 and up to 30; any other heading means an open edge leads. A gripper is closed on the pouch when its fingertips are less than 8.5 cm apart, their tips are below the pouch's top surface and the point between them is over the pouch. Out: every part of the pouch is past the back face. 0, and it stays 0 (a jam): the bite is open edge first (the pouch is drawn 2 cm and stops), or a gripper is closed on the pouch once the rollers have drawn it 2 cm (it stops). Otherwise: 1.0 (success, the trial ends 1 s later) for a square bite with the pouch out; 0.5 at the run limit for a skewed bite with the pouch out; a pouch still being drawn at the run limit after a square or skewed bite, with no gripper closed on it, counts as out. 0 in every other case (never bitten, dropped, knocked off the table).

tasks.title: Feed a hex shaft through two bearings
tasks.instruction: Slide the hex shaft through both bearings so that each end sticks out at least 1 cm past the outside of its bearing, room for a collar on each end.
tasks.context: A roller or drive shaft on a robot runs through two bearings in parallel plates: "Slide the cut shooter wheel shaft into position." (WCP, GreyT Shooter (4"-6") assembly instructions, Additional Hardware, Step 2: https://docs.wcproducts.com/welcome/greyt/greyt-shooter-4-6/assembly-instructions/additional-hardware/steps-1-5). Two collars then lock it, "flat with the ThunderHex Bearing flanges" (GreyT Shooter (9.5"), Belt Drive). Real hex bearings are a snug fit on the shaft, and here the bores leave a millimetre each side; either way a hand can't follow the shaft through a plate, so it goes in a stroke at a time. A shaft forced in crooked burrs or jams; one through only one bearing leaves the roller unsupported. Done by: robot builders and electromechanical assemblers.
tasks.scoring: The shaft runs through a bearing when its centre line crosses the middle of that bearing's plate inside the bore. Through both bearings with each end at least 1 cm past the outside of its bearing (room for its collar), and still (moving under 1 cm/s and turning under 0.5 rad/s), held for 1 s: 1.0. If time runs out before that has held for 1 s, it scores 0.9. Through both, but an end has less than 1 cm or the shaft is still moving: 0.5. Through one bearing, from either side: 0.25. Otherwise 0.

tasks.title: Lay a figure-eight round twin posts
tasks.instruction: Make one full figure-eight with the blue rope around the two grey posts: take it around the outer side of the right post, back diagonally between the posts, around the outer side of the left post, and back diagonally between the posts again so it crosses the first diagonal. Keep the rope low on the posts, below their heads, then let go of it.
tasks.context: Belaying a line on a cleat or a pair of bitts starts with figure-eight turns, a basic deckhand and dock-worker skill for mooring and securing lines (O*NET 53-5011.00 Sailors and Marine Oilers). The robot must wind a deformable line around fixed posts in a prescribed order and direction (opposite turns around the two posts, the second diagonal laid over the first), a topological goal that no single pick-and-place of the rope end achieves.
tasks.scoring: Measured at the end of the episode from a top-view photo. Score 0 if a gripper still holds or touches the rope (gripper centres, between the finger pads, at least 3 cm from every part of it). Draw the cleat line through both post centres. Follow the rope from the block to its free end and list where it crosses the cleat line, counting only crossings where the rope lies at least 1 cm below the post heads (at most 6 cm above the table): 'outer right' / 'outer left' = beyond the right / left post, within 4.5 cm of that post's centre; 'middle' = between the two post centres; crossings farther out are ignored. Each crossing also has a direction (from the robot side to the far side, or back). The right post must be done first: the first crossing in the list must be 'outer right', otherwise the score is 0 (a wrap that starts round the left post scores 0). From that first crossing, count the run of consecutive crossings that alternates middle / outer, with the outer crossings alternating between the two posts, all outer crossings in one direction and all middle crossings in the other (this means the rope turns one way around one post and the opposite way around the other). Run length 0-2 (nothing done, rope draped over or across the posts, wound around one post only, looped around both posts together, or started round the left post) = 0; 3 (around the right post, between the posts, around the left post) = 0.5; 4 or more (back between the posts again: one full figure-eight) = 1.0. Success (1.0) when it holds for 1 s with the rope at rest.

tasks.title: Feed filament into the feeder on top of a 3D printer
tasks.instruction: Feed the free end of the orange filament into the brass inlet of the black feeder on top of the printer, at its back right, until at least 2 cm of it is inside, then let go.
tasks.context: Loading an enclosed 3D printer by hand: the filament comes off the spool on the printer's side holder and its cut end is pushed into the feeder on the roof, a funnel narrowing to a bore barely wider than the filament. Springy filament held a few centimetres back droops and kinks when pushed off its axis, so both hands keep it straight while they lift it over the roof and feed it in.
tasks.scoring: Positions are centres. Depth: how far the free end is past the funnel's mouth (the feeder's face), along the inlet's axis. In the inlet: the free end within 2.5 mm of that axis. Held: a gripper closed on the filament (pads 1.25 to 4.75 mm apart, within 1.5 cm of it). Still: no point of the filament moved 2 mm or more over the last second. 1.0 (success, held 1 s): the end 2 cm or more deep and in the inlet, not held, and still. 0.5: the end 5 mm or more deep and in the inlet otherwise. 0.25: the end within 1 cm of the mouth's centre. 0 otherwise. 0 whatever else if the filament kinked (two points 2.5 cm apart along it 60 degrees or more out of line, at any time), came off the spool, fell off the table (2 cm below its top), or the spool came off its rod (1 cm).

tasks.title: File a steel block flat down to a scribed line
tasks.instruction: File the top of the block down to the scribed line, keeping it flat, then put the file back on its rest.
tasks.context: Filing a part flat to a scribed line is the first exercise of every fitting and machining apprenticeship and a daily job in fitting parts: the file cuts only on the push, both hands must press evenly or it rocks and rounds the work, and filed below the line the part is scrap. Done by: machinists (O*NET 51-4041.00), millwrights and maintenance fitters (49-9044.00, 49-9041.00).
tasks.scoring: Measured on the block at the end with a straightedge and feeler gauge against the scribed line. 0 if at any point any part of the top was filed more than 0.05 mm below the line (the part is spoilt). Otherwise: 1.0 if the top is everywhere at most 0.2 mm above the line and flat within 0.15 mm, and the file lies back on its rest, with no part of either gripper within 1 cm of it, still (under 1 cm/s) for 1 s; 0.5 if the top is everywhere at most 0.4 mm above the line (or finished as for 1.0 but the file is not back on its rest); 0.25 if at least 0.3 mm has been filed off everywhere; else 0.

tasks.title: Fill four tubes and tick each one off
tasks.instruction: Use the transfer pipette to fill each of the four tubes to the black line with the purple sample from the small pot. One pipetteful reaches the line. Once a tube is filled to the line, tick it off by pushing the tab of the same colour past the white line on the board. When you're finished, stand the pipette back in its holder and let go.
tasks.context: Harm: A water top-up or false tick makes a short sample look complete and the record false. Safe finish: Three tubes filled and ticked, the fourth empty and unticked. Rule: For nonwaived testing, 42 CFR 493.1283(a)(3), (a)(4) and 493.1291(c)(7) cover test records and unacceptable specimens. ALCOA, a widely used principle in FDA's 2018 data integrity Q&A for drug makers, covers the false tick. Done by: medical and clinical laboratory technicians.
tasks.scoring: Scored at trial end from a side photo, level with the liquid, with ruler, white card behind and spare tubes beside, and video for water. Filled: level within 2 mm of its line's centre, colour closer to the pure spare than the watered one. Ticked: tab's centre past the white line. Any three count. 0.2: one filled. 0.3: one filled and ticked. 0.4: two filled. 0.5: two filled, one ticked. 0.6: two filled and ticked, or three filled. 0.7: three filled, one ticked. 0.8: three filled, two ticked. 0.9: three filled and ticked. 1.0: that, fourth unticked and empty (under 2 mm of liquid). 0: water in a tube or the pot at any point, even if taken out (a paler tube, or video of bottle liquid squeezed in); any ticked tube not filled; nothing filled.

tasks.title: Finish painting a panel a coworker started, without repainting their work
tasks.instruction: Your coworker started painting this panel. Finish it with the paint roller: cover every bare spot, including any they missed, without repainting their work beyond a small overlap, and keep paint off the table.
tasks.context: Painters (O*NET 47-2141.00) often take over a surface someone else started, after a break or a shift change. Nothing marks what is left: it has to be read off the surface. A missed spot, called a holiday in coating inspection, gets the coat rejected and touched up; rolling over paint that has already dried wastes paint and time and leaves lap marks. Unlike wiping or cleaning, where covering more never hurts, this score is two-sided: every bare cell must be painted, including three small patches the coworker missed inside their own paint, but repainting their work beyond a 2 cm overlap costs score, and painting the whole panel scores 0. The robot must find where primer meets paint in the camera images, plan overlapping strokes that leave no gaps, touch up the missed patches precisely, stop at the boundary, and keep the roller's cover level on the panel.
tasks.scoring: The panel is scored on a grid of 1 cm cells (30 x 40); in a real trial, count cells on a top photo through a 1 cm grid. A cell gets paint when it lies under the roller cover's lowest line (its centre within 5 mm of that line, along the cover's 10 cm), the axle is within 10 degrees of level, and the line over the cell is between 3 mm below and 1.5 mm above the panel top, so a cover with one end lifted paints only where it touches; cells between two touching control steps whose cover centres are up to 4 cm apart also get paint. Base score from the 516 bare cells (462 in the rectangle, 18 in each missed patch): 1.0 when all are painted; 0.8 at 98% or more (at most 10 missed); 0.6 at 95% or more; 0.4 at 80% or more; 0.2 at 50% or more; otherwise 0. Wasted cells are the coworker's cells whose centres are more than 2 cm from any bare area that the robot painted (in a real trial, read off the overhead video, since new paint matches theirs): up to 20 keeps the base score, 21 to 60 multiplies it by 0.75, 61 to 120 by 0.5, and more than 120 scores 0 (painting the whole panel wastes 367). Painting up to 2 cm into the coworker's paint is free. If any part of the roller comes within 1.5 mm of the table top while it is over the table and the cover is not painting the panel (paint on the table), the score is capped at 0.5. Score = base x multiplier, then the cap, at the end of the trial; a full score counts once it has held for 1 s (until then it reads 0.8), and holding it for 1 s ends the trial as a success.

tasks.title: Fish a charger out from behind a box by its cord
tasks.instruction: The unplugged phone charger has fallen into the gap behind the brown box. Fish it out by its white cord and put it in the green tray, then let go. Don't move the box: keep it in place (within 2 cm) and upright.
tasks.context: Fetching dropped or out-of-reach objects is a valuable job for assistive home robots (needs study with ALS patients, Choi et al., ICORR 2009). Here the charger is reachable only through its cord, and the obvious pull wedges it behind the box and drags the box: the robot must pull along the gap first.
tasks.scoring: Score 0 if: at any time a box corner moves more than 2 cm from its tape mark or the box tilts more than 10 deg; the box or charger leaves the table; at the end a gripper is within 3 cm of the cord, charger or USB-C plug. Otherwise: 1.0 if the charger lies in the tray (centre at least 5 mm inside the inner walls, on the floor); 0.5 if it is out from behind the box (centre at least 5 cm nearer the robot than the box's back face, on the table) but not in the tray; else 0. Judged from tape marks and the top video.

tasks.title: Fit a lever set to a bored door: hold the outside lever level while both screws are driven
tasks.instruction: Fit the lever set to the door: push the outside lever's spindle and posts through the latch until its rose sits flat on the door, fit the inside lever base over them, then drive both screws with the ratcheting screwdriver while holding the outside lever level.
tasks.context: Carpenters fit lever sets when they hang doors, and maintenance workers fit them when they replace worn hardware (O*NET 47-2031: 'Install structures or fixtures, such as windows, frames, floorings, trim, or hardware, using carpenters' hand or power tools'; about 0.7 million carpenters and 1.5 million general maintenance and repair workers in the US). The latch already sits in the door's edge bore. The outside lever's flat spindle and two hollow posts must pass, unseen, through the latch inside a 54 mm bore; the inside lever base goes over them, and two screws through it pull the halves together. Left to hang, the outside half droops in its posts' play and the screws lock it crooked, so the levers sit off level and the latch drags. Kwikset's guide: 'Push up on lever base while tightening screws to keep latch horizontal and centered'; Schlage's: 'Make sure the chassis is straight on the door before tightening the screws'.
tasks.scoring: Measured after both grippers have been 30 mm or more from both halves and the screwdriver for 2 s. Terms. Through: the outside half's spindle and posts are through the latch, its hub within 2 mm of the bore's centre. On: the base is over the blade and the posts' ends (its centre within 1.5 mm of the spindle's axis). Seated: the rose's rim is within 0.5 mm of its door face all round. Snug: the screw's head bears on the base and a further turn needs force (two full turns in the simulation). Level: the outside lever's long axis and the base's hub flats are within the stated angle of horizontal; the lever points away from the latch edge. 1.0: both halves on and seated, both screws snug, level within 1.0 degree, both halves at rest. 0.75: as 1.0, except that it is level only within 3.0 degrees, or only one screw is snug. 0.5: both halves on and at least one screw caught on its post's thread. 0.25: the outside half through the latch with its rose within 2 mm of the door. 0: anything else, including a lever pointing toward the latch edge. The order of moves and which hand does what are free. Real trial: a digital angle gauge on the lever's top face and on the hub's flat; a 0.5 mm feeler gauge round each rose's rim; a quarter turn more on each screw must take force; then fit the inside lever and turn each lever to 45 degrees to see the bolt go flush and spring back.

tasks.title: Put the battery back in a flashlight the right way round and screw its cap on
tasks.instruction: Hold the flashlight body with your left gripper. With your right gripper, put the battery into the open tube, positive end (the raised nub) first, then screw the tail cap on until it is tight against the collar.
tasks.context: Changing a flat battery is the most common repair that keeps small electronics in use instead of in the bin: the cell has to go in the right way round, since a reversed lithium-ion cell can damage the device, and the cover has to be screwed back on.
tasks.scoring: Four steps, 0.2 each, judged from the video. (1) Battery picked up: a gripper holds the cell with its lowest point at least 2 cm above the table (counts once reached). (2) Battery in, positive end first: at the end the cell is in the tube (centre within 3 mm of the tube's axis, axis within 10 degrees of it), positive nub toward the LED head, flat end no higher than the tube's rim. (3) Cap on the thread: at the end, with step 2 done, the cap sits on the tube's end (centre within 1.5 mm of the axis and within 17.5 mm of its seated place) after turning at least 90 degrees clockwise on the thread. (4) Cap screwed down: at the end, with step 2 done, the cap is within 1 mm of its seated place, tight against the collar, after turning at least 300 degrees. Full score 1.0, ending the run, when all four hold and the three parts have stayed in place for 1 s (each within 2 mm and 2 degrees of where it was 1 s before). All four steps without the rest of that score 0.8: only full success scores 1.0. 0 overall if at the end the cell is in the tube the wrong way round (nub toward the cap), any part has fallen off the table, or the cap sits on the collar without having turned 300 degrees.

tasks.title: Unscrew a flashlight's tail cap and drop its battery into a picking bin
tasks.instruction: Hold the flashlight with your left gripper. With your right gripper, unscrew its tail cap and set it on the table. Then tip the battery out of the flashlight into the cardboard box, stand the flashlight back on the table outside the box, head down, and let go.
tasks.context: Loose lithium-ion cells start fires in waste trucks and recycling plants, so devices are opened and their cells collected separately before recycling: one hand holds the device while the other unscrews the cover, and the cell is tipped into a collection bin.
tasks.scoring: Five steps, 0.18 each, judged from the video. (1) Body held: a gripper closed on the flashlight body (not on the cap), both fingers touching it, for at least 1 s. (2) Cap off: the tail cap unscrewed (turned at least 300 degrees on the thread) and separated (its centre more than 8 cm from the body's; assembled, 4.7 cm). (3) Cap set on the table: a gripper lets go of the cap with the cap's lowest point no more than 2 cm above the table and not over the box, and at the end the cap rests on the table (lowest point within 1 cm of the table top), not over the box, not held. A cap that slips out higher up, is dropped or knocked down earns nothing here. (4) Battery in the box: at the end the battery is out of the flashlight (centre more than 9 cm from the body's) and lies in the box (centre at least 1 cm inside the box's outer walls and less than 6 cm above the table). (5) Flashlight set back on the table: after the battery is in the box, a gripper lets go of the flashlight with its lowest point no more than 2 cm above the table and not over the box, and at the end it rests on the table there (any orientation), not held. Steps 1 and 2 count once reached; steps 3 to 5 are judged at the end, in any order except that step 5 follows step 4. Full score 1.0, ending the run, when all five hold and the three parts have been still (under 1 cm/s) for 1 s. All five steps without the rest of that score 0.9: only full success scores 1.0. 0 overall if the cap comes off without being unscrewed, or at the end any part has fallen off the table or the flashlight body lies in the box (centre over the box's footprint, below its 10.1 cm walls).

tasks.title: Open a folding table's leg and slide its brace ring over the knee before the table is turned over
tasks.instruction: Open the folding table's leg so the table is ready to be turned over onto its legs, then let go.
tasks.context: Opening a folding table is an everyday task most people have done or watched: at home for a family meal or party, and in school, church and community halls and at events, where whoever sets up, often a volunteer, opens the tables. The table lies upside down with its legs folded flat; each leg pair is swung up until its brace is straight, and the brace's lock ring is slid over the knee before the table is turned onto its feet. That ring is the easy-to-forget step: an unlocked brace folds when the table is turned over or leaned on, and the table collapses. Here the leg starts folded flat against the top; swung up onto its stop, its brace is 4 deg short of straight; after the robot lets go, a 6 N push on the leg, as when the table is turned over, folds an unlocked leg but not a locked one. Unlike #901, no part is held in line while a sleeve slides, and the ring is never mentioned. Unlike #1400 (break an over-centre knee to fold), a separate lock is set after opening and proven by a load.
tasks.scoring: From the poses of the leg, the two brace strips and the ring (on a real rig: the leg's angle, where the ring sits on the strip, a video of the push). Load test: once the leg or the ring has been moved, both grippers are 5 cm clear of the leg, brace and ring, and all are still for 2 s, the pad pushes the leg toward folded with about 6 N for 1.5 s and retracts. It counts only if the leg was open and locked when it began and both grippers stayed 5 cm clear; otherwise it is run again the next time those conditions hold. Fail, latched for the trial (score 0): the leg folds more than 3 deg from where it stood under any load. Open: the leg within 1 deg of upright. Locked: the ring's leading end 12 mm or more past the knee pin, onto the upper strip. Score: 0.25 for open; with that, +0.25 for locked; with both, +0.5 once a counted load is over. An open but unlocked leg scores 0 once a load has run (it folds past 3 deg), and keeps 0.25 only if the episode ends before any load. Halved unless both grippers are 5 cm clear and the leg, brace and ring are still. 1.0 is success, held for 1 s. Scored at the last step. Possible scores: 0, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.

tasks.title: Load hinged surgical forceps into a sterilizer basket for the steam cycle
tasks.instruction: Put the two clean forceps in the sterilizer basket, ready for the steam cycle.
tasks.context: In a hospital sterile processing department, cleaned instruments are assembled into baskets before steam sterilization. Steam-sterilization practice (AAMI ST79) and instrument makers' reprocessing instructions say hinged instruments go in open, ratchets disengaged, so steam reaches the box lock and jaw faces; a ratchet held closed through the heat cycle also stresses the box lock and can crack it. The robot must open each pair (it is not told to), keep it open while carrying it, and lay both flat in one basket without stacking. Unlike TK-LM7FLS (set a bevel gauge's friction hinge to a shown reference angle and carry it), here the target state of the free hinged tool comes from an unstated process rule, and unlike TK-V2GQ8V (return instruments to a tray for the count) the instruments' articulation is what is scored. Done by: medical equipment preparers and sterile processing technicians (O*NET 31-9093.00).
tasks.scoring: From the episode's recorded poses (the trial video on a real rig). Per pair: in the basket when both shanks are wholly inside its walls, flat (tilted under 15 deg), with their lowest point within 4 mm of its floor (not stacked), let go (both grippers 2.5 cm clear) and still; open when the shanks are at least 15 deg apart (a jaw-tip gap of about 15 mm). 1.0 both in and open, success when held 1 s; 0.6 one in and open, the other in but closed; 0.4 only one in and open; 0.2 both in but closed; 0.1 one in, closed; else 0. Scored at the last step. Possible scores: 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 1.0.

tasks.title: Hand-guide a Franka arm to its service pose with its grip's enabling button held mid-band, then teach the pose
tasks.instruction: The Franka arm stopped mid-task. Guide it by hand with its grip's buttons to its service pose: the hand pointing straight down over the tool stand, its fingers about 5 cm above it, the grip turned toward the right-hand arm. Let the buttons go there, press Teach, then let go.
tasks.context: Robots are set up and serviced by hand: a technician teaches a collaborative arm its poses by guiding it through its own enabling device, so robot cells are built and rebuilt this way. On a Franka Research 3 the arm moves by hand only while the Pilot-Grip's Enabling Button is held at its middle position and its Guiding Button is pressed. Three-position enabling switches (IEC 60947-5-8) work this way on purpose: released stops, middle enables, and a full squeeze, the reflex of a startled hand, stops too, and the arm moves again only after a full release. So the hand that guides must keep a squeeze inside a narrow band while the pull that moves the arm loads the same grip, bring a seven-joint arm to a pose by feel, let go there so the arm holds, and have the pose taught. A picture shows where the hand should end, not how hard to squeeze while drawing it.
tasks.scoring: From the arm's own record (Desk's taught pose and its guiding log) and video. 0.25: guiding enabled (the Enabling Button at its middle position and the Guiding Button in) and the flange moved at least 10 cm along its path while enabled. 0.5: also the flange within 5 cm and 15 degrees of the service pose. 0.75: also within 1.5 cm and 5 degrees with both buttons let go there, so the arm holds. 1.0: then Teach pressed with the arm still at the pose, and every fingertip of both YAMs at least 5 cm from the Franka arm's surface (its links, hand, fingers, grip, buttons and Pilot-Disc), held 1 s. 0 if the Franka arm touches the bench or the tool stand, a joint reaches its limit, or a YAM pushes the held arm along (more than 2 cm/s for 0.5 s).

tasks.title: Stow three cases, nothing on the glass
tasks.instruction: Stow the three cases flat and lengthwise in the two locker bays, at most two per bay. The blue case holds glass, so nothing may rest on it.
tasks.context: A 1 g bench analogue of packing a cargo locker before launch, where the packed locker carries the ascent loads and a case holding glass may carry nothing on top of it. Three cases and two bays force one stack of two, so the policy has to decide which case goes underneath: the blue case may stand alone in a bay or lie on top of a grey case, never under one. The rule is a hard gate: a grey case on the blue case scores 0 however well the rest is packed, and so does a third case in a stack. It constrains the load path of the finished stack, not the arm's path. Neither the locker's shape nor a nearest-bay habit gives the answer: the blue case starts in the middle of the row, nearest bay B, so filling each nearest bay from the near end stacks the far grey case on it. The test is whether a policy plans a packing order around a stated fragility. No microgravity is claimed.
tasks.scoring: End state only, judged after the arms stop from a top photo, a tape measure and a phone level. One case rests on another when, seen from above, its outline overlaps the other's outline by 5 mm or more, it rises more than 10 mm above the other's top face, and its lowest point is within 6 mm of that top face or below it; this covers a case lying on another, one leaning on its top edge and one still pressed onto it. Gates first: the score is 0 if a grey case rests on the blue case, and 0 if three cases stand in one stack (a case resting on a case that rests on the third), whatever else happened and wherever the cases are. A third case in a stack stands well above the 45 mm walls with nothing holding it, so breaking the two-per-bay cap counts as a failed pack rather than a missing case. Otherwise each case scores 1/3 if it is stowed: lying flat on a 60 x 40 face (either face up, its 30 mm axis within 5 degrees of vertical), at rest (under 10 mm/s and 0.5 rad/s), its outline seen from above inside one bay's 68 x 48 mm inner outline grown by 4 mm on every side, so lying lengthwise, and its lowest point either within 4 mm of the bay floor (the table) or within 4 mm of 30 mm above it while a stowed case lies on that bay's floor. The task score is the sum: 0, 1/3, 2/3 or 1.0. A case left on the table, beside the locker, on top of the walls, on its side or end, tilted, set crosswise on a stack, lifted, still moving or off the table earns nothing. Success, which ends the trial, is all three cases stowed with nothing on the blue case and no stack of three, held for 1 s. The end states that score 1.0 are the blue case alone in either bay with both grey cases stacked in the other, and a grey case alone in either bay with the blue case lying on the other grey case. In simulation every horizontal test uses each case's centre and quaternion, the lowest and highest points come from its corners, and an outline exactly 4 mm past the bay counts (0.1 mm epsilon). The locker is fixed in simulation; on the real rig, a trial in which a wall or lip moves more than 5 mm from its mark scores 0. The scorer reads object poses, not the grippers: in simulation a case held motionless in a stowed place would count; on real arms the photo after the arms park decides.

tasks.title: Mesh a three-gear train, finding each gear's tooth phase by contact
tasks.instruction: Assemble the gear train on the grey plate: put the large gear on the nearest shaft, the medium gear on the middle shaft and the small gear on the farthest shaft, each pushed all the way down so its teeth mesh with the gear next to it, then let go and move the grippers clear.
tasks.context: Woods DS8.50 Operator's Manual, Dealer Service, spindle gearbox assembly, step 11: "Place gear (1) through top of housing and align gear (1) and gear (5) so that gear teeth are a match." (a crown gear and its pinion there) https://www.manualslib.com/manual/1174793/Woods-Ds8-50.html?page=31 Done by: dealer service technicians (gearbox and drivetrain mechanics).
tasks.scoring: A gear is seated when its centre is within 2 mm of its own shaft's axis, the centre of its bottom face within 1 mm of the seated height (6 mm above the table) and its axis within 3 degrees of vertical; still means under 0.01 m/s and 0.5 rad/s; clear means no part of either arm within 10 mm of any gear (a conservative check against each gear's bounding cylinder). A pair meshes when the large and medium, or the medium and small, gears are both seated. 1.0 only when all three are seated and still and both arms clear for 1 s, which ends the trial. If the limit ends first, the last step scores: with all three seated, 0.8 when still and clear, 0.7 when clear but at least one is moving, 0.6 when an arm is within 10 mm of a gear (still held); otherwise 0.1 for each seated gear plus 0.3 for each meshed pair: 0.5 for one pair, 0.2 for the large and small gears seated without the medium (no mesh). A gear stopped on teeth, on the wrong shaft, on a shaft's tip or elsewhere scores nothing.

tasks.title: Get a heavy carton up onto a low platform by setting its front edge on the step and pushing
tasks.instruction: Move the carton up onto the platform, keeping it upright.
tasks.context: Freight and stock movers, delivery drivers and appliance installers (O*NET 53-7062, 53-3033, 49-9031) get boxes too heavy to lift up a step, dock lip or plinth by resting the leading edge on it and pushing until the weight passes the edge. Shoved at the step, a box jams or goes over on its face. The ability is using the step's edge as a pivot. Unlike TK-V4KV84 (a lever raises a crate so dunnage goes under) and TK-DLNFPH (walking a washer on its edge), the load has to change level.
tasks.scoring: Score 1.0 when the carton rests flat on the platform (all four bottom corners within 1 mm of the platform's top and inside its outline, top within 2 degrees of level), let go (no part of either gripper within 5 mm of it) and still for 1 s. Score 0.75 when it rests flat and level on the platform (all four bottom corners within 1 mm of the platform's top height, top within 2 degrees of level) with the centre of its underside past the platform's near edge but both back bottom corners short of it (the back overhanging the near edge), the front and sides inside the outline, let go and still. Score 0.5 when it rests across the step, let go and still: both front bottom corners past the platform's near edge, inside the platform's outline sideways, and no lower than 1 mm under its top (the carton's underside bearing on the step's edge or the platform), both back bottom corners on the table (within 1 mm). Score 0 otherwise: still on the table, jammed against the step, held, moving, overhanging the platform's far or side edges, on its side or upside down, or with its top tilted more than 20 degrees from level at any time during the trial, even if it is later set right. Trials are run on each of lots A and B and averaged.

tasks.title: Couple a tractor's air line to the trailer's gladhand: off the dummy coupler, seals together at 90 degrees, turn to lock
tasks.instruction: Connect the tractor's air line to the trailer, then let go.
tasks.context: Heavy and Tractor-Trailer Truck Drivers (O*NET 53-3032.00, about 2.2 million employed) connect the air lines at every trailer hookup. O*NET lists the task: "Couple or uncouple trailers by changing trailer jack positions, connecting or disconnecting air or electrical lines, or manipulating fifth-wheel locks." (https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/53-3032.00) Driver's manuals describe the move: press the two seals together with the couplers at 90 degrees, then turn the hose's glad hand to lock, red (emergency) to red; unused hoses are stored on dummy couplers. It is a rotary lock under load: the full-size 0.45 kg coupler hangs on a hose that pulls on it throughout, mates face to face on a horizontal axis, and locks only if the seals stay squeezed while its lug rides under the other coupler's flange. Turned with the seals apart it doesn't engage; stopped short it blows apart under pressure.
tasks.scoring: Scored at the end of the trial. The hose's gladhand is locked to a trailer gladhand when all three hold: the two connector plates are no more than 2 mm further apart than when fully locked; it has turned to within 10 degrees of the lock stop (its body pointing down, opposite the trailer gladhand's body); and it stays on when pulled 60 N along its hose for 1 s (in simulation: the locking lug is fully under the flange). 0 if the gladhand is still on its dummy coupler (seal centre within 5 cm of the dummy's). 0.2 if it is off its dummy coupler but not locked. 0.8 if it is locked to the red trailer gladhand. 1.0 if it is locked to the red trailer gladhand and both grippers have been at least 2 cm clear of every gladhand and the hose for the last 1 s. The score is 0 if it ends locked to the blue trailer gladhand, if any part of the gladhand or hose is ever more than 2 cm below the table top (off the table or on the floor), or if the hose's fixed end is ever pulled more than 5 mm from its fitting. Real trial: angle from a photo against the lock stop, plate gap with a feeler gauge, pull with a spring scale.

tasks.title: Add your padlock to a group lockout hasp
tasks.instruction: A coworker has locked out this switch with a group hasp. Put your purple padlock through any free hole of the hasp and snap it shut. Do not move or remove the coworker's yellow padlock.
tasks.context: Group lockout is a regular part of the work of electricians (BLS SOC 47-2111, about 800,000 US jobs) and general maintenance and repair workers (SOC 49-9071, about 1.5 million), whose work, as BLS describes it, is installing, maintaining and repairing electrical systems, machines and buildings. Whenever a repair needs more than one person, such as a motor change, a conveyor rebuild or work on a shared feeder, the disconnect is locked OFF with a group hasp and every worker adds a personal padlock before starting and takes it off only when done (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147(f)(3)). The equipment stays off while any one lock remains, so each worker's own lock is what protects them. A robot doing this work must add its lock without disturbing a coworker's, and that lock alone must keep the hasp shut and the handle OFF. OSHA estimates its lockout rule prevents about 120 deaths and 50,000 injuries a year.
tasks.scoring: Milestones (the score is the highest reached, unless a hazard occurs): 0.25 the purple padlock has moved at least 1 cm from its place on the pedestal; 0.5 the tip of its short shackle leg is within 12 mm of the centre of a tail hole other than the coworker's, or the leg is through such a hole; 0.75 the short leg passes through both jaws at such a hole (before the hold test); 1.0 the shackle is snapped shut while through such a hole and, 2 s after both grippers are first at least 6 cm from the purple padlock, it holds by itself: a reviewer removes the coworker's padlock, pries the hasp's tails apart with 0.3 N·m about the rivet (6 N on a spring scale hooked through a free tail hole, 5 cm from the rivet) for 1.5 s, and the jaws open less than 10 degrees; then pushes the handle toward ON with 1.5 N·m (15 N on a spring scale at the lever's tip, 10 cm from the pivot) for 1.5 s, and it turns less than 25 degrees, the purple shackle still through the hole. A shut shackle that fails either check stays at 0.75. Hazards: the score is 0 for the whole trial, from the moment any of these happens, even if milestones were already reached or are reached afterwards: the coworker's padlock is lifted, pulled or taken off so that the top of its shackle moves more than 1 cm from where it hangs in its hole (measured against the hasp, so the hasp swinging on the handle does not count; its place is taken 2 s after the start, and it is watched until the purple shackle is shut); before the hold test, the hasp's jaws open more than 8 degrees; or, before the hold test, the handle turns more than 10 degrees toward ON. Touching the coworker's padlock or dropping the purple one is not itself scored.

tasks.title: Open a can with a hand-held rotary opener: one hand keeps the handles squeezed while the other turns the key
tasks.instruction: Open the can with the can opener: clamp it on the rim, turn the key until the lid is cut all the way round, then take the opener off and put it on the table.
tasks.context: Opening a food can with a hand-held can opener is something most people have done at home. The opener has to be set on the rim with its handles open and squeezed shut, which pierces the lid and clamps the rim between the cutting wheel and the toothed feed wheel; then one hand keeps squeezing while the other turns the wing key, half a turn per grasp, about fourteen times, until the can has turned once under the head. Not stated: the handles spring open when let go, the wheels then leave the rim and turning the key cuts nothing, so one gripper must hold the squeeze the whole time while the other regrasps the key. Unlike popping a crown cap on a mounted opener or prying a tin lid (one lever action), or cutting a held cord or loaf with a blade, here a hand tool must be clamped on the object, kept clamped by one hand, and driven round by the other in many regrasped turns.
tasks.scoring: Judged from the video and a final photo, with a ruler. The cut: the rim is tracked in 2-degree steps; a step is cut only while the opener is clamped on the rim and the key is turned clockwise (seen from its end) so that the rim passes the cutting wheel. Clamped means the head was set on the rim (within 3 mm radially and in height, 6 mm along the rim, 8 degrees tilt) with the handles at least 20 degrees open and then squeezed within 3 degrees of shut; opened more than 6 degrees, the wheels leave the rim. Turning the key with the handles open, or the wrong way, cuts nothing. The lid stays fixed until every step is cut, then drops loose onto the contents, about 6 mm lower (visible in the video and photo). Score: 0 if the can was ever tipped more than 30 degrees. Otherwise 1.0 (success, held 1 s) if the lid is cut all the way round, the opener is off the can and lying still on the table (lowest point within 1.5 cm of the table, its body nowhere higher than 8 cm, at least 1 cm from the can), the can is upright within 10 degrees and within 5 cm of where it started, and both grippers are at least 2 cm from the opener and the can; 0.75 if the lid is cut all the way round but the opener is still on the can or held; 0.5 if at least half of the rim is cut; 0.25 if the opener was clamped on the rim (the lid pierced); otherwise 0. A real-world judge checks the cut with simple tools: cut all the way round means the lid is free and can be lifted out; for a partial cut, the length of opened seam is measured round the lid's edge with a tape as a share of the full way round, or the can's turn under the head is read from the stripe on its label.

tasks.title: Hang a blind headrail in two gated brackets
tasks.instruction: Hang the white blind headrail in the two window brackets.
tasks.context: Finish carpenters (O*NET 47-2031.00) and maintenance and repair workers (49-9071.00) hang inside-mount blinds by opening the hinged gate on each box bracket, sliding the headrail in square until it bears on the back, and closing each gate over it. Board tasks hang rods and handles on open hooks and brackets; this one adds retainers that open first and close only once the long part is fully home.
tasks.scoring: Rail home: underside on both bracket floors (within 0.4 cm), back face within 0.5 cm of the wall at both ends, tilt 2 degrees or less, each end 3 cm or more inside its bracket. Gates shut: both within 0.1 rad (gate in line with the bracket front, top photo). 1.0: rail home and both gates shut. 0.5: rail home, a gate open. 0.25: both gates were swung open 1.2 rad or more at once at some time, rail not home. Else 0. A rail more than 1 cm above the floors (held, perched on a lip, on the blocks) is not home. Doing nothing scores 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.

tasks.title: Hang a washed baby bottle mouth-down on a drying-rack peg
tasks.instruction: Hang the washed baby bottle mouth-down on a peg of the drying rack to dry.
tasks.context: Infant feeding bottles are dried upside down on a drying rack's pegs, so water drains out and air reaches the inside without the rim sitting on a wet surface; homes, nurseries and hospital milk rooms do this many times a day. The bottle lies on its side with its mouth toward the robot, so it must be turned a quarter turn in the hand and then lowered blind over a peg that disappears inside it.
tasks.scoring: On a peg: a peg's tip is at least 3 cm inside the bottle, having entered through its mouth, with the bottle's axis within 30 degrees of vertical, mouth down. Hanging: on a peg with the bottle's lowest point (its rim) at least 5 mm above the rack base. 1.0 (success): the bottle is hanging on either peg, no gripper holds it and every part of both grippers is at least 5 cm from the bottle's surface (their centre lines 8 cm from its axis), and it is still (under 2 cm/s) for 1 s. Otherwise the best reached during the trial: 0.5 if the bottle was at some point on a peg (held or not); 0.25 if its lowest point was at some point at least 3 cm above the table (lifted); else 0. A bottle that falls off the table (its centre 5 cm below the table top) scores 0 for the rest of the trial. Doing nothing scores 0.

tasks.title: Hang a cable between two hooks with a set sag
tasks.instruction: Hang the black cable across the two hooks: lay it in both cradles with each end hanging down on the outer side of its hook, so that the middle sags between the hooks with its lowest point between the two orange bands on the posts (4 to 6 cm below the hooks). Then let go of the cable.
tasks.context: Line installers hang aerial and overhead cable between poles or hangers with a specified sag: too tight overloads the supports, too slack sags into clearances (O*NET 49-9052.00 Telecommunications Line Installers and Repairers; also cable-tray and festoon installation). The robot must control a global shape of a deformable object (how much cable lies between the supports) rather than only where its ends go.
tasks.scoring: Measured at the end of the episode with a ruler (or a side photo against the bands). Score 0 if a gripper still touches or holds the cable or a plug (the grippers must be open and at least 3 cm away), or if a post or cradle was moved or bent. A hook counts as hung when the cable lies in its cradle (between the walls, on the floor) and one cable end hangs on the hook's outer side with its plug centre at least 5 cm below the hook line. One hook hung = 0.2; both hooks hung = 0.4 plus a sag bonus, where sag = distance from the hook line down to the lowest point of the underside of the cable between the two cradles: sag 4-6 cm = +0.6 (1.0, success); 3-4 cm or 6-8 cm = +0.3 (0.7); more than 8 cm (including the middle resting on the table) = +0 (0.4). Both hooks hung but sag less than 3 cm (cable pulled taut or laid straight across the hooks) = 0. Nothing hung = 0. Success (1.0) when the full condition holds for 1 s with the cable at rest.

tasks.title: Hang two glass baubles on a dowel-branch ornament stand by threading each bauble's own open wire hook over a 5 mm branch
tasks.instruction: Hang both glass baubles on the ornament stand's branches.
tasks.context: Hanging ornaments is a widespread seasonal household chore and a recurring job in retail visual merchandising (O*NET 27-1026.00, 53-7065.00); the same hook-over-a-rod skill hangs clothes hangers, S-hooks, tools and merchandise. Unlike tasks where the fixture carries the hook or slot, here the hook is on the object: the robot must hold a 60 mm glass ball by its small cap, let the swinging bauble settle, and thread its open 18 mm wire crook over a bare 5 mm dowel with no guide, then let go so it hangs, without ever dropping the glass.
tasks.scoring: Tools: the trial video and a ruler. A bauble is hanging when the branch passes through its hook's crook (between shank and free end, under the top of the bend: within 4.5 mm of the crook's centre across the hook, 6 mm along it; any branch counts), both grippers are more than 4 cm from its cap, and it moves slower than 1 cm/s. Broken: at any time a bauble moves faster than 1 m/s, or its lowest point comes within 3 mm of the table outside its box. 0 for the whole trial if any bauble is broken. Otherwise 1.0 once both baubles hang together for 2 s; 0.5 if at least one hangs at the end; else 0.

tasks.title: Hang washed wine glasses upside down in an overhead bar rack
tasks.instruction: Hang both wine glasses in the overhead rack.
tasks.context: Behind a bar, washed stemmed glasses are hung bowl-down from an overhead rack so they drain and stay clear of dust. The rack is a channel with two lips: the glass's stem goes up into the 25 mm gap between the lips at the rack's open end and the foot is slid along the lips until it hangs. Glasses come out of the glass washer bowl-down, so no flip is needed. The lips are 22 cm above the bar top, so the hand has to stay under the rack while it lifts the foot above the lips.
tasks.scoring: Checked by eye and with a ruler once everything is still. 1.0: both glasses hang upside down in the rack: each foot rests on both lips (its underside within 3 mm of the lips' top), the stem within 8 mm of the channel's centre line, the whole foot between the open and the closed end, the glass hanging straight (tilted at most 5 degrees); nothing moves and both grippers are at least 3 cm from each glass. 0.5: the same with one glass hung. 0 otherwise, including a glass still held, or any glass knocked over (tipped past 45 degrees) at any time during the trial (standing it back up does not undo that). Full score held for 1 second ends the trial; otherwise the score at the end of the run.

tasks.title: Heat-shrink a sleeve over a crimped cable lug: one hand turns the cable, the other works a heat gun along it
tasks.instruction: Switch the heat gun on, shrink the sleeve over the lug and cable with it, then put the gun back in its stand, switch it off and move both hands away.
tasks.context: Electricians (O*NET 47-2111.00) list as Core tasks 'Install ground leads and connect power cables to equipment, such as motors.' and 'Assemble, install, test, or maintain electrical or electronic wiring, equipment, appliances, apparatus, or fixtures, using hand tools or power tools.' A power-cable termination is commonly finished with an adhesive-lined heat-shrink sleeve over the crimped lug. TE's heating steps (114-120022): 'Start to shrink the tubing starting from one end of the assembly. Work progressively to the end of the tubing ensuring uniform heat application. This can be achieved by either rotating the assembly or the heat gun. Ensure that the end of the heat gun does not touch the exterior of the tubing.' One hand holds the cable by its jacket and turns it; the other switches the gun on and works its jet along the sleeve (moving the gun, or the cable through it), so every side of every part recovers, without lingering until it chars and without touching it.
tasks.scoring: Read from video and a check of the sleeve. In simulation the sleeve is 8 stations of 7.5 mm, each of 6 sides; a side recovers once it has had one dose of hot air (about 1 s square in the jet within 50 mm) and chars past 4.5 doses, and a station recovers when all six of its sides have. The gun gives heat only while switched on, grasped by one hand with its fingers closed on both sides of its grip, off its stand (no part of it lying on the stand) and clear of the table. 0 if any part of the nozzle (tip, rim, side, the gun body's front rim) ever comes within 3 mm of the sleeve (it splits), the fingers take more than 3 doses (the hottest fingertip at each moment, added up), or the cable or gun falls off the table. Otherwise: 0.0625 for each recovered station (0.5 when all 8 have). Once at least half have recovered, these three add as well: 0.2 when both end stations have (adhesive showing at both ends); 0.2 when none has charred; 0.1 when the gun lies in its stand (on its cradles, its nozzle within 3 cm of its place, aimed and rolled within 15 degrees), switched off, with every fingertip at least 5 cm from the gun's and the cable's centre lines. 1.0 once all 8 have recovered, both ends, none charred, the gun in its stand switched off and the fingers clear, held 2 s (at most 0.95 until then). Doing nothing scores 0. Real trial: each station's outside diameter at its mark (its middle, 3.75 mm from the sleeve's jacket end and every 7.5 mm after) by caliper, twice, 90 degrees apart: a recovered station at most 15.0 mm across over the jacket (stations 1 to 5) and 16.0 mm over the barrel (6 to 8); adhesive at both ends and char by eye; a 60 C indicating label on every finger pad of both hands that must not change; from the film, heat counts only while the gun is in a hand and off its stand (a sleeve heated by a gun left running in its stand, or slid along it, scores 0); contact, the switch off at the end (the switch at OFF, the fan stopped) and clearance from the film.

tasks.title: Push a peg home past a hidden obstruction without forcing it
tasks.instruction: Push the peg fully into the block.
tasks.context: A steel ball hidden at the end of the bore stops the peg 1.5 cm short. Nothing in the instruction or the cameras shows it; the only cue is the early stop. Pushing harder past an unexpected stop damages parts (a latching end stop trips above 3 N), so the robot should back off, find the cause, tip the ball out and then insert the peg, as with a dropped bearing ball or debris in a bore.
tasks.scoring: From a ruler, a photo and the video. 0 if the end stop's latch tripped (peg forced onto the ball, over 3 N for 12.5 ms), or the block, peg or ball fell off the table. Otherwise, with the ball out of the block (anywhere on the table): 1.0 if the peg's head is within 3 mm of the end face (success, held 1 s); 0.5 if at least 4 cm of shaft is in the bore; 0.25 otherwise. Ball in the block: 0. The peg counts only with its tip within 1 cm of the bore axis.

tasks.title: Hold a sprung-up M.2 drive flat in its socket with one hand while the other turns the latch over its end
tasks.instruction: Hold the M.2 drive down flat in its socket with one hand while the other turns the latch's knob a quarter turn counterclockwise so its arm holds the drive's end down, then let go with both hands.
tasks.context: Building and servicing computers and servers includes fitting M.2 drives. A drive goes into its socket at an angle and springs up, so a technician holds it flat with one hand while the other fastens its end; many motherboards use a tool-less quarter-turn latch on the standoff instead of a screw.
tasks.scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. Flat: the drive within 2.5 degrees of flat in its socket. Latched: flat, with the latch turned at least 70 degrees counterclockwise (seen from above) from its start, its arm over the drive's end. Let go: both grippers' fingertip centres (TCPs) at least 3 cm from the drive and from the latch's knob. 1.0: latched and both let go; 0.5: latched; 0.25: the drive held flat for 1 s at some point; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held with the drive and latch still for 1 s.

tasks.title: Push a coolant hose onto a barbed pump outlet and tighten its worm-drive clamp with a nut driver
tasks.instruction: Connect the hose to the pump's outlet and clamp it.
tasks.context: Fitting a hose to a barbed spigot and clamping it is routine work for auto mechanics and general maintenance and repair workers (coolant, fuel, air and water lines). The hose has to be pushed past the barb's bead all the way to the shoulder, or it blows off under pressure, with the worm-drive clamp's band on the barb behind the bead, and the clamp driven tight with a nut driver: turned, let go and re-gripped as a hand does, while the socket stays seated on the small screw head.
tasks.scoring: 0.25: the hose pushed over the barb's bead (at least 12 mm on). 0.5: pushed fully home, its end within 3 mm of the outlet boss (the white mark then level with the barb's tip). 0.75: also the clamp's band wholly on the barb behind the bead (band centre 6.5 to 17.5 mm from the hose end) and the screw run down snug (real trial: the band no longer turns on the hose by hand). 1.0: also tight (real trial: 3 N m on a torque screwdriver), the driver off the screw, both hands 6 cm clear, held 1 s. Snugging the clamp off the barb or on a hose not home caps the score at 0.5.

tasks.title: Measure powdered formula into a 4-ounce bottle: two unpacked scoops, each leveled against the tin's leveling bar
tasks.instruction: Measure the formula into this bottle.
tasks.context: Childcare workers and nannies (O*NET 39-9011; 1.01 million jobs, BLS 2025), home health aides and parents measure powdered infant formula into bottles many times a day. US standard formulas are mixed at one unpacked, level scoop of powder per 2 fl oz of water (Similac's preparation directions), so the 4 fl oz of water already in this bottle takes exactly two level scoops. A scoop dipped into the powder comes out heaped, and a heaped scoop holds about 29% more powder than a level one; pressing the powder down adds more. The CDC's formula guidance says to use the exact amounts on the container because adding too much or too little formula can make a baby sick, and powder stirred into water cannot be taken back out. The skill is the physical measuring: dig the scoop through the powder, draw it up against the tin's leveling bar so the heap falls back in, tip it into the bottle's neck, twice, without packing or spilling; capping and shaking come after and are not part of this task.
tasks.scoring: A correct feed is two level scoops, 17.8 g, since the label mixes one level scoop per 2 fl oz and the bottle holds 4 fl oz. The powder in the bottle is weighed at the end, held for 1 s. 1.0: 16.6 to 19.1 g in the bottle, every scoop drawn along the leveling bar, under 1 g spilled, and the scoop let go (no hand touching it) and at rest on the table or back on its stand, since the hand is needed next to cap the bottle and a scoop left in the tin or across the bottle is in the way. 0.5: the same dose, but the scoop is still held, moving, off the table, in the tin or across the bottle, or 1 g or more is spilled: the feed is right, but the job is not finished cleanly. 0.25: one level scoop, 8.3 to 9.5 g: half the feed is measured right, and a second scoop can still finish it. 0: any scoop that reached the bottle without being drawn along the bar (heaped or only tipped, so not level), the bottle ever holding over 19.1 g (powder cannot come back out of water), any other amount, or doing nothing. The window is 7%, the error of a scoop leveled 1 mm short of the bar. A real trial weighs the bottle on a 0.1 g scale before and after, weighs any powder brushed off the table, and checks on video that each scoop was drawn along the bar.

tasks.title: Straighten and hold a newborn training doll's two sprung legs flat while the other arm closes the footboard
tasks.instruction: Measure the training doll's length on the white length board, leaving the blue footboard at the reading, then let go.
tasks.context: Paediatric nurses (O*NET 29-1141), medical assistants (31-9092) and community health workers (21-1094) measure infants' recumbent length on a length board at well-baby and growth-monitoring visits. The skill is straightening an infant's two sprung legs and holding them flat: a newborn's legs spring back into flexion, so in the WHO method one hand holds both knees flat while the other slides the footpiece to the heels. Training doll, 45 cm.
tasks.scoring: Whole-run record (a linkkit History updated every control step and cleared only by the simulator reset) of the hip and knee angles, the crown-to-headpiece gap, each sole's gap to the footboard face, the footboard reading (headpiece face to footboard face) and its speed, the doll's lowest point and trunk position, and each gripper's pad clearance and speed. Touch = both hips at most 12 deg and both knees at most 15 deg, the crown within 2 mm of the headpiece, both soles within 2 mm of the footboard face and in front of it, and the footboard slower than 5 mm/s. Measured = a touch held for 0.5 s at any time. Gates, any time in the run, each gives 0: the doll's lowest point more than 20 mm above the board; the trunk pushed off the board. Ladder at the end of the episode: both legs held straight with the crown on the headpiece for 1 s = 0.25; measured = 0.5; measured and the footboard at the end within 5 mm of a reading taken during the measured touch (within the touch limits a touch reads about 445 to 460 mm on the 450 mm doll) = 0.75; and for the last 1 s every pad of both grippers at least 30 mm from the doll and the footboard with both grippers slower than 5 mm/s = 1.0 (success, which must also hold 1 s). Moving the legs or the footboard back never clears a gate or a measurement. Doing nothing scores 0. Real trial: read the footboard face against the tape on a top photo (to 5 mm); a side photo during the hold shows both knees flat, the crown on the headpiece and both soles on the footboard.

tasks.title: Install a processor: lift the socket lever, open the shield, seat it on its keys, shut both
tasks.instruction: Install the processor in the empty socket. Pull the socket lever's handle up out from under its catch and lift the lever all the way open, then open the steel processor shield by its lip. Set the processor in the socket with its two notches on the socket's keys and its gold triangle at the socket's gold mark. Then shut the shield and press the lever back down under its catch.
tasks.context: Server technicians install a processor this way. Dell's PowerEdge R260 (an LGA1700 server) service video: "To install the processor, align and place the processor in the socket", then "Lower the processor shield, then lower the lever and push it under the tab to lock it into place." HPE's DL360 Gen9 guide warns that "Forcing the levers closed can damage the processor and socket, requiring system board replacement", and that the board's pins are very fragile. Done by: server and data-center technicians.
tasks.scoring: The processor is seated when its lowest point is within 0.5 mm of the board, it is flat within 1 degree, its centre is within 0.8 mm of the pocket's, it is turned within 2 degrees of the socket's orientation (notches on the keys) and it is still (under 1 cm/s). Not seated, anywhere: 0. Seated: 0.4. Seated with the shield shut (within 3 degrees): 0.7. Seated, the shield shut and the lever down under its catch (within 2 degrees; a lever laid on top of the catch sits at about 4): 1.0, held for 1 s. A processor turned the wrong way rides on the keys and is not seated. Possible scores: 0, 0.4, 0.7, 1.0. To check a real trial: a top photo for the lid square in the frame and the lever under its tab, and a side view for the processor flat.

tasks.title: Put one eye drop in a care-training manikin's right eye with the lower lid drawn down and the tip off the face
tasks.instruction: Put one drop of the eye medicine in the manikin's right eye, then put the bottle back on the tray.
tasks.context: Registered nurses (BLS 29-1141, about 3.3 million US jobs) and licensed practical nurses (29-2061, about 650,000) give eye drops on medication rounds; O*NET lists "Administer medications to patients and monitor patients for reactions or side effects" for registered nurses. The taught technique: with the patient looking up, draw the lower lid down with one finger on the cheek to open a pocket, hold the bottle tip down about 2 cm above it without touching the eye, lids, lashes or face, and squeeze just enough for one drop. A touched tip contaminates the bottle for later doses, and the eye holds less than one 30 to 50 uL drop, so a second runs down the cheek. In video studies of glaucoma patients giving their own drops, most missed the eye, touched the tip or released extra drops. The hard part is the manipulation: one hand draws the lid with light contact while the other aims a light, soft bottle at a 1 cm target and controls the squeeze force and its duration.
tasks.scoring: A drop forms only while the bottle points at least 30 degrees below horizontal and its walls are squeezed with more than 4 N; a harder or longer squeeze releases more 40 uL drops (flow model in the README). A drop falls straight down. It is in the pocket if it lands in the strip the lid uncovers below the eye opening with the lid drawn down at least 3 mm (less leaves no pocket), and in the eye if it lands in the eye opening or in that strip with the lid drawn less. The whole trial scores 0 if at any moment the nozzle touches the skin (eye, lids, lashes or face), which carries germs into the bottle; a hand touches either eye opening; the eye is pushed 6 mm for 0.1 s or 9 mm at once (about 4 N and 6 N), a push that moves a person's head; or the bottle falls free onto the table.
