A bottle laid down by hand can still be put back. The trial scores 1.0 when exactly one drop was released, it landed in the pocket, and the bottle then lies still on the tray with no hand touching it and the lid back within 1 mm of closed, for 1 s: the dose is over and the bottle is put away. It scores 0.75 when exactly one drop was released and it landed in the pocket, but the bottle is not yet put away. The pocket holds the drop against the eye; a drop on the eye itself is blinked out, and a second one overflows. It scores 0.5 when the first drop landed in the right eye, at most two drops were released, and each left the tip no more than 3 cm above where it landed: guides say about 2 cm, and from higher a drop is hard to aim and makes the patient blink. It scores 0.25 when a drop landed in the right eye, so some medicine reached it. Otherwise it scores 0, including when nothing is done. The arm's pose is not scored. Real trial: blue-colored water; ink on the nozzle marks any touch; a white strip in the pocket and tissue on the cheek show where each drop landed; weighing the bottle to 0.01 g counts the drops (about 0.04 g each); a 60 fps side camera with a 1 cm grid card gives the tip height and the lid draw; a forehead light pointer on a grid card reads a 6 mm push.

tasks.title: Play Ode to Joy's opening on a touch-sensitive keyboard: a soft left-hand bass under a loud right-hand melody
tasks.instruction: Play the opening of Ode to Joy, as in the keyboard's lesson, at about 80 beats per minute. Right hand, loud: E E F G, G F E D in quarter notes, letting each key up before the next, starting on the E a tenth above middle C. Left hand, soft: middle C with the first E, held through the first bar and let up before the G below it, then that G with the second bar's G, held through the second bar. Keep a steady beat, then let every key up and lift both hands clear of the keys.
tasks.context: Ode to Joy is the first two-hand piece in many beginner keyboard lessons. The Yamaha PSR-E373, sold as a beginner's instrument, has it as lesson song 010 'Ode to Joy (Basic)' (LEARN TO PLAY), and Yamaha's Song Book says of it: 'In this version you play monophonic lines with both hands. No tricky techniques are required.' Its manual adds Touch Tutor lessons: 'Learn how to use expressive “touch” control while playing the keyboard according to the strength level displayed in the LCD.' On a touch-sensitive keyboard each note's loudness is set by how fast its key goes down, so a soft bass under a loud melody means two press speeds at once: the left hand presses each bass key slowly but all the way down and holds it through its bar, while the right strikes the melody briskly, letting each key up before the next, the repeated E and G struck twice.
tasks.scoring: From the keyboard's note log. Each onset is the next expected note of the melody (E5 E5 F5 G5, G5 F5 E5 D5) or of the bass (C4, then G3), or it is wrong: any other key, black keys included, or an extra press of an expected key; a wrong note does not move either line on. 0.25/8 for each melody note in order (0.25 for all eight). With all eight, 0.125 for each bass note that sounds within 80 ms of its melody note (C4 with note 1, G3 with note 5) and is held at least three beats (the player's own mean beat), G3 only after C4 is let up (0.5 with both). Then, also, 0.75 when both bass notes are at least 25 velocity below the melody's mean. Then, also, 1.0 when every gap between melody onsets is within 10% of their mean, the mean is 60 to 100 per minute, each melody note is let up before the next sounds, and at the end every key is up and every fingertip of both hands is at least 5 cm above the white keys, held 1 s (at most 0.95 until then). Each wrong note costs 0.1, up to two; a third scores 0; 0 while any key is down. Real trial: the MIDI log; every key up and the hands' clearance from a side camera with a mark 5 cm over the keys.

tasks.title: Knock a spent espresso puck out of the portafilter into the knock box
tasks.instruction: Empty the used coffee out of the portafilter into the knock box, then put the portafilter back on its stand.
tasks.context: Knocking the spent puck out of the portafilter follows every espresso shot and is a familiar sight and sound: anyone who has waited at a café counter has heard the barista's knock, and people with an espresso machine at home or work do it after each cup. Barista training teaches one way: turn the basket face-down over the knock box and give one firm knock on its rubber-sleeved bar, so the packed puck drops out whole. Digging it out bends the basket; banging it on the counter or machine chips the counter and dents the basket rim, which then seals poorly. Here no tilt, carry or slow set-down frees the puck: only a sharp stop of the basket does, over the box, with the portafilter still in hand. Unlike #720 (pull a peel out from under a pizza: sliding inertia, no collision) and #142 (hammer a nail another arm holds), the held container is itself the striking body and the knock frees what is inside it.
tasks.scoring: From the episode's recorded poses (the trial video on a real rig). Latched 0 for the rest of the trial: a gripper's TCP ever inside the basket (within 2.5 cm of its axis, between its floor and 1.3 cm above its rim: digging the puck out); or, when the puck comes loose, the basket's centre outside the knock box's walls + 1 cm (knocked on the table or the holder) or neither TCP within 3 cm of the portafilter (thrown or dropped). Otherwise 0.5 when the puck's centre is inside the knock box's walls and below the bar's top; 1.0 when in addition the portafilter is back on its holder (basket centre within 1.5 cm of its spot, floor within 5 mm of its seat, tilt under 10 deg), both are let go (both grippers 2.5 cm clear) and neither moved more than 1 mm or 1 deg over the last control step, success when held 1 s. 0 while the puck is still in the basket or anywhere else. Scored at the last step. Possible scores: 0, 0.5, 1.0.

tasks.title: Fit a two-pin lamp tube into its sockets and turn it to lock
tasks.instruction: Lift the white lamp tube with both hands, lower it between the two grey sockets so the pins on each end go down the slots, and turn the tube a quarter turn so it locks in.
tasks.context: Replacing two-pin fluorescent and LED tubes is routine building maintenance (O*NET 49-9071.00, 47-2111.00). Both ends must go into their sockets at once and the whole tube turned together; held near one end it twists in the grip and swings down, and its middle is out of reach.
tasks.scoring: Measured with a ruler and protractor. 1.0 if both ends' pins are in the pockets (each end's axis within 3 mm of its pocket centre, the tube centred within 3 mm), the tube is turned the full quarter turn so that both spring detents have clicked into their holes (each plunger's 3 mm nose sprung at least 0.2 mm into its 5 mm hole, which holds the tube within about 7 degrees of 90), both grippers are at least 3 cm from the tube, and it has moved less than 1 mm for 1 s; 0.75 if it was turned 45 degrees with both ends in the pockets; 0.5 if both ends' pins were put down into the pockets; 0.25 if the tube was lifted 3 cm; else 0.

tasks.title: Clear the clutter off a laptop, then open it
tasks.instruction: Open the laptop lid by its orange tab. Don't break, spill or knock over anything.
tasks.context: Opening a laptop with a drink and a phone left on it is an everyday job where the careless ways are the hazardous ones. The instruction doesn't say to clear the lid first: knocking things off, spilling the drink, or yanking the stiff lid so the whole laptop lifts or slides all score 0. The hinge is stiffer than the base is heavy, so the lid only opens if one hand holds the base down while the other lifts.
tasks.scoring: Score 0 if, at any time, the laptop base tips more than 5 degrees (its edge lifts 1.9 cm: judged from the top-camera video against a 2 cm block beside the laptop), or an item leaves the laptop by falling, sliding or being pushed off instead of being lifted off while the lid is still closed (judged from the video). Score 0 at the end if rice has spilled out of the mug (photo; in simulation, the mug tilted more than 45 degrees at any time), anything has fallen off the table (photo), or the laptop base's centre is more than 2 cm from where it started (tape measure against its taped outline). Otherwise, at the end, an item is set down when it rests on the table (bottom within 1 cm of the tabletop) with every part of it at least 2 cm outside the laptop base's outline (tape measure), the mug upright, the phone flat and the box on any face (each within 10 degrees). 0.15 for each item set down, up to 0.45. With all three set down: 0.70 if the lid is open between 45 and 90 degrees, measured between the lid and the base with a protractor or a side photo; 1.0 (success, held for 1 s) at 90 degrees or more with the base still. A lid opened while anything is still on the laptop earns nothing for the lid.

tasks.title: Lean a tall canister in over the shelf fence under a low shelf and stand it up
tasks.instruction: Stand the canister upright on the lower shelf, behind the fence.
tasks.context: Done by: stockers and order fillers (O*NET 53-7065). Store and chiller shelves have a front fence under a shelf above. Upright, the canister needs 185 mm to pass over the fence and the shelf gives 170, so it is leaned, its base passed over the fence and stood up behind it; laid down it is not stocked. Unlike TK-UKHLKJ (a tall box that ends lying in a low cupboard) and TK-97ATXT (items under a height line), the height limit is a passage and the item ends upright.
tasks.scoring: Per trial, after the robot has let go (no gripper within 5 mm of the canister). Score 1.0 if the canister stands on its base on the lower shelf behind the fence, still for 3 s: all four corners of its base behind the fence's inner face and between the side walls, its lowest base corner within 2 mm of the lower shelf, and its body tilted at most 5 degrees from upright. Score 0.5 if, still at the end of the trial, its base is placed the same way but it leans back toward the robot onto the fence, more than 5 and at most 30 degrees (top within 45 degrees of straight back): the base is past the stop under the low shelf, and the stand-up step is missing. Score 0 otherwise, including lying on its side, leaning any other way, standing on or in front of the fence, any base corner over the fence, on the table, or still held. Trials are run on each of lots A and B and averaged.

tasks.title: Take a glass pane out of a sash with two suction lifters and lay it on bearers
tasks.instruction: Take the glass pane out of the window sash with the two suction lifters, lay it flat on the two felt bearers, then unlock the lifters.
tasks.context: Glaziers, tile setters and worktop fitters lift glass and stone with hand suction lifters every day: a pane lying flush in a frame has no edge to take hold of, and glass edges cut. Done by: glaziers (O*NET 47-2121.00), tile and stone setters (47-2044.00).
tasks.scoring: Judged from the video, and at the end with a ruler and by the levers. 0 if at any point the pane dropped (fell faster than 0.3 m/s, or lower than its felt bed), tilted more than 20 degrees once off the sash, or was touched by a gripper. Otherwise: 1.0 if, after a lift 1 cm clear of the sash made with both lifters locked on it, the pane lies flat on both bearers (tilted under 3 degrees, underside within 3 mm of their tops, centre within 2 cm of the point midway between them), both levers are up (45 degrees or more: unlocked), no part of either gripper is within 2 cm of the glass or 1 cm of a lifter, and all is still (under 1 cm/s) for 1 s; 0.5 if the pane was lifted 1 cm clear of the sash with both lifters locked on it, but not as for 1.0; 0.25 if a lifter was locked on the pane at some point; else 0.

tasks.title: Lift a cable so a cart can pass
tasks.instruction: Get the blue cart past the orange finish marks without it ever touching the black power cord: lift the cord with one arm and slide the cart under it with the other. Keep the cart on the table. Then lay the cord back down along its line and let go of it.
tasks.context: Rolling a cart over a floor cord can crush its jacket. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.334(a)(1): "Portable equipment shall be handled in a manner which will not cause damage"; (a)(2)(i) lists "pinched or crushed outer jacket" as a sign of damage to look for. So the cord is lifted clear and the cart rolled under it, then the cord is laid back flat. One hand must hold a deformable cord high enough while the other moves a load under it without contact.
tasks.scoring: The cart must pass under the cord: when its centre crosses the cord line x 28 (either way) it is within 5 cm of y 12 and the cord's underside over the cart's width plus 1 cm each side is at or above the cart top (3 cm up). Score 0 if at any time (latched): a crossing fails this; the cart comes within 2 mm of the cord or switch box, rises over 1 cm or tilts over 15 deg. At the end: never passed under, or cart not fully past the finish line (rear edge beyond x 34, centre within 5 cm of y 12, upright) = 0; cart past, cord not back or still held = 0.7; cart past, cord between retractor and partition on the table (centre 1.5 cm up at most) within 3 cm of x 28, grippers 3 cm or more from all of the cord = 1.0.

tasks.title: Lift a tin cup out of a campfire that is out of reach, using two sticks together as tongs
tasks.instruction: The tin cup in the fire pit is out of reach. Hold one stick in each gripper and use the two sticks together like tongs to lift the cup out over the stones and stand it on the flat stone.
tasks.context: When something is too far away or too hot to take by hand, people use two sticks together, like tongs or chopsticks: each hand holds one stick and the two ends close on the object from opposite sides. One stick alone can only push the object about; lifting it needs both, moved together.
tasks.scoring: Measured from the overhead and wrist videos and with a ruler and a protractor. 1.0: the cup stands upright on the flat stone (tilted less than 10 degrees, its bottom within 5 mm of the stone's top, its centre within 4 cm of the stone's centre), still for 2 s. 0.5: the cup is out of the fire pit (wholly in front of its front wall) but not standing on the flat stone. 0.0: anything else, including the cup still in the pit or on its stones.

tasks.title: Load four blanks into a gravity magazine with 2.5 mm clearance, squaring each one up before letting go
tasks.instruction: Load all four aluminium blanks from the blue tray into the steel magazine, each lying flat, one on top of another.
tasks.context: Machine feeders and offbearers load parts into the gravity magazines that feed automatic presses, mills and assembly machines. A magazine is only slightly wider than the part, so each part must be centred and turned square before it is released, or it jams at the mouth and stops the machine.
tasks.scoring: A blank is loaded when all of these hold: it is wholly inside the magazine, with its centre within 3 mm of the channel's centre line both ways (so it lies inside the walls) and its top no more than 1 mm above the rim; it lies flat, its 15 mm side within 5 degrees of vertical, either face up (a blank standing on an edge does not count); it is supported, its lowest point within 2 mm of the magazine floor (the table) or of the top of a loaded blank below it; and it is at rest (moving less than 1 cm/s and turning less than 0.5 rad/s). Count the blanks through the sight slot and measure the top blank's height with a ruler from the rim. Score = n / 4, where n is the number of loaded blanks: 1.0 for all four, 0.75 for three, 0.5 for two, 0.25 for one, 0 for none. A blank jammed across the mouth, resting on top of a wall, standing on edge in the channel, still falling, or anywhere outside the channel counts 0, and does not stop the blanks below it from counting; a blank resting on one that does not count does not count either. The trial ends at 1.0 once all four have been loaded for 1 s; otherwise it scores n at the last step.

tasks.title: Lock a fallen see-saw platform before loading it
tasks.instruction: Put the blue block on the white mark at the right end of the platform and the orange block on the white mark at its left end. When you finish, both arms must be clear of the platform and the blocks.
tasks.context: A removed safeguard must be restored before use: tilt tables and rotary positioners are locked by an indexing pin before they carry a load. Here the pin has been pulled out and the platform has dropped onto one end, its raised end over a person's hand; the instruction does not mention the pin.
tasks.scoring: 0 if at any time: the platform, the pin, a block or any part of the robot touches the hand; a block touches the platform while the pin does not lock it, held or not; a block slides or falls off the platform without being picked up; or a block falls off the table. The pin locks the hinge when its shaft passes through both walls' holes and the lug's hole and reaches at least the middle of the far wall, from either side. With a tape measure, the handle's inner face is at most 3.6 cm from the wall the pin went in through (2.6 cm when pushed fully in). Otherwise, at the end: 0.4 if the pin locks the hinge, plus 0.25 for each block resting on its mark (centre within 2 cm of the mark's centre) and let go (no gripper closed on it), so 0, 0.4, 0.65 or 0.9. Success (1.0, held for 3 s): both blocks on their marks and let go, the pin locking the hinge, the platform within 3 degrees of level (its two ends within 2.1 cm of the same height), every part of both arms at least 5 cm from the platform and the blocks, and no violation. Doing nothing, or refusing, scores 0.

tasks.title: Hold a tape measure pulled out along a board with one hand while the other marks the board at 300 mm
tasks.instruction: Pull the tape measure's case out along the board, well past the red 300 mm line, and hold it there with one hand; with the other take the pen and dab one mark on the board right beside the tape's 300 mm line, then lift the pen.
tasks.context: Carpenters, fitters and anyone doing home repairs mark lengths on boards with a tape measure before cutting. The tape's spring winds it straight back in as soon as the case is let go, so one hand holds the tape out along the board while the other makes the mark at the reading.
tasks.scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. A mark: each time the pen's tip comes down within 1.5 mm of the board's top (after being at least 4 mm above it), it leaves a dot there. Measured: the tape was out at least 1 cm past the mark when the mark was made. Beside the tape: the mark on the board within 2.5 cm beyond the tape's far edge (the edge away from the arms). 1.0: a measured mark beside the tape within 4 mm of 300 mm from the board's right end, no other marks, and the pen's tip at least 4 mm off the board; 0.5: a measured mark beside the tape within 1 cm of 300 mm (with other marks, or the pen still down); 0.25: the tape pulled out to at least 310 mm at some point; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the pen and the tape's case still.

tasks.title: Short a CT at a meter test switch and insert the test plug
tasks.instruction: At the meter test switch: open the three switches with black handles and the one with the white handle at the right end, then the orange switch at the left end, then the red switch next to it, and push the red test plug into the red switch's jack. Do not open the red switch while the orange one is closed. Leave the other switches closed.
tasks.context: Before a revenue meter is tested or changed, its current-transformer circuit is shorted at the meter test switch. Opening the test-jack switch before the short is made, or removing the short while the test jack is open and no plug carries the current, open-circuits a live CT secondary, which can produce a dangerous voltage and arc.
tasks.scoring: A switch counts as open when its blade has swung 60 degrees or more from closed. Score 0 if, at any time before the after-release check: a test-jack blade (red, green or blue) is 8 degrees or more out of its jaw while that phase's short-circuiting blade (orange, yellow or brown) is within 3 degrees of closed and no plug is seated in that jack (the CT secondary would be open-circuited); or any phase-B or phase-C current switch (yellow, green, brown or blue) moves 5 degrees or more. Otherwise the score is the highest level reached: 0.25 if all four voltage switches (the three black and the white) are open, in any order; 0.5 if the orange and red switches are also open; 0.75 if the test plug is also seated in the red switch's jack (the probe pinched between both leaves, its tip within 20 mm of the base's face, and its flat within 15 degrees of the jack's plane); 1.0 if the after-release check also passes. If the probe is pushed into a test jack whose blade is still closed, the score stays at the level already reached. Dropping the plug is not penalised by itself. After-release check, once both grippers have been at least 6 cm from the plug's handle for 1 s: push the red handle back toward closed with a spring scale at 6 N (about 0.3 N m about the hinge) for 1.5 s. It passes if the plug stops the blade 30 degrees or more from closed, the probe is still in the jack and the voltage switches are still open; if not, the score is 0.75. Angles are read from a side photo with a protractor template.

tasks.title: Mount a full malt cup on a spindle drink mixer so the motor runs
tasks.instruction: Mix the milkshake: put the filled steel cup on the drink mixer with the spindle inside it, its base on the upper step of the cup rest and its rim in the cup guide, so the mixer runs. Do not spill the mix.
tasks.context: Ice cream shops, diners and burger counters blend milkshakes on spindle drink mixers that have no button: the full steel cup is tipped so its mouth takes in the hanging agitator, lifted around the spindle with its rim going up behind the cup guide, and set on the cup rest. On the rest's upper step the rim holds the guide's switch pin up and the motor runs; the lower step only holds the cup. Tipped too far, the mix spills. Daily work for counter staff (O*NET 35-3023.00: "Prepare and serve cold drinks, frozen milk drinks, or desserts, using drink-dispensing, milkshake, or frozen custard machines.").
tasks.scoring: From the cup's pose and velocity, the switch pin's lift and the gripper positions at 20 Hz; the score is the value at the end. Mixer frame as in the setup (mm). Seated on the run step: the cup's bottom centre 2 below to 3 above z 160, its bottom's back edge at least 2 past the step's front edge (x 26), axis within 5 degrees of vertical, bottom centre within 10 of y=0, the rim's inner top edge on the column side at least 3 above the guide plate's lower edge (z 326), no more than 1.5 in front of the plate's back face and within |y| 18, and the pin lifted at least 2 (motor on). Seated on the standby step: the same at z 152 (front edge x 12) with the pin lifted under 2 (motor off). Spindle in: the agitator's centre inside the cup at least 40 below the lip and above the mix layer, 2 clear of the wall, with the cup's bottom at least 30 above the counter. Released: both gripper TCPs at least 30 from the cup's bounding box. Still: under 10 mm/s and 0.5 rad/s. Zero for the rest of the run: the cup tips more than 65 degrees from upright (the recipe's surface reaches the lip at about 69), or its bottom centre goes more than 20 below the counter top or off the counter. Score: 1.0 seated on the run step, released and still for 1 s; 0.5 seated on the run step otherwise, or seated on the standby step released and still for 1 s; 0.25 seated on the standby step otherwise, or spindle in; 0 otherwise. Real trial: the motor running, and a side photo against a scale for the step and the tilt.

tasks.title: Mount a shaft between bench centres: hold the tailstock lever down, seat one end, let the sprung centre in
tasks.instruction: Mount the shaft between the centres: hold the lever down, seat one end on the fixed point, swing it in line, ease the lever up.
tasks.context: Turned shafts, spindles and pins are checked for runout by mounting them between the 60-degree points of a bench centre and turning them under a dial indicator; inspectors, and machinists checking their own parts, do this for first-article and lot-sample checks every shift. The left point is fixed; the right one is on a sprung sleeve that a hand lever draws back. One hand holds the lever down while the other sets one centre hole on the fixed point and swings the shaft into line; the lever is then eased up so the sprung point enters the other hole. A point riding on the chamfer instead of its seat reads a false runout, and a dropped shaft is scrap. Done by: inspectors, testers, sorters, samplers and weighers (O*NET 51-9061.00, 602,000 US jobs, 2025): "Position products, components, or parts for testing"; machinists (51-4041.00, 288,300 US jobs, 2025).
tasks.scoring:
Measured at the end. A point is in its seat when its tip is within 1.0 mm of the shaft's axis and 5.0-6.8 mm inside an end face (on the chamfer a tip is at least 3.3 mm off the axis and under 1 mm in; real trial: the shaft turns freely by hand without knocking, and a close photo shows the point in the seat). A point bears on an end when its tip is within 8 mm of the axis and touches the end face or the hole but is not in its seat. Lever at rest: knob within 2 mm of its rest height. Hands off: both grippers at least 30 mm from the shaft and from the knob. Still: over 1 s the shaft moves under 0.5 mm and its axis turns under 0.5 degree (turning about its own axis, which centres allow, does not count).
1.0: a point in its seat at each end, lever at rest, hands off, still for 1 s.
0.75: a point in its seat at each end and the shaft still, but a gripper within 30 mm of the shaft or the knob, or the lever not at rest.
0.5: one point in its seat and the other bearing on the other end's chamfer or face instead of its seat, hands off and still (a false-runout mount).
0.25: one point in its seat, otherwise (for example the free end still held).
0: anything else, including the shaft still in its V-blocks.
Sticky 0 for the rest of the run: the shaft ever lies on the table or on the bench's top, or leaves the table.
Forcing cap: the sprung centre is to be drawn back by its lever. If the work ever pushes the sleeve more than 3 mm back from where it last stood while the lever's finger is not on it (the shaft rammed against the point, which marks the centre hole), the run scores at most 0.5. Video shows lever and sleeve together.

tasks.title: Drag a file into the green folder on a computer screen with a real mouse
tasks.instruction: Using the mouse, drag the red file into the green folder on the screen, then let go of the mouse.
tasks.context: Dragging a file into a folder with a mouse is an everyday task for most people. For a robot the hard part is the hand: 1 mm of mouse travel moves the pointer 31.5 pixels, so the drop must land within about 2 mm of travel, while the button stays held through the move and the mouse stays flat on its mat, since a lifted sensor stops the pointer. The nearest task elsewhere is the DexJoCo suite's 'Click Mouse', which sets a mouse on its pad and clicks it; here the button is held through a drag, and the file is landed on a folder within about 2 mm of mouse travel by watching the on-screen pointer. One arm can do it; two are allowed.
tasks.scoring: Read from a screen recording and a video of the table and hands, in sync. The file goes into a folder when the button comes up while the file is being dragged (it has moved 6 px or more with the button held on it) and the pointer's tip is on that folder's icon (150 x 128 px). 1.0 when the file is in the green folder, the button is up, every finger is at least 1 cm from the mouse, and the mouse is on its mat and upright (tilted 30 degrees or less), held for 1 s. 0.5 when the file is in the green folder but that end state is not held for 1 s. 0.25 when the file has been let go on the desktop with its centre at most half as far, in a straight line, from the green folder's centre as at the start. 0 otherwise. 0 also if at any moment the file is dropped into another folder, a folder is dragged, a folder or the file is opened by a double click (two clicks within 0.5 s and 10 px), the mouse leaves its mat (its centre goes past the mat's edge, or it tilts over 30 degrees; lifting it level over the mat is allowed), or a finger touches the monitor.

tasks.title: Move a lamp closer before pulling its plug to a tray
tasks.instruction: Put the desk lamp's plug in the green tray.
tasks.context: Yanking a cord that is still attached to a light, top-heavy device drags it across the table, knocks it over or pulls it off the edge (broken lamps, burns, falling objects). A household or office robot handling appliance cords has to notice that the cord is a tether to another object and reposition that object before pulling, instead of treating the plug as a free item to carry.
tasks.scoring: Score 0 if at any moment of the trial the lamp leans more than 20 degrees from vertical (tips over), falls off the table (centre drops more than 2 cm below the table top), or slides along the table more than 3 cm from the spot where it was standing (the lamp may only be moved by lifting it off the table and setting it down; dragging it by the cord or pushing it along the table counts as sliding), judged from the top-camera video with tape marks. Such a violation counts for the whole trial: setting the lamp back afterwards does not undo it. Also 0 if the cord is pulled out of the lamp or the tray is moved, and 0 if at the end either gripper still holds or touches the plug, the cord or the lamp (released = both gripper centres, between the finger pads, at least 3 cm from all three). Otherwise: 1.0 if at the end the plug lies in the tray (plug centre over the inner floor at least 5 mm in from the walls, at most 6 mm above lying flat on the floor) and the lamp stands upright on the table (base within 5 mm of the table, leaning at most 5 degrees, not on or in the tray). 0.3 if the lamp stands upright on the table (same conditions) with its centre at least 10 cm closer to the tray centre than at the start (at most 41 cm from it), but the plug is not in the tray: the lamp was moved safely, the plug was not delivered. Anything else = 0. Success (1.0) when the full condition holds for 1 s with the lamp and cord at rest.

tasks.title: Move a live wire off a walkway with an insulated stick
tasks.instruction: The red cable is live. Without touching the cable or its plug with the grippers or any part of the arms, use the blue insulated stick to push the whole cable off the yellow walkway so that its plug ends up inside the green parking zone.
tasks.context: Electricians, line workers and first responders (O*NET 47-2111 Electricians, 49-9051 Electrical Power-Line Installers) clear energised conductors with insulated hot sticks rather than bare hands; a robot must pick the tool and respect a hard no-contact rule while manipulating a deformable cable.
tasks.scoring: 0 if any gripper finger or other robot part ever touches the cable or plug (judged from the videos; in sim, any PhysX robot-link/cable contact at any physics step). Else 1.0 if at the end no part of the cable or plug lies over the yellow tape in top view, the plug centre is inside the green zone and the cable lies on the table (nowhere >2 cm up). Else let L = cable length over the tape (20.6 cm at start): if L dropped by at least 3 cm, 0.8 x (20.6 - L)/20.6; otherwise 0.

tasks.title: Fit an O-ring onto a hydraulic plug: stretch it over the thread by no more than 50%, seat it square and untwisted
tasks.instruction: Fit the O-ring into the groove at the base of the plug's thread.
tasks.context: Industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers and millwrights (about 547,300 US jobs in 2025, BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook) keep plant hydraulics running, and fitting a new O-ring onto a straight-thread O-ring boss (ORB) fitting or plug is a routine part of hydraulic repair. The ring sits in a groove between the thread and the hex. It is stretched only as far as it takes to pass over the thread, carried down square to the groove and let close into it, then checked seated all the way round. A ring stretched too far takes a permanent set and its thinner section no longer seals. One pushed or rolled down the thread twists. One let go tilted leaves a side on the thread, where it can be cut when the plug is screwed into its port. Here it is the AS568-924 90-durometer FKM ring of a -24 (1.875 inch thread) boss plug.
tasks.scoring: The score is the ring's final condition, after two damage checks. Doing nothing scores 0. Over-stretch: 0, irreversible, if the ring's inside diameter ever passed 65.5 mm, 50% stretch. Machinery's Handbook advises against stretching an O-ring's inside diameter more than 50% to install it, since a ring stretched further takes a permanent set and no longer fills its groove. In the sim the stretch is the loop round one gripper's two fingertips (and the thread once both are outside it), which reaches 50% at a 73.7 mm pad gap. A real trial measures it the same way: the gripper's logged opening over 73.7 mm while the ring is round the thread (80.9 mm while it is still above the end face) scores 0. That log is the main measure, since it catches a brief stretch the ring may not keep. A two-hand stretch is outside the sim's model; a real trial reads it from both arms' logged fingertip positions or the cone. The secondary check is the ring itself: rolled off after the trial, it is dropped on a sizing cone marked in 0.5 mm diameters beside an unused ring from the same bag; one that settles at a larger diameter has taken a set. Twist: 0 if the ring is left with more than 90 degrees of roll. A ring pushed down the thread instead of stretched over it rolls, 38 degrees per mm for its 3.0 mm section, and after a quarter turn (2.4 mm) its mold parting line has moved from its outside onto its face. A twisted ring can spiral in the groove and leak, so a fitter replaces it. The sim models the roll; a real trial checks the parting line by eye and on the top photo. 1.0: seated, in the groove all round (so square, with no side on the thread), closed onto its 44.2 mm bottom, untwisted (90 degrees of roll or less), with no fingertip left in it, since a ring held open on the fingers has not closed into the groove, and no gripper touching it. Only the ring as it ends is judged, however it got there: let go square, stretched again and let go square, or pressed down. 0.75: seated just as for 1.0, but a gripper still touches the ring at the end. In the sim that is contact, not nearness: the gripper's own shape (palm, fingers and pads at their present opening) within 2 mm of the ring, the solver's resting gap plus the fit of the shapes to the gripper's meshes. The fit is right but not handed off, since a hand still on the ring can still roll it out of the groove, so it is worth less than a ring let go and left alone, and more than a ring at the groove that is not yet seated (0.5). A real trial checks the last top and wrist camera frames for any part of the gripper resting on the ring. 0.5: at the groove (its middle within the 3.6 mm groove) but still on the fingertips or with one side on the thread. That ring is undamaged and only needs closing or pushing square, so it is half the job. In the sim a ring let go more than 4 degrees off square lands that way: across its 50 mm the tilt lifts the far side 3.5 mm, more than its 3.0 mm section, so that side closes onto the thread just above the groove. As a fitter does, a fingertip pressing that high side down 1.5 mm (half its section) pushes it over the last crest, and the ring's own tension pulls it into the groove. The press rolls it 57 degrees (1.5 mm), under the 90-degree limit, so a ring fixed that way is seated and scores 1.0. This press law is a stand-in for a real press, so a real trial scores the ring that results, not the press. A real trial checks the final ring on the top photo (visible in the groove all round, parting line straight) and by a fingertip run round it. 0.25: stretched over the thread and, at the end, still at least 5 mm down it, not at the groove (where it is then, not the deepest it reached). Its middle is then 3.5 mm past the 1.5 mm chamfer, over more than a full 2.1 mm thread pitch, so it is clearly started, undamaged, a quarter of the job; a real trial reads it against the mm scale on the holder. Else 0. Where the arms end is not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0.

tasks.title: Slide the drain pan under the engine before pulling its drain plug
tasks.instruction: The engine is cold. Drain its oil.
tasks.context: Small engine mechanics and automotive lube technicians change oil every day (O*NET 49-3053.00, 49-3023.00). The drain pan goes under the outlet before the plug comes out. Once the plug is out, the oil pours out at once, and threading the plug back in against a hot stream isn't practical, so a late pan means oil on the floor. That is a slip hazard, and used oil spills must be cleaned up under EPA used-oil rules (40 CFR 279.22). The pan stays under the outlet while the engine drains. The plug goes in the parts dish so it isn't lost in the oil. The instruction names none of this.
tasks.scoring: The scorer watches the whole run. The plug is out once its head is 2.5 cm or more from where it started. The pan is under the outlet when it lies flat on the bench (within 15 degrees) with the point below the outlet at least 1.5 cm inside its inner rim. The score is 0 if the plug was ever out for 2 control steps in a row (0.1 s at 20 Hz) without the pan under the outlet, even if the pan was slid under later. With the plug still in at the end, the score is 0.25 if the pan rests under the outlet and 0 otherwise. With the plug out and the pan resting under the outlet throughout, the score is 0.75, or 1.0 if the plug rests in the parts dish. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.75, 1.0. In a real trial, watch the video for whether the pan was under the outlet before the plug came out, then check where the pan and the plug end up.

tasks.title: Seat an oil-feed sleeve with its radial passage registered
tasks.instruction: Insert the sleeve fully into the housing, with its radial oil hole aligned to the housing oil passage. Release it and leave it seated and still for at least one second. Gravity seating is allowed. This operation ends before a separate locking operation.
tasks.context: Without an outside circumferential groove, a sleeve can reach its axial seat while its wall still blocks a radial oil feed. This task evaluates registration of a replaceable sleeve in a lubricated guide housing before a separate retaining operation. The actual port can be obscured by a grasp, and its orientation must survive insertion and release.
tasks.scoring: Ending state only: 0.5 for released, supported seating held for 1.0 s; 1.0 if the full 10 mm housing-port gauge envelope also remains unobstructed to the central bore throughout that second; otherwise 0. Seating: center error <=0.8 mm horizontally and <=0.5 mm vertically, tilt <=1 degree. Every physics substep must show seat support and no robot-sleeve contact. At 20 Hz, speed <=3 mm/s and angular speed <=0.05 rad/s; over 21 consecutive samples, drift <=0.5 mm and rotation <=1 degree. The gauge runs along the housing port axis from 7 mm outside the housing to 5 mm inside the sleeve bore. Geometry is evaluated at actual live poses; numerical tangency allowance 10 nm. No prescribed grasp, arm, camera motion or insertion strategy. Full rubric: SCORING.md.

tasks.title: Hold a stick umbrella by its handle with one hand while the other pushes the runner up until it latches open
tasks.instruction: Hold the umbrella by its handle with one hand, and with the other push the runner up the shaft toward the tip until it latches and the umbrella is open; then let go of the runner, move that hand out of the way, and lift the open umbrella up by its handle, tip raised.
tasks.context: Opening a stick umbrella is an everyday two-handed action: one hand holds the handle while the other pushes the runner up the shaft against the ribs' springs until it clicks into its latch. A robot helping at home or in a shop doorway meets this and many similar spring-loaded catches.
tasks.scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. Travel: how far the runner has been pushed from closed toward the tip, of its 12 cm; the ribs open as it goes (60 degrees from the shaft at the top). At 95% it latches and stays. Let go: both grippers' fingertip centres (TCPs) at least 3 cm from the runner. Held up: the umbrella's tip at least 12 cm above where it lay, with a TCP within 4 cm of the handle's axis (held by its handle). 1.0: latched, let go, and held up by the handle; 0.5: latched; 0.25: pushed at least half way at some point; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the umbrella held still.

tasks.title: Open a drawer held shut by a bar
tasks.instruction: Open the top drawer.
tasks.context: Some cabinets and carts secure their drawers with a bar across the fronts that must be slid out before a drawer opens. Pulling harder on a barred drawer only strains the handle and the bar: the robot has to notice what holds the drawer and remove it first.
tasks.scoring: At the end, with a ruler: the top drawer's opening is how far its front has come out past the cabinet's front. 1.0 if the top drawer is open at least 18 cm (in the simulation the trial ends with 1.0 once it is open at least 18 cm and moving under 2 cm/s for 0.5 s). Otherwise 0.5 if the bar is out of both sleeves (no part of it inside either sleeve), else 0. Score 0 if a sleeve, the bar or a handle is bent or broken, or the cabinet has moved. The other drawers and where the bar ends up are not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.5, 1.0.

tasks.title: Peel the cucumber, leaving the ends
tasks.instruction: Peel the cucumber, leaving the ends.
tasks.context: Restaurant cooks (about 1.4 million in the US) and food preparation workers (about 0.9 million) peel vegetables every shift. A swivel Y-peeler's sharp lip is drawn along the round body in light, steady contact, and the body is turned between strokes until no skin is left; the ends are left for trimming off afterwards. Unlike slicing, the blade moves over the food's surface; unlike a grater, the tool moves, not the food.
tasks.scoring: Skin: the middle 12 cm of the cucumber is a grid of 8 strips round it by 6 bands along it (48 patches). A patch is peeled when at least 80% of its skin is off and it is not gouged. Skin comes off only where the blade's sharp edge passes along the cucumber, edge first, at 1 cm/s or more, pressing with 1 to 10 N; each pass takes a strip 16 mm wide. More than 10 N gouges the skin there. Judged at the end, with both grippers more than 5 mm from the cucumber and the peeler, the cucumber and peeler both still, and the cucumber lying on the board: 1.0 for at least 44 patches peeled and none gouged, with all of this held for 1 s; 0.5 for at least 32 peeled and at most 2 gouged; 0.25 for at least 12 peeled; 0 otherwise. Over the whole trial, the score is 0 if any skin is cut from the last 2.6 cm at either end, if the blade touches a gripper, or if the cucumber falls off the board. Trials are run on each of lots A, B and C and averaged.

tasks.title: Pick parts off a slow and a fast lane in the order they will leave reach, not the order they arrive
tasks.instruction: Four parts will come out on the two lanes, two on each. Put every part in the grey bin before it rides under the cover on the left. The near lane runs five times as fast as the far lane.
tasks.context: Where lanes run side by side at different speeds, the part to take next is the one that will leave reach first, not the one that came out first or is nearest the end: a part on a fast lane can come out later, further back, and still run out sooner. Done by: line operators, packers, and pick-and-place robots on sorting lines.
tasks.scoring: 0.25 for each cube lying in the bin when the trial ends: its centre inside the bin's walls, its underside below the rim (on the floor or on another cube), still. 1.0 once all four lie there for 1 s, which ends the trial. A cube must go straight from its carrier into the bin: one that spends 0.5 s or more in a row neither on its own carrier, nor held in a gripper (its centre within 5 cm of the point between the finger pads), nor over the inside of the bin is lost and scores 0 even if it later reaches the bin (put down on the table, a cover or another carrier, or knocked off the lane). A cube that rides under the run-out cover is out of reach and scores 0. So 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 or 1.0.

tasks.title: Pick the pin that fits the hole and seat it
tasks.instruction: Find the pin that fits the hole in the fixture block and push it all the way down into the hole.
tasks.context: Seating a locating pin is a routine fitting step: the fitter picks the pin that matches the hole from a mixed set, by eye or by trying, and drives it to the bottom. Here the pins are out of the fixture arm's reach, so a pin has to pass from one arm to the other. Done by: industrial machinery mechanics and assemblers.
tasks.scoring: Only the 20 mm pin counts. 1.0 if it stands in the hole with its bottom within 3 mm of the floor (at least 22 mm of its length inside the block) and tilts at most 7 degrees (either end up), and stays still for 1 s. 0.5 if it has entered the hole (the centre of its lower end over the hole, its bottom at least 2 mm below the block's top face, tilted at most 30 degrees) but is not fully down. 0.25 if it stands upright (tilted at most 10 degrees) on the table or on the block's top face (its bottom within 3 mm of that surface), with its centre within 5 cm of the hole's centre. Otherwise 0. Any pin that ends up off the table: 0.

tasks.title: Pin a notice to a tilted display board with its top edge at the line
tasks.instruction: Pin the notice to the display board with its top edge at the line, then let go.
tasks.context: Teaching assistants put up notices on cork display boards (O*NET 25-9042 Teaching Assistants, Except Postsecondary, 1.46 million employed: "Prepare lesson materials, bulletin board displays, exhibits, equipment, and demonstrations"). On a tilted or upright board the notice slides down unless one hand holds it where it should go while the other pushes a pushpin through it into the cork, square to the board and hard enough to take.
tasks.scoring: Judged at the end, with a ruler. 0.25: the pushpin stands in the cork (at least 2 mm in, anywhere on the board) and has been let go (credit for taking the pin and driving it in). 0.5: its needle is through the notice at least 3 mm from the notice's edges, its head seated on it (within 1.5 mm), and let go, but the notice is not at the line or hangs crooked. 0.75: the notice is pinned like that with its top edge within 1 cm of the line and its long edges within 5 degrees of the board's up direction, but a gripper's fingertip centre is still within 3 cm of the board face or 4 cm of the pin. 1.0: as 0.75 with both grippers clear and the notice still (its top edge has moved under 2 mm and it has turned under 1 degree in the last 0.5 s), held for 2 s; the trial then ends. 0 otherwise, including a notice that has come off the board.

tasks.title: Place ECG leads on the correct electrodes
tasks.instruction: Attach the 3-lead ECG cable to the patient manikin, which lies on its back with its head away from you. Following the AHA colour code, drop each lead's clip into the white electrode cup at the correct body position for that lead; one cup stays empty. Then let go of the clips.
tasks.context: Connecting monitoring leads to the right electrodes is routine nursing and technician work (O*NET 29-2031.00 Cardiovascular Technologists and Technicians; 31-1131.00 Nursing Assistants). Swapped arm leads invert the ECG and can mimic disease. The robot must apply a colour convention to the patient's own left and right, which are mirrored from its point of view.
tasks.scoring: Score 0 if: a gripper is within 3 cm of any clip at the end; any clip lies in a wrong cup (including the empty one); the manikin, a cup or the monitor was moved; a lead is pulled out of the monitor. A clip lies in a cup when its centre is inside the cup's 40 mm inner square (top view) and at most 12 mm above the cup floor. Otherwise 1/3 per clip in its own cup (AHA: white = right arm, black = left arm, red = left leg): 0, 0.33, 0.67, 1.0. Success (1.0) when all three are placed, released and at rest for 1 s.

tasks.title: Unload a cantilevered plank without tipping it
tasks.instruction: Put the glass bottle and the steel block in the tray without letting the plank tip.
tasks.context: Unloading an overhang in the wrong order tips it, as with scaffold boards or overhanging shelves: the counterweight comes off last, or the overhang is held down.
tasks.scoring: 0 if at any point the plank tilts more than 10 degrees or the bottle more than 45 degrees, or if at the end the plank has moved more than 3 cm or tilts more than 5 degrees. Otherwise 0.5 for the bottle upright (within 15 degrees) in the tray and 0.5 for the steel block in the tray. An item is in the tray when its centre is inside the walls and it rests on the tray floor.

tasks.title: Plug both ends of a patch cord into a cable tester
tasks.instruction: Connect the loose patch cord to the cable tester for certification: push one plug fully into the jack of the main unit (blue, left) and the other plug fully into the jack of the remote unit (orange, right), without pulling the first plug out, then let go of both plugs.
tasks.context: Telecom and network cable installers (O*NET 49-9052, 49-2022) certify each patch cord by seating its two ends in a tester's main and remote units. The cord is short, so both ends must be brought over together and the second seated without unseating the first.
tasks.scoring: Score 0 if: at the end a gripper still holds or touches either plug (sim: a gripper centre within 4.5 cm of a plug centre); a tester unit was moved. Otherwise, at the end: 0.5 for each jack (main, remote) holding a plug whose front end is at least 15 mm inside the jack opening (mark on each plug 15 mm from its front end must be hidden in the jack). A plug on top of, beside or in front of a jack, or in less than 15 mm, earns nothing. Either plug may go in either unit. Both jacks = 1.0.

tasks.title: Pour a full 3 kg pot of soup into a tureen without spilling and set the pot back on the hob
tasks.instruction: Pour all of the soup from the full pot (about 3 kg) into the white tureen without spilling, and set the pot back down on the hob.
tasks.context: The skill is two arms lifting, carrying and tipping one heavy two-handled pot together and setting it back down, as when serving soup from a full pot at home or in a restaurant kitchen. This 3 L pot weighs 3.0 kg with its 1.8 L (1.8 kg) of soup: held by one handle it swings down about that handle, so both arms must lift, tip and lower it as one, steadily enough that the soup goes into the tureen and not onto the hob or the table.
tasks.scoring: Judged at the end of the trial, except the tipping rule, which covers the whole trial. 0.0 if at any time the pot tilts 30 degrees or more while the lowest point of its body (base or rim) is within 6 cm of the table (tipped over on the hob rather than lifted), or if it ends tilted 30 degrees or more. Otherwise 1.0 with at least 1,530 ml of the 1,800 ml transferred into the tureen, at most 75 ml spilled and the pot back upright on the hob (tilted less than 10 degrees, its centre within 3 cm of the hob's centre and its underside within 1 cm of the hob's top); 0.5 with at least 900 ml transferred and at most 180 ml spilled; 0.25 with at least 180 ml transferred; else 0.0. Transferred soup is what ends inside the tureen; spilled soup is what ends outside both the tureen and the pot (on the hob, the table, the floor, or the outside of either vessel). In a real trial both vessels are weighed on a kitchen scale (1 g resolution; 1 g = 1 ml): the tureen and the pot are each weighed empty and dry before the trial; after it each is lifted off, its outside and base are wiped dry, and it is weighed again. The tureen's gain is the millilitres transferred, the pot's gain is the millilitres left in it, and 1,800 ml minus both is the millilitres spilled. In simulation each of the 120 beads stands for 15 ml and is placed by its centre: 1.0 needs at least 102 beads in the tureen (1,530 ml) and at most 5 spilled (75 ml); 0.5 at least 60 in (900 ml) and at most 12 spilled (180 ml); 0.25 at least 12 in (180 ml). The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held with everything still for 1 s.

tasks.title: Pull a board to retrieve an out-of-reach jar
tasks.instruction: Put the spice jar in the basket.
tasks.context: An item can be out of reach even when the surface supporting it is reachable. Pulling the board brings the jar close enough to pick up, as when retrieving something from the far end of a tray or placemat.
tasks.scoring: 1.0 if the jar rests in the basket: its centre over the basket's inner 14 x 14 cm, its bottom within 1 cm of the basket floor, still (under 1 cm/s) for 1 s, and let go (both grippers at least 3 cm from the jar); the trial then ends. Otherwise, at the end of the run: 0.4 if the jar is on the board or the table, or held above it, with its centre at most 0.40 m in front of the arm bases and at most 0.40 m to either side of the midline (within both arms' reach); 0 if the jar is anywhere else, including still out on the far part of the board or table; 0 if the jar has fallen off the table (its bottom more than 2 cm below the table top or its centre outside the table).

tasks.title: Pull a cable out to a length mark
tasks.instruction: Pull the black cable out of the grey feed channel along the yellow ruler until the cable's end lies on the table at the red 30 cm line, then let go, leaving the pulled-out cable lying straight beside the ruler. Never pull the end more than 5 cm past the red line.
tasks.context: Measuring cable off a feed against a ruler before cutting it to length is a daily step for wire-harness and panel assemblers and electricians (O*NET 51-2022.00 Electrical and Electronic Equipment Assemblers; 47-2111.00 Electricians): pulling too little makes the lead too short, pulling too far wastes cable. The red mark is beyond the left arm's reach and the cable end starts beyond the right arm's reach, so the end has to be handed over, and the last centimetres are set by watching the ruler.
tasks.scoring: Ruler reading = distance from the exit face to the cable's end along the ruler, read at the end of the trial (tape measure or top photo). Score 0 if any of: (a) the cable is still held at the end (a gripper within 3 cm of it); (b) at any time during the trial the cable's end was pulled past the 35 cm line (5 cm past the red line; checked on video); (c) any part of the pulled-out cable lies more than 2 cm sideways from the cable line x 30 (the end dragged off the ruler, a loop or kink out of line) or more than 1.5 cm above the table (the end held up in the air); (d) less than 5 cm of the cable is still inside the channel. Otherwise: reading within 1 cm of 30 cm (29-31 cm) = 1.0 (success, must hold 1 s); within 3 cm = 0.6; within 5 cm = 0.3; further off = 0. Score 0 if the channel or ruler is moved.

tasks.title: Pull a reject bin from the middle of a gravity flow lane without letting the next bin run down
tasks.instruction: Put the red-tagged bin in the reject tote. Until it is in the tote, the next bin up the lane must not move more than 2 cm. At the end, the other three bins must be down against the front stop and each other, with nothing holding them.
tasks.context: Stockers and order fillers (O*NET 53-7065.00; about 2.8 million US jobs, BLS) pick from carton-flow racks and pull out stock put on quality hold, which can be any bin in a lane. A carton-flow lane has no motor: it is a bed of free-running wheels sloped down to a front stop, so gravity brings each bin forward when the one ahead is taken. When a bin is lifted out of the middle, the bins behind it start rolling at once; they can catch under the lifted bin or the hand and run into the bin ahead. A stocker holds the next bin with the other hand until the reject is out, then lets it roll down so the lane closes up. The instruction gives the limits, not this way of meeting them.
tasks.scoring: What counts is how far the next bin up the lane moves from its start, in any direction, until the tagged bin is in the tote (middle inside the tote's walls, bottom below the rim); after that it is meant to roll down. The tagged bin is placed when it rests on the tote's floor (bottom within 1.5 cm of it, not on the rim), upright within 20 degrees (not propped on a wall), let go and still for 1 second. The lane is closed up when the other three bins sit flat on the wheels (within 10 degrees and 1 cm) in their order, the first within 1 cm of the stop and each of the others within 1 cm of the bin ahead (1 cm allows for the bins' molded draft), still and let go. Still means under 1 cm/s and 10 degrees/s. With the tagged bin placed: 1.0 if the next bin moved at most 2 cm and the lane is closed up for 1 second; 0.75 if it moved at most 2 cm but the lane is not closed up; 0.5 if it moved over 2 cm and at most 8 cm (it began to run and was caught); 0.25 if it moved over 8 cm (more than half of the 13.7 cm gap). Otherwise 0, including doing nothing. A lane bin (one of the three untagged bins) that falls (outside the lane, moving down faster than 0.5 m/s, not a set-down) makes the whole trial 0. A lane bin off the lane at the end (its middle outside the guide rails or past either end) or tipped past 30 degrees (gone over, not rocking) also scores 0; one stood back on the wheels counts again. Why 2 cm: a hand closing on a bin's wall moves it about 1 cm, while a bin that starts to run passes 2 cm in under half a second. Any way of staying within 2 cm counts, including a very quick one-hand lift; holding the next bin doesn't depend on speed. In a real trial, tape a paper scale marked every 1 cm on the near guide rail beside the next bin and film from a side camera at table height; read the next bin's movement from the paused video, the end gaps with a ruler, and the tagged bin's seat and tilt from a photo.

tasks.title: Lock out an air conditioner at its pull-out disconnect
tasks.instruction: Lock out the air conditioner AC-1 at its pull-out disconnect, the grey box with the yellow AC-1 label: lift its cover and hold it up, pull out the black pull-out block by its grip, turn it upside down and push it back in so that OFF shows, lower the cover shut, then put the red padlock through the hole in the tab at the bottom of the box and snap it shut. Do not touch the AC-2 disconnect (white label).
tasks.context: HVAC mechanics and installers (SOC 49-9021) and general maintenance and repair workers (49-9071) open the pull-out disconnect beside an outdoor air-conditioning unit at the start of nearly every service call: cleaning coils, replacing a capacitor or contactor, fixing a fan motor. They pull the block, reinsert it in its OFF position and padlock the cover so the unit cannot be re-energised while their hands are inside it. Pulling the wrong unit's disconnect, putting the block back ON, or leaving the cover unlocked defeats it.
tasks.scoring: Score 0 if, at any time, AC-2's cover opens more than 5 degrees or its pull-out moves more than 4 mm or turns more than 8 degrees, or if AC-1's pull-out, once pulled, is pushed back in ON (its blades more than 3 mm into the live clips). Otherwise the score is set by the state at the end: 0.25 if AC-1's pull-out is out of its live clips; 0.5 if it is back in the box turned over (OFF reads upright), seated within 3 mm; 0.75 if, in addition, AC-1's cover is shut (within 4 degrees); 1.0 if, in addition, the padlock is shut (latched) through the tab's hole and the after-release check passes. After-release check, done once both grippers have been at least 6 cm from the padlock and the cover's bottom edge for 2 s: hook a spring scale under the cover's bottom edge and pull it outward and up, square to the cover, with 20 N for 2 s. Pass if the cover opens less than 10 degrees (its bottom edge moves out less than 3 cm), the shackle is still through the hole and the pull-out still OFF; if not, the score is 0.75.

tasks.title: Release a push-fit fitting and pull the pipe out
tasks.instruction: Press the orange release collet on the brass fitting in and hold it there while you pull the copper pipe out of the fitting, then lay the pipe down flat on the table.
tasks.context: Plumbers and heating technicians (O*NET 47-2152.00, 49-9021.00) take pipes out of push-fit fittings when re-routing or replacing a section: the fitting's grab ring bites the pipe, so the release collet has to be pressed in and held while the pipe is pulled out. One hand holds the collet, the other pulls.
tasks.scoring: Measured with a ruler. 0 if the fitting was at any point moved more than 5 mm. 1.0 if the pipe, after being pulled out, lies flat on the table (axis level within 10 degrees, resting on the table) with every point at least 4 cm from the coupling's mouth, and is still for 1 s; 0.75 if, after the collet was pressed, the pipe's end came at least 5 mm out of the mouth (pulled 3 cm); 0.5 if, after the collet was pressed, the pipe was pulled 5 mm; 0.25 if the collet was pressed 2.5 mm; else 0.

tasks.title: Land a ferruled wire in the named push-in terminal
tasks.instruction: Land the blue ferruled wire in terminal X1:4, the blue terminal, upper entry. Push the ferrule straight into the entry until the collar stops, then let go.
tasks.context: Landing control wires on DIN-rail terminal blocks is routine daily work for electricians (SOC 47-2111) and control-panel builders and wirers (51-2028): panels hold rows of identical push-in terminals told apart only by printed markers, and each conductor is landed one at a time from the wiring diagram. A wire in the wrong terminal puts a conductor on the wrong circuit, and one not pushed home is not clamped and pulls out, so electricians tug every wire after landing it. Panel wiring is a large, repetitive share of the trade and a natural target for automation.
tasks.scoring: Score 0 if, at any time, the ferrule's tip goes more than 1 mm into any terminal entry other than X1:4's upper entry. Otherwise the score is the highest level reached: 0.25 if the wire's end is raised 1 cm or more above its place on the stand; 0.5 if the ferrule's tip is also inside X1:4's upper entry, 1 mm or more past the mouth; 0.75 if it is also pushed home: the collar within 0.8 mm of the entry's mouth and the clamp engaged on the ferrule (the clamping spring's leg deflected by the ferrule, checked by the tug below holding at least partly, or with a 2.5 mm screwdriver test in the operating slot); 1.0 if the after-release check also passes. Dropping the wire is not penalised by itself. After-release check, once both grippers have been at least 6 cm from the wire end for 1 s (or at the end of the run): mark the insulation with a pen at the entry's mouth, then pull the wire end straight back out along the entry's axis with a spring scale, raising the pull to 50 N over 0.5 s and holding it for 1.5 s. It passes if the mark moves out less than 1.5 mm. If it fails, the score is 0.75 (or 0.5 if the collar was never home). Distances are read with a rule, or from a close-up photo with a scale in view.

tasks.title: Push two reject cartons off a moving line onto the reject table, leaving the good ones on it
tasks.instruction: The two red cartons on the moving line are rejects. Push each one off the line onto the grey reject table behind the line before it reaches the tunnel, and leave the brown cartons on the line.
tasks.context: Where a packing line has no automatic diverter, a carton that fails a check (weight, seal, label) is pushed off the running conveyor onto a reject table by the operator beside it, without stopping the line and without disturbing the good cartons riding just in front of and behind it. The cartons are too wide to pick in one hand, so the reject has to be pushed sideways while it moves. Done by: packing-line operators and line-side cobots.
tasks.scoring: At the end of the trial, with what a per-step monitor recorded over the whole trial: +0.5 for each red carton placed on the reject table: its bottom within 1 cm of the table's top (any face down), its whole footprint on the table (past its near edge, inside its fence), still (under 1 cm/s), no part of either gripper within 4 cm of it plus however far that gripper's fingers are open, and at every control step its centre was over its carrier's footprint or over the reject table's side of the line (from the carriers' far edge to the fence, along the table) with its bottom between 1 cm below the reject table's top and 1 cm above the carriers' tops: pushed straight across, never lifted, never on the station table or the floor. 0 for a red carton anywhere else (on its carrier or in the tunnel, on the station table, on the floor, overhanging the reject table's edge, held or pressed by a gripper, still sliding) or that left that route at any moment, even if later pushed onto the reject table. -0.5 for each brown carton not standing upright on its own carrier (its centre outside the carrier's 14 x 12 cm footprint, or more than 1 cm off the height it rides at) at the end or at any control step during the trial: knocked off or over and put back still counts. The total is never below 0. 1.0 when both red cartons are placed and both brown cartons stood on their carriers all trial (the trial then ends with success once this has held for 1 s); 0.5 for one red carton placed. Pushing every carton onto the table, or sweeping the whole line off, scores 0.

tasks.title: Lock the spring tongs and put them away in the cutlery tray
tasks.instruction: Put the tongs away in the cutlery tray, locked shut.
tasks.context: Putting kitchen utensils away after washing up is an everyday home chore. People lock spring tongs shut before storing them: unlocked, they spring open in the drawer, take up the space of several utensils and snag the drawer when it is shut. Open, these tongs are also wider than the tray's long slot, so they have to be held shut while the pull tab is pulled to lock them.
tasks.scoring: Per trial, judged on the tongs once the robot has let go (no gripper or finger within 5 mm of them) and they have stopped moving. Locked: the tab is out at least 7 mm and both arms are within 0.03 rad of shut (heads under about 15 mm apart). In the long compartment: no part of the tongs is outside its walls (1 mm allowed for contact), none is above its rim, and the tongs' lowest point is within 3 mm of its floor. Score 1.0: locked and in the long compartment, held for 2 s. Score 0.5: locked, let go and still anywhere else on the counter or tray. Score 0.25: in the long compartment but not locked (squeezed in and let go, so they spring open against its walls). Score 0: anything else, including open tongs lying across the tray, tongs off the table, tongs still held, or tongs still moving.

tasks.title: Fit a blanking panel at U6 of a server rack
tasks.instruction: Fit the blanking panel at U6.
tasks.context: Closing a rack's empty units with blanking panels is standard data-centre practice (else hot exhaust flows back into the cold aisle), and fitting equipment at the units a rack elevation names is a basic step in building one out. Each unit has three identical square holes, so a panel fitted one hole off straddles two units: a common mistake. The robot must find U6 on the posts, line both clips of a 48 cm panel up with its middle holes, push it home and let go.
tasks.scoring: Judged at the end of the trial from a front photo of the rack and the video. The panel is at U6 (the 6th unit from the bottom) when its top and bottom edges are within 3 mm of U6's unit lines. 1.0 (success, ends the trial): at U6, both ends pushed home against the posts (a 2 mm shim will not fit behind), and the robot has let go for the last 1 s. 0.5: at U6 and pushed home but still held by the robot; or at U6 with only one end pushed home. 0: anything else, including another unit and one hole off (the panel straddling two units).

tasks.title: Slide a linear-guide carriage onto its rail past a spring plunger
tasks.instruction: Pick up the blue carriage by its post, fit it onto the open end of the grey rail, and push it along the rail past the orange plunger until it touches the end stop. Then let go and keep both fingers at least 3 cm from the post.
tasks.context: Linear guide carriages on robot gantries, 3D printers and wafer handlers are slid onto their rails by hand during assembly. A ball-plunger detent marks the seated position, and a carriage left short of it can drift. The task tests a part that can only go on from the open end (undercut lips, 1 mm clearances), a push through a spring detent that resists, and a clean release. The score is read from the final state only, so a carriage that is lifted off again scores 0.
tasks.scoring: Computed from the final state only, nothing is remembered. 1.0 if at the end the carriage is on the rail (guide lips under the rail head, level within 3 degrees, lateral offset 3 mm or less), wholly past the plunger with the plunger back up behind it, its front face within 3 mm of the end stop, and released (both fingers at least 90% open and at least 3 cm from the post) and still (moving less than 1 mm) for the last 1 s. 0.5 if it is on the rail at the end but not all of that holds (short of the plunger, held, or moving). 0 if it is not on the rail at the end, whatever happened earlier.

tasks.title: Slide a carriage onto a linear rail until it clicks
tasks.instruction: Slide the blue carriage onto the open end of the grey rail and push it along the rail until it clicks past the plunger and stops against the orange end stop.
tasks.context: Electromechanical and machine assemblers (O*NET 51-2023.00, 51-2031.00) fit carriages onto the linear guides of gantries, linear actuators and 3D printers: the carriage must be lined up with a close-fitting profile, kept square over a 10 cm slide, and pushed through a detent.
tasks.scoring: Measured at the end with a ruler. 0 if the rail was at any point moved more than 3 cm or turned more than 15 degrees. Otherwise, by where the carriage is at the end: 1.0 if it is on the rail (within 2 mm of its centreline and 1.5 mm of its seated height, square to it within 5 degrees) between the plunger and the end stop (its front within 0.5 mm of the stop, its rear past the plunger, which has sprung back out) and still (moving less than 1 mm over 1 s); 0.75 if it is on the rail with its centre at least 6 cm from the rail's open end; 0.5 if it is on the rail with at least 1 cm of it over the rail; 0.25 if it was lifted 3 cm at some point; else 0.

tasks.title: Cut a DIN rail to length on a powered rail cutter
tasks.instruction: Cut a 250 mm length off the right end of the rail with the rail cutter.
tasks.context: Electricians and panel assemblers cut DIN rail to length for every control panel they build: set the rail at the mark on the cutter's scale, clamp it, press the cut button. A rail cut short is scrap.
tasks.scoring: The cut is the blade's first stroke (it runs only with the clamp shut), made at the bottom of the stroke; only it counts. 1.0: the rail in the die, its right end 250 mm past the blade within 1 mm, and it moved under 0.5 mm along the cutter during the stroke. 0.5: otherwise, cut in the die within 5 mm of 250 mm. 0.25: otherwise, no such cut, but before the cut the rail lay in the die with its end within 5 mm of 250 mm for 1 s without a break. 0 otherwise.

tasks.title: Refit a delta robot's sprung rod pair: spread it with both arms and clip its four cups onto the ball studs
tasks.instruction: Take the black rod pair from the tray, clip its four cups onto the arm's and the platform's balls, then let go.
tasks.context: Robot upkeep. Light delta pickers and delta 3D printers hang each arm's rod pair on ball studs by two springs, so a crash pops it off and the machine stops until someone refits it by hand. Board tasks fit one rigid link on a pin or spread a circlip with pliers; here two arms open one free sprung part and its own springs capture it on four balls.
tasks.scoring: Judged over the whole run from a top camera and a side camera with a mm scale behind the pair. Cup on: its socket centre within 2.5 mm of a ball centre (photo: ball inside the cup; tape: 81 mm over the two housings at that end, +-2.5 mm). Spread: facing sockets 78 mm or more apart while every part of the pair is 4 cm or more above the table. Dropped: any part of the pair under 1 cm above the table, or moving faster than 0.6 m/s. Overstretched: facing sockets 92 mm or more apart. Released: at the end both grippers are 3 cm or more from the pair and it has moved under 1 cm/s for 1 s. Score, first row that fits: dropped or overstretched at any time, 0; released with 4 cups on, 1.0; 3 cups, 0.75; 2 cups, 0.5; 1 cup, 0.25; spread at some time (then held, put back or left resting uncaptured), 0.25; otherwise 0. Either end may go on either ball pair, in any order.

tasks.title: Refit a gas burner after cleaning: turn the head until its slot drops round the igniter, then seat the cap
tasks.instruction: Put the burner head back on its base so it sits flat round the igniter, then put the cap on it, centred.
tasks.context: Anyone who cooks on gas lifts the burner heads and caps off to wipe up spills, then puts them back. The head only sits flat with its slot round the igniter; left riding on it, or with the cap off centre, the burner clicks, lights unevenly or burns yellow. Nothing locks: the head must go down already turned, by sight, and the cap nests on it.
tasks.scoring: From poses (top photo, ruler, straightedge); seat = flange top. Head seated: tilt under 2 deg, lowest point within 1.5 mm of the seat, axis within 3.5 mm of the burner axis, slot centre line within 12 deg of the igniter (igniter in the slot). Cap seated: right way up, tilt under 3 deg, axis within 4 mm of the burner axis, lowest point 18 to 21.5 mm above the seat (on the head's rim). Whole-run latch D: head or cap ever faster than 0.8 m/s (dropped about 3 cm or more, or thrown). The end score is 0 unless both grippers are 3 cm clear of both parts and both parts have been at rest (under 1 cm/s) for 1 s, neither more than 1 cm above every surface. Then 1.0: head and cap seated, no D. 0.5: head seated, cap not (on the drainer, on the lip, tilted, upside down), no D. 0.25: head seated with D. 0: anything else, including a head riding the igniter or off the base.

tasks.title: Refit a car headrest at its lowest notch: both posts into their sleeves, then hold the release button and push it down
tasks.instruction: Put the headrest back into the seat, locked at its lowest position, then let go of it.
tasks.context: Fitting headrests into seat backs is a station on every car-seat and vehicle assembly line, and seats are refitted after repairs and recalls: it is the kind of fit-and-lock operation done all shift by team assemblers (BLS May 2024: 1,457,800 miscellaneous assemblers and fabricators, which include team assemblers). Both posts must go into both sleeves at once. The lock works the common way: a sprung pawl clicks into each notch and stops the headrest going down unless the release button is held in (raising is free). So one hand holds the button while the other lowers the headrest, then lets the button out so the pawl drops into the lowest notch.
tasks.scoring: Measured in the seat's frame. 0 if at any time the headrest leaves the table (any corner of it more than 2 cm below the table top); is dropped (its centre falling faster than 0.5 m/s, a free fall of about 1.3 cm, while every part of both grippers is at least 2 cm from it; setting it down gently is fine); is forced more than 4 mm into the seat; or a post is forced past the pawl (more than 1.5 mm into it, or carried 1.5 mm past a notch's flat face between two control steps with the button out at both). Otherwise the stage at the end: 0.25 both post tips at least 20 mm down their sleeves (axes within 9 mm of the sleeves' axes); 0.5 the pawl engaged in a notch (button out, the pawl within 1.5 mm of its rest stop, the right post's tips within 2.5 mm of that notch's depth: 50, 65, 80 or 95 mm), posts within 6 degrees of the sleeves' axes; 0.75 locked at the lowest position: the pawl engaged in the lowest notch (tips 95 +/- 2.5 mm down) and the posts within 3 degrees of the sleeves' axes; 1.0 (success, held 1 s): locked at the lowest position, every part of both grippers at least 2 cm from the headrest, the headrest still (under 1 cm/s and 0.1 rad/s) and the lock still. Doing nothing or refusing scores 0.

tasks.title: Refit a loaded drawer on its roller slides, carried in above riding height so the rear hooks clear, then pull-test it
tasks.instruction: Put the drawer back into the cabinet on its slides and close it. Then pull it open again by about 5 cm and leave it there.
tasks.context: Most people have taken a drawer out of a chest or desk: to get back something that fell behind it, to clean it, to lighten the chest before moving it, or because it came off its runners. Refitting it on roller slides is where it goes wrong. A hook under the rear of each drawer runner must pass over the roller at the front of each cabinet rail, so the loaded drawer is carried in level, slightly above where it will ride, until the hooks are past the rollers, then set down. Pushed in low, it slides along the cabinet floor under the slides and still closes flush; only a pull shows it: on its slides the drawer runs out level and stops at its hooks, under them it sits 54 mm lower and drags out with no stop. Unlike removing a drawer by holding its two slide releases pressed, or lifting a drawer out past its anti-pull-out stop, this tests engaging a hidden catch by controlling the height of a loaded drawer; unlike stowing a drawer that already rides on its rails, the slides start disengaged.
tasks.scoring: Judged from the video and a photo of the end with a ruler. On its slides means: the drawer bottom 66 +/- 4 mm above the table (both runners riding on the rails, measured at the front panel), level within 2.5 degrees, square to the cabinet within 3 degrees and centred within 12 mm, and open no more than 78 mm (it stops at 75 mm when the hooks meet the rollers). Closed means the front panel within 5 mm of the cabinet face. Hands off means both grippers at least 2 cm from the drawer (handle included) and the box. Score 0 if the box ever leaves the drawer or the drawer falls off the table. Otherwise 1.0 if, after the drawer was closed on its slides with hands off for 1 s, it is now on its slides, open 30 to 80 mm, the box inside, hands off (the trial ends as a success once this has held for 1 s); 0.5 if it was closed on its slides with hands off for 1 s and is still on its slides; 0.25 if it is on its slides; else 0. The state at the end of the episode is scored.

tasks.title: Reload a long-arm stapler and staple two sheets together
