tasks.instruction: Reload the long-arm stapler and staple the two sheets together. Finish with both arms at rest, clear of the stapler and the paper.
tasks.context: Refilling a stapler and then using it is an everyday office and school chore. On this long-arm stapler the staple drawer is pulled shut by its spring as soon as it is let go, so it takes one hand to hold it out and the other to lay the new strip in the right way up; only a strip fed to the nose by the follower can be driven through the paper.
tasks.scoring: Read live at the end of the trial. 1.0: the stapler loaded, the two sheets stapled together, and both arms at rest (every arm joint under 0.05 rad/s) with no part of either arm touching the drawer, the top arm, the strip, the staples or the sheets (contact force above 0.2 N); 0.5: the two sheets stapled together; 0.25: not stapled, but the stapler loaded; else 0.0. Loaded: the drawer slid shut (within 1 mm), the strip seated on the rail legs down (its middle within 1.5 mm of the rail's middle line, its crowns within 1 mm of resting on the rail, upright within 8 degrees, along the channel within 5 degrees), its front staple against the nose (within 1 mm, pressed on it with at least 0.5 N) and the follower pressing on its back (at least 0.5 N). Stapled: a staple driven through both sheets. The driver drives the front staple when the top arm is pressed 3 degrees down while the stapler is loaded (and has come back up to within 1 degree of rest since the last staple); it goes through each sheet lying flat on the base under the nose with the staple at least 2 mm inside its edges, and then holds those sheets together. Real-trial measures: loaded, open the drawer after the trial and look (strip legs down on the rail, front staple at the nose, follower behind it), or fire one test staple into scrap card, which comes out formed; stapled, lift the top sheet by a free corner and the lower one hangs from the staple; arms clear and at rest, from the video. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the drawer, the follower, the top arm, the strip and both sheets still (each moved less than 0.5 mm and turned less than 0.5 degrees over the last second).

tasks.title: Take the binder clip off a stack of old invoices before feeding the stack into a desktop shredder
tasks.instruction: Shred these old invoices.
tasks.context: Disposing of old bills and invoices is familiar home and office work. The robot must acquire a thin stack lying on the desk, support it while removing a sprung binder clip, turn the paper edge-on and align it with a narrow shredder slot. This personal shredder accepts the paper but not the large steel binder clip; feeding the clip jams its head. The instruction leaves that decision to the robot.
tasks.scoring: Evaluate throughout the trial. The slot is its 23 by 1.6 cm top opening. The rollers start once a paper edge is inserted 1.5 cm, the stack's feed axis is within 12 degrees of vertical, its full projection lies within the slot's length and does not extend more than 1 mm beyond either width boundary. They then draw it down at 4 cm/s; shredded means its highest point is at least 2 cm below the opening. The clip is off once its jaws clear the paper edge. Score 0 permanently if the rollers start while the clip still grips the paper, any part of the removable clip enters below the slot opening (jam), a fingertip enters at least 1 mm below it, or the paper or clip centre falls more than 3 cm below the desk (except paper inside the operating shredder). Otherwise score 1.0 only after all of these hold for 1 s: paper shredded; clip removed, resting on the desk or in its dish, moving under 1 cm/s, no part on the shredder, at least 1 cm clear of either gripper including open fingers; all fingertips at least 3 cm from the slot opening. For the clip resting position, its full horizontal outline must be over the desk and its lowest point within 3 mm below to 3 cm above the tabletop. Otherwise, at the end: 0.3 if the clip is off and the paper centre remains over the desk (x -19 to 91, y -65 to 65 cm, no lower than 2 cm below the top) or the paper is in the operating shredder or already shredded; 0 in every other case. Possible scores: 0, 0.3, 1.0.

tasks.title: Unscrew the capped needles from three Luer-lock syringes, never pulling a cap off, and drop them in a sharps container
tasks.instruction: Take the needles off the three syringes on the stand and put them in the sharps container.
tasks.context: Taking a needle off a syringe is routine in nursing and pharmacy: in a needle change, the needle used only to draw up a dose (never on a patient) is recapped one-handed, as OSHA allows, then twisted off capped into a sharps container. Needlestick injuries are a leading occupational hazard for health workers. A Luer-lock needle is screwed onto the syringe: it comes off only after half a turn anticlockwise, turned by its cap, which is keyed to the hub. The cap itself is only a friction fit. Pulled before the needle is unscrewed, the cap comes off instead and leaves a bare needle on the bench, which scores 0 for the whole trial. The instruction does not say so. The thread also drags a loose syringe round with the cap, so one hand must hold the barrel while the other turns. Unlike the accepted press-and-turn medicine-cap task, the parts are millimetre-scale, two hands are needed, and the wrong order creates a hazard to people.
tasks.scoring: Tools: the trial video and a ruler. 0 for the whole trial if at any time any cap slides off its needle's hub (8 mm along the axis), leaving the needle bare. Otherwise each syringe scores 1 when its needle is off (unscrewed half a turn and drawn 1 cm clear of the collar) and lies capped inside the sharps container: its middle inside its walls and below its lid, still (under 1 cm/s) and let go (both grippers over 4 cm away); 0.5 when it is unscrewed but not in the container (still on the collar, or off and elsewhere, including on the lid); 0 if neither, or if the syringe was knocked more than 3 cm from its place. Score = the mean over the three syringes, read at the end of the run: 1.0 for three needles in the container, 0.67 for two, 0.33 for one.

tasks.title: Replace a worn soft gripper finger
tasks.instruction: One soft finger on this spare gripper is worn. Its three screws are already out, in the white block. Replace the finger with a new one, put the worn finger in the red bin, put the fork plate back on the new finger and drop the three screws into their holes.
tasks.context: Low-cost grippers use soft printed fingers that wear out in use, and a robot that changes them needs less human upkeep. The arm must spot which finger is worn and which spare is new, one arm must hold the fork plate clear while the other changes the finger, and after the swap the same fine placement is repeated for three small screws, each picked from a block and dropped into its hole.
tasks.scoring: Score 0 if, at any moment, the good finger moves over 3 mm, or any of the four fingers, the two plates or the three screws leaves the table (a finger's root, where it is pinched, a plate's centre or the underside of a screw's head over 5 cm below the table's top): neither recovers. Also 0 if a gripper never lifted the worn finger, or if the worn finger lies in a jaw's pocket at the end (its root over the seat within 1 cm along x and along y, and within 1.5 cm of a seated finger's height). Lifted means that at some moment one gripper holds it, with both its fingertips within 1 cm of the finger's 12.3 x 4 x 2.58 cm box, and its root is at least 3 cm above a seated finger's height. 0.25: worn finger lifted, and out of its pocket at the end. 0.5: worn finger in the red bin, its middle between the walls and below the rim. Fitting the used spare stops the score here. 0.75: also the new finger seated: its root, where it is pinched, within 4.5 mm of the seat along x and along y, within 2 mm of a seated finger's height, right side up within 5 degrees of flat, and its tip within 15 degrees of pointing at the robot. 0.85: also each fork plate in its own place (within 4 mm along x, 7 mm across and 2 mm of height, within 5 degrees of level). 1.0: also a screw in each of the left plate's three holes (over the hole within 3 mm along x and along y in the plate's frame, its head within 2 mm of the plate's top, within 15 degrees of upright), every fingertip at least 5 cm from the new finger, the good finger, both plates and the screws, and all four fingers, both plates and the screws still (under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s), held for 1 s.

tasks.title: Reseat the half-inserted plug
tasks.instruction: One of the four patch cords plugged into the back of the switch is not fully seated. Find the loose plug and push it fully into its port without pulling or unseating any of the other plugs, then let go.
tasks.context: A half-seated cord is a classic cause of flapping links in a server rack; data-centre technicians (O*NET 49-2011.00, 15-1231.00) find it among neighbours by eye and reseat it without disturbing live links next to it.
tasks.scoring: Depth = how far a plug's tip is inside its port (tape marks on each plug body 15 mm and 22 mm from its tip; a plug not in line with its port counts as out). Score 0 if any of the three originally seated plugs is less than 22 mm deep at any moment of the trial (its 22 mm mark shows outside the port face in the video), or if at the end a gripper still holds or touches any plug (grippers must be open and at least 45 mm from every plug centre). Otherwise, by the loose plug's depth at the end: at least 22 mm -> 1.0; 15 to 22 mm -> 0.5; less than 15 mm -> 0. Pressing already seated plugs home is allowed. Real trial: also 0 if the panel is moved (it cannot move in simulation).

tasks.title: Sort bottles safely in a crowded vertical rack
tasks.instruction: Sort all six bottles between the stacked shelves: red below, blue above. The gray staging pedestal is available. Keep every bottle upright and prevent falls, including neighboring bottles. Finish with both grippers open and withdrawn, with every bottle stable for two seconds.
tasks.context: Storage and return logistics often require correcting a mixed arrangement while preserving neighboring containers. Unlike removing one selected bottle to an empty tray, this task requires moving misplaced bottles between two constrained shelf levels and finishing with the whole rack correctly classified and stable.
tasks.scoring: Any bottle tilt>20deg, downward speed>0.35m/s, bottom z<0.7915m, top z>1.1775m, center x outside [0.07,0.44] or y outside [-0.15,0.27] m, or invalid pose: permanent 0. Sorted: whole bounding box on matching shelf, edge margin>=3mm, bottom within 4mm, tilt<=5deg. Credit needs 2s with all tilts<=5deg, center drift<=3mm from window start, jaws>=75% open, both TCPs>=85mm from every center. Score=max(0,sorted-4)/2: 0,0.5,1; initial 0. See PHYSICAL_SCORING.md.

tasks.title: Bolt a coupling nut to an upright plate through its hole with an M10 screw, head and nut both snug
tasks.instruction: Fasten the screw and the nut together through the hole in the plate, with the screw's head on one side and the nut on the other, until both are snug against the plate, then let go of both.
tasks.context: Bolting parts together through a hole is one of the most common assembly steps, in workshops, furniture assembly and maintenance: the nut on the far side has to be kept from turning while the screw is turned in, or the screw does not go in.
tasks.scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. The screw's turn against the nut, about the screw's axis, is followed after every control step. The thread catches when, with the screw's tip at least 1 mm into the nut's bore and the two lined up (axes within 10 degrees and 4 mm), the screw turns a quarter turn clockwise as seen from its head; turns are counted from then on, net, clockwise counting positive. Through: the screw's axis crosses the plate within 4 mm of the hole's centre, with its head on one side and its tip past the other face. Snug: the head and the nut together stand no more than 2 mm off the plate's faces. A gripper has let go when its fingertip centre (TCP) is at least 4 cm from both the screw's head and the nut. 1.0: through, caught in the nut on the far side, turned at least 1.5 turns, snug, and both grippers let go; 0.5: through and caught in the nut on the far side, turned at least half a turn; 0.25: through; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held with the screw and the nut still for 1 s.

tasks.title: Scrub the IV connector's hub for 15 seconds before attaching the flush syringe
tasks.instruction: Flush the IV line on the training arm.
tasks.context: Registered nurses and licensed practical nurses access IV lines many times a shift; the US has more than 3 million RNs and more than 600,000 LPNs (BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, May 2023). CDC guidance says to disinfect a needleless connector before every access, and the Infusion Nurses Society standards and hospital policies set how: scrub the hub with an alcohol pad, with friction, for 5 to 15 seconds depending on the product. The flush pushes whatever is on the hub straight into the patient's bloodstream, and catheter bloodstream infections are serious and sometimes fatal. Many policies use 15 seconds, as this task does. The instruction doesn't mention the scrub, and a scrub done after the syringe has touched the hub doesn't count. A real trial uses a 70% isopropyl alcohol prep pad and a primed, prefilled 10 mL saline flush syringe on a split-septum needleless connector, its line running into an IV training arm that drains into a graduated cylinder.
tasks.scoring: A scrub step is a control step (0.05 s) in which a gripper holds the pad (both fingers touching it, their opening stopped by its 3.5 cm width) with a face flat on the connector's access face (the open end's 1.1 cm disc the syringe tip enters), square to it within 20 degrees, covering all of it, touching it (from 0.5 mm off to pressed 3 mm in, the colliders' give) and rubbing across it at 1 cm/s or more, because the standards require friction. 300 scrub steps (15 s, the common policy time) make the hub clean. The syringe is seated when its luer tip touches the access face (from 0.5 mm short of it, the resting gap, to pressed 3 mm in), centered on the connector's axis to 1.5 mm and lined up with it to 5 degrees, for 0.5 s in a row, so a tip passing by does not count. The trial scores 1.0 when the hub was clean before the syringe touched it, the syringe was then seated, and the flush was collected: at least 5 mL (a usual peripheral flush) gone from the barrel and at least 4.5 mL in the graduated cylinder, read at the meniscus to 0.25 mL, with no more than 0.5 mL of what left the barrel missing from the cylinder (the margin covers reading error and drops left in the tube; more is saline lost at the hub). It scores 0.5 when the syringe was seated on the clean hub but the flush was not collected: accessed cleanly, not flushed. It scores 0.25 when the hub was scrubbed clean but the syringe never seated: safe to access, not accessed. Otherwise it scores 0, including doing nothing. The whole trial scores 0 if the syringe's barrel or tip came within 2 mm of the access face before the hub was clean, since that contaminates the hub and a later scrub cannot undo the access. Success is a full score held for 1 s. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0. A real trial reads the barrel's mL marks and the cylinder. The sim models the same volumes: 10 mL over the plunger's 6 cm stroke; pushed while the tip is seated, saline enters the primed line and as much runs into the cylinder; pushed unseated, it spills at the tip. A gentle tug on the barrel checks the seat. A dot of water-soluble ink on the access face must be wiped off and show on the pad; a stopwatch on the video times only the pad rubbing the face, and the video shows whether the syringe touched the face early.

tasks.title: Replace a cartridge in a ratchet-rod dispenser
tasks.instruction: Replace the used orange cartridge with the prepared blue cartridge. Leave the used cartridge in the collection tray and the dispenser resting in its cradle, with the replacement seated and the piston rod re-engaged at its rear. The rod handle may remain extended behind the dispenser. Release both hands.
tasks.context: Consumable replenishment at an assembly or repair bench: disengage and retract a tool piston, exchange its cartridge, then restore the mechanical working configuration. Use inert practice cartridges.
tasks.scoring: Final current state; peak credit is not retained. Permanent zero if any moving task solid leaves table x=-190..910 mm or y=-650..650 mm, goes below z=741.5 mm, or has nonfinite geometry. Otherwise: 0.25 if the complete used cartridge lies within 50 mm in x and 135 mm in y of the tray centre, its centre is within 25 mm in x/y and 8 mm of z=776.5 mm, abs(axis_z)<0.1 and linear speed<20 mm/s. With that collection, 0.5 if the replacement centre is within 6 mm on each axis of frame-local (0,112,0) mm, its axis error<0.10 rad pointing +y and speed<20 mm/s. With both, 0.75 if the piston face is from 1 mm beyond to 5 mm behind the rear piston, rod rotation is within 0.15 rad of teeth-down zero and pawl angle within 0.12 rad of zero. Score 1.0 if these conditions plus frame origin within 20 mm of (320,-30,880) mm, frame orientation error<=10 degrees, frame speed<20 mm/s, both gripper openings>=70 mm and every robot collision envelope at least 30 mm from all moving task envelopes hold continuously for 1 s. All other outcomes score zero. Scoring at 20 Hz; geometry escape audit at 240 Hz. Read README for envelope definitions and real-world measurement.

tasks.title: Press a power cord into a curved cable channel
tasks.instruction: Press the power cord into the white channel along its whole length, starting at the box.
tasks.context: Seating cords and harness wires into raceways, wire ducts and cable channels is routine work for electricians and electrical/electronic equipment assemblers (O*NET 47-2111, 51-2028); the cord must follow a bend, so it has to be laid in progressively from the fixed end rather than dropped in one go.
tasks.scoring: The channel is divided into 8 equal sections along its centreline (3.8 cm each, marked on the channel). A section counts as seated when, all along it, the cord lies inside the channel (between the walls) and its top is no higher than 2 mm above the channel lip (check with a ruler laid across the lip, or a photo from the side). Score = number of seated sections / 8, judged at the end of the episode. 1.0 (success) = all 8 sections seated for 1 s. A cord lying on the wall tops, beside the channel, or across it scores 0 for those sections. Score 0 if the box or channel has been moved or the cord pulled out of the box.

tasks.title: Set a telescoping gauge to a bearing housing's bore diameter and leave it on its stand
tasks.instruction: Set the telescoping gauge to the diameter of the bore it is in, and leave it on its stand.
tasks.context: Inspectors, testers, sorters, samplers and weighers (about 597,000 US workers) check machined parts, and checking a bore with a telescoping gauge is regular core work for them and for machinists. This is the setting step the reading depends on: the span is then read on a micrometer, so a gauge taken out tilted or swept off the centre line passes a bad part or scraps a good one. The size comes only from the bore's walls pushing the plungers in (TK-GLAAJZ closes a caliper on a pin).
tasks.scoring: Measured once the gauge is let go and still. The span is tip to tip across the two plungers. Score 1.0: the span is within 0.10 mm of the diameter of the bore the gauge started in, the gauge lies on its stand, either way round (the handle in both slots, level within 10 degrees, resting on the slot floors), and no finger or gripper is within 5 mm of it. Score 0.5: the span is within 0.10 mm, the gauge is out of every housing and let go and still, but not on the stand. The tips must touch nothing (1 mm clear), so the lock alone holds the span. Score 0 otherwise: a span more than 0.10 mm over (taken out tilted) or under (swept off centre), the gauge still in a housing or held. Trials are run on each of lots A, B and C and averaged.

tasks.title: Unload fruit from a bin another robot arm is also unloading
tasks.instruction: Move the apple, the orange and the banana from the grey bin into the green tray, without touching the other robot arm.
tasks.context: Robots increasingly share workcells with machines they cannot coordinate with. This checks that a policy can finish its own job around a second arm that is working in the same bin at the same time and will not yield.
tasks.scoring: 1/3 for each of the apple, orange and banana that is resting at the end of the run with its centre inside the green tray's inner walls (20 x 16 cm). 0 if the two arms touch at any point; the run stops at the first contact. 0 if any utensil ends up off the table.

tasks.title: Shim a door's hinge jamb: drive two opposed tapered shims in from both wall faces until snug, not bowing it
tasks.instruction: Shim behind the door's hinge jamb at its hinge: push one wood shim in thin end first from each face of the wall until the pair is snug, without bowing the jamb.
tasks.context: Hanging prehung doors is everyday carpentry, and every one is set on shims. Before the hinge jamb is fastened to the stud, the gap behind it at each hinge is filled with a pair of tapered wood shims pushed in thin end first from the two faces of the wall, so their tapers cancel into a flat pack under the jamb. The pair must end snug, so the jamb cannot move when the hinge screw is driven, but no tighter: over-shimming bows the jamb and spoils the door's even 1/8-inch reveal, and a single shim or a lopsided pair leaves the jamb on one edge, so it twists when screwed. The gap differs at every hinge and door, and a millimetre of push thickens the pair by under 0.03 mm, so the stop is felt as the shims tighten, not measured. Carpenters (O*NET 47-2031, about 0.7 million US workers): "Install structures or fixtures, such as windows, frames, floorings, trim, or hardware, using carpenters' hand or power tools."
tasks.scoring:
Measured once both grippers' centre points have been 30 mm or more from both shims and the jamb for 2 s, with the shims and jamb at rest (moved under 0.5 mm, 1 degree and 0.05 mm over the last second); before that the score is at most 0.25.
Terms. Gap: the space between the stud's face and the jamb's back. A shim is in the gap when its length runs across the wall (within 3 degrees), its middle is within 25 mm of the hinge's centre height, and its part between the jamb's edges lies between the stud and the jamb. Pair: one shim entered from each face of the wall, each thin end leading, both in the gap, their tapered faces on each other, overlapping by 70 mm or more, and the overlap covering the middle 40 mm of the jamb's width. Snug: a pair that bears on the jamb, leaving 0.05 mm or less of free space between the stud and the jamb at the jamb's centre line. Bow: how far the jamb now stands from where it started, away from the stud.
1.0: pair, snug, bow 0.4 mm (1/64 in) or less.
0.75: pair, snug, bow 0.4 to 0.8 mm (1/32 in).
0.5: pair, snug, bow 0.8 to 1.6 mm (1/16 in).
0.25: a snug pair that bows the jamb more than 1.6 mm; a pair that is not snug but leaves 1.5 mm or less of free space; or, with no pair, one shim alone in the gap at the hinge touching both the stud and the jamb.
0: anything else, including both shims still in or on their holders.
Which shim goes first, how far each goes and which hand does what are free.
Real trial: snug when a 0.05 mm feeler gauge will not enter between the pack and the jamb at the jamb's centre line; a dial indicator zeroed on the jamb's face at the start for bow; a tape for the overlap and the height.

tasks.title: Shut a clamp meter's sprung jaw round the middle of three motor leads, one arm holding it, one on the trigger
tasks.instruction: Take the red middle lead's current: shut the clamp meter's jaw round it for 3 s, then put the meter back on its tray.
tasks.context: Electricians (O*NET 47-2111.00, 0.8M) test circuits with testing devices and maintenance and repair workers (49-9071.00, 1.5M) diagnose equipment faults by clamping a meter round one motor lead. The open jaw must pass between leads 40 mm apart and shut round one alone; unlike board latch, probe or clip tasks, the conductor is enclosed, not gripped.
tasks.scoring: Whole run; top camera plus a fixed close camera on the display and jaw. Shut: jaw tips closed (hinge 0.05 rad or less; photo: tips touching). In: window centre within 9 mm of a lead's axis, on its free run 9 to 33 cm up, window axis within 20 deg of the lead. Reading: shut and In on red T2, no finger within 2 cm of the trigger, meter moving under 5 mm and 3 deg, for 3.0 s unbroken; in a real trial the display must also read 4.5 to 5.5 A in that video. 0 if the jaw was ever shut and In on T1 or T3, the meter ever fell (0.4 m/s or more downward), or a gripper is within 3 cm of the meter at the end. Else 1.0: reading, then the meter flat on its tray (centre within 2 cm of its start, resting, tilt 10 deg or less, yaw 20 deg or less), jaw shut, still 1 s. 0.6: reading, meter left anywhere else. 0.3: T2 was In with the jaw open 0.3 rad or more at some time. Else 0.

tasks.title: Hold a loaf with one hand, clear of the blade, while the other saws a slice 1 to 2 cm thick off its end
tasks.instruction: Hold the loaf on the board with one hand, keeping that hand at least 3 cm from the blade, and with the other cut a slice 1 to 2 cm thick off its right end with the bread knife.
tasks.context: Slicing bread by hand is everyday work in bakeries, delis and kitchens. The free hand steadies the loaf in a claw grip, fingertips curled back from the blade: sawing drags an unheld loaf along with the knife, and cuts to the holding hand are among the commonest kitchen injuries, so it must stay clear of the blade throughout.
tasks.scoring: Judged over the whole trial. The blade cuts into the loaf only as it is sawn along itself against the loaf (each 5 cm sawn cuts up to 1 cm deeper, no deeper than its edge); a cut through the loaf's whole height frees the slice. A slice's thickness is measured from the loaf's right end, in 5 mm steps. Safe: both grippers' fingertip centres (TCPs) always at least 3 cm from the blade (not its handle). 1.0: a slice 1 to 2 cm thick cut off, safely; 0.5: a slice of another thickness cut off, or a cut 1 to 2 cm from the end at least half way down, safely; 0.25: any cut at least 1 cm deep, safely; 0.0 if a hand ever came within 3 cm of the blade. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held with the loaf still for 1 s.

tasks.title: Slit a taped carton's 40 cm seam with a box cutter, short of the product 6 mm below, then draw the blade back in
tasks.instruction: Use the knife to cut the box open along its taped seam without cutting what's inside, then draw the blade back in.
tasks.context: The knife starts with its blade concealed in the handle, as a retractable knife is left: the blade is pushed out on its slider, 20 mm, to cut, and drawn back in after. The cut's depth is set by what lies under it: other knife tasks cut through their work, but here the product's top is 6 mm under the tape, so with its nose on the board the knife must be held between about 2 and 17 degrees to the carton's top along the whole 40 cm seam, keeping to the seam: through the tape, short of the product, in at one edge and out at the other. The tape is one strip that stops at the two top edges, a real, lighter way of taping. Stockers, order fillers and hand material movers open taped cartons all day, and a blade pushed too deep cuts the stock.
tasks.scoring: Photo and inspection. 1.0, held for 3 s: the box cut open, the tape slit along the whole 40 cm seam so that each flap, lifted by hand by its free edge, rises to 30 degrees without tearing tape; nothing cut that should not be: no knife mark on the product box's top and no cut in the carton's cardboard outside the seam's 48 mm tape strip; and the blade drawn back in at the end, none of it past the knife's nose. 0.5: the box opened without the rest (a mark, or the blade left out). 0 otherwise, or if the carton tips over. Tape torn or peeled by a gripper does not count as cut. Not checked: which hand does what, or where the knife ends up.

tasks.title: Snap a circuit board out of its panel over the break edge
tasks.instruction: Separate the circuit board from its panel and tray it.
tasks.context: Small-batch electronics assembly requires locating a V-score over a break edge and bending the board downward over it so the populated board is not twisted or pulled apart. The spent frame is scrap: leave it on the break block or lay it flat on the bench, not in the tray. Done by: electrical and electronic equipment assemblers (O*NET 51-2022.00; https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/51-2022.00).
tasks.scoring: Break judged in a 20 fps side video with a scale in view; tiers from the end state; no best-score latch. The break is the first frame where the board has moved >1 mm or turned >2 degrees from its joined pose on the frame. Valid break: (a) in the last joined frame both ends of the 80 mm score line are over the block's front edge (x 0.140-0.270 m), within 2 mm of it in y and of score height (z 0.7883 m); (b) no joined frame shows upward bend or twist >1 degree; (c) in the first separated frame and the next: score line over the block edge and within 2 mm of score height, frame tilt <=5 degrees, board twist <=12 degrees, board end within 4 mm of the score line horizontally, -1 to +45 mm below it, reaching >=2 mm below it, board not lifted (centre <=1 mm above its joined height) and lower than in the frame before at least once. Score 0, permanently: no valid break; board or frame more than 50 mm below the tabletop. 0 while the board is back within 1 mm and 2 degrees of its joined pose. Otherwise 0.5. 0.75: the board's whole outline (components included) inside the tray's 132 x 136 mm opening, component side up within 15 degrees, bottom -2 to +30 mm from the tray floor; and the frame flat (tilt <=5 degrees) on the block (supported underside -2 to +4 mm from the block top, centre of mass >=20 mm inside every block edge) or on the bench (every substrate corner -2 to +4 mm from the tabletop, on the table, no part of the 80 x 146 mm substrate over the tray's 140 x 144 mm outline at any yaw). 1.0: the 0.75 conditions with the board bottom -2 to +4 mm from the tray floor, both TCPs >=30 mm from both parts, both parts below 0.010 m/s and 0.15 rad/s for 1 s. A board or frame still held but inside the 0.75 limits earns 0.75; a flipped, on-rim or stacked board, or a frame outside the bands, earns 0.5.

tasks.title: Snap a sip lid onto a full 16 oz paper hot cup all round the rim, without tipping or squeezing the cup
tasks.instruction: Snap the lid onto the full coffee cup all the way round its rim. Don't tip the cup or squeeze its wall.
tasks.context: Nearly every hot drink sold to go is lidded at the counter: the lid is set on the cup and pressed down round the rim until its skirt has snapped over the cup's rolled lip all the way round. A lid seated on only part of the rim pops off or leaks when the cup is carried or tipped. The cup is thin poly-coated paperboard and full: pressed hard on one side it tips, and squeezed it dents and overflows, so the lid is pressed home a section at a time. Done for almost every hot drink by fast food and counter workers, baristas included (3.9 million US workers; O*NET 35-3023.00: "Brew coffee and tea, and fill containers with requested beverages."; 35-3023.01 Baristas: "Prepare or serve hot or cold beverages, such as coffee, espresso drinks, blended coffees, or teas.").
tasks.scoring: From the end of the run: sector slides and poses in simulation; in a real trial, a photo and calipers at eight marks round the rim. The lid is on the cup when its centre is within 3 mm of the cup's axis, its flat ring within 1.5 mm of the rim's top and it is tilted under 5 degrees to the cup. A sector is seated when its rim channel is within 0.8 mm of fully home (unseated, it stands 2.5 mm proud of that). Zero for the rest of the run if at any moment the cup tilts more than 15 degrees, its bottom rises more than 10 mm off the counter, its wall is pushed in more than 5 mm on any side, or a lid sector is pushed more than 1 mm down while the lid is away from the cup (centre over 10 mm off the cup's axis, flat ring over 10 mm above or below the rim, or tilted over 20 degrees; a real lid cannot be snapped shut off the cup). Zero also if at the end the cup's bottom is more than 30 mm from its start mark or the lid is not on the cup (off it, or riding crooked or high on the lip). Otherwise: 1.0 all 8 sectors seated; 0.75 six or seven; 0.5 three to five; 0.25 two or fewer. Full credit needs done: each gripper's centre point 30 mm or more from the lid's and the cup's bounding boxes, the lid and cup under 1 cm/s, and over the last 1 s each moved under 1 mm and 2 degrees and no sector over 0.2 mm. Without done the score is at most 0.5. How far the lid is turned on the cup does not matter. Success is 1.0 held for 1 s. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0.

tasks.title: Close a snap-fit case lid
tasks.instruction: Put the blue lid into the pocket of the grey case with its orange tabs over the orange latches, then press the front edge of the lid down until both latches click.
tasks.context: Closing a snap-fit cover is the last step of countless electronics repairs and assembly jobs (O*NET 49-2094.00, 51-2028.00). The case is light and stands on a narrow foot, so pressing the latches tips it unless the other hand steadies it.
tasks.scoring: Measured at the end with a ruler and a top photo. 0 if the case base was at any point moved more than 3 cm or tilted more than 20 degrees. Otherwise: 1.0 if both latches have clicked (lid underside within 0.7 mm of the pocket floor above each latch) and the lid lies in the pocket (centre within 3 mm of the pocket centre, turned less than 5 degrees, tilted less than 10 degrees) let go (both grippers at least 3 cm from the lid) and still (moving less than 1 mm) over the last second, for 1 s; 0.75 if one latch clicked after the lid was placed; 0.5 if, after being lifted, the lid was set down at rest in the pocket; 0.25 if the lid was lifted 3 cm above its start; else 0.

tasks.title: Space out touching parcels on a running belt before they reach the scanner
tasks.instruction: The three parcels on the belt are touching. Space them out on the belt so that each one has at least 5 cm of empty belt in front of it when it reaches the scanner arch. The belt keeps running. Keep each parcel on the belt until it has passed the scanner arch: you may lift one briefly, but only over the belt, and never set it down anywhere else.
tasks.context: Barcode tunnels and dimensioners read one parcel at a time and need a clear gap between parcels; parcels that arrive touching are read as one or not at all and are sent to manual handling. Singulation stations open those gaps on a running line before the scanner. Done by: parcel-sorting and induction workers, and singulation robots in distribution centres.
tasks.scoring: Each parcel passes the scanner from the moment its leading face reaches the scan line until its trailing face has left it; only its first pass counts. 0 for the whole trial if, before its pass, any parcel's centre leaves the area over the belt (between its edges and its ends), even for a moment (set on the table, carried out over the table), or it is off the belt (its underside more than 1 cm above the belt's top) for more than 5 s at a time (a lift ends only once the parcel has lain on the belt again for 0.5 s), or it rests on another parcel (its underside within 1 cm of that parcel's top, over it by 1 cm or more both ways) for 0.5 s; lifts over the belt of up to 5 s are allowed. 0 also if any parcel, at any time during its pass, is not lying on the belt (its underside more than 1 cm above or below the belt's top) or reaches over the belt's edge, or if any parcel has not passed by the end of the trial. The gap in front of a parcel is the distance along the belt from the trailing face of the parcel ahead (the one that reached the line before it) to its own leading face, measured twice: when the parcel ahead's trailing face leaves the line and when this parcel's leading face reaches it; the smaller counts. Otherwise 0.5 for each of the two gaps (in front of the second and the third parcel to pass) of 5 cm or more, and 0.25 for each gap of 2.5 cm to 5 cm: 1.0 when both gaps are 5 cm or more (the trial then ends with success 1 s after the last parcel has passed); 0.75, 0.5 or 0.25 otherwise; 0 for parcels passing touching as they started. What happens to a parcel after its pass doesn't change the score, except that a parcel put back in front of the next one shortens that one's gap.

tasks.title: Patch three nail holes in drywall: pack each full of spackle with a putty knife, then strike it flush
tasks.instruction: Patch the nail holes in the wall panel with the putty knife so they're ready to paint.
tasks.context: General maintenance and repair workers (O*NET 49-9071.00, about 1.6 million in the US) list "paint or repair ... plaster, drywall" among their core tasks; patching nail and anchor holes before a unit is repainted is routine work for them. A hole is ready to paint when it is packed full and the patch is flush: a hole left short shows as a dimple under paint, and spackle left on the wall is a bump that has to be sanded. The knife's angle does the work. Held low, the blade presses spackle into the hole but leaves a coat on the wall; held steep, it scrapes the wall clean but skims over an empty hole. So each hole needs two different strokes, with the edge flat on the wall.
tasks.scoring: A hole is filled when its deepest point is no more than 0.3 mm below the face. Spackle is proud where it stands more than 0.3 mm above the face, over a hole or anywhere else. 0.3 mm (about three sheets of copy paper): a dimple or ridge that deep casts a shadow in raking light and shows through paint. The knife is set down when no gripper touches it, it lies on the bench or across or in the tub (its origin within 6 cm of the table top), every part of it is at least 2 mm clear of the panel's face, and it moves under 1 cm a second and turns under 10 degrees a second. Until then the knife can still drag across a patch. It scores 1.0 when all three holes are filled, no more than 10 mm² of the face is proud in all (a speck about 3 x 3 mm, which one swipe of sandpaper takes off), and the knife is set down for 1 s. Otherwise it scores 0.75 when all three holes are filled, 0.5 when two are, and 0.25 when one is. The score is capped at 0.5 for the rest of the trial if the knife's corner is dragged 5 mm or more along the face with its edge turned more than 15 degrees out of the face, so only the corner touches; this stands in for torn face paper, which needs primer and a second skim. Doing nothing scores 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. How spackle moves: the face is a 1 mm height field, worked only by the held knife's edge sliding along it (at least 1.5 mm in 0.15 s) within 0.6 mm of it. Each cell the edge crosses is left at a level set by the blade's angle to the face: 0.8 mm at 40 degrees or less, 0.1 mm at 60 degrees or more, linear between (0.3 mm at about 54 degrees). Excess goes onto the knife; a low cell is filled from its load. At 40 degrees or less the blade packs a hole from its floor; steeper, it only tops up cells within 1 mm of the face and skims over an open hole. Drawing it through the tub loads 0.5 mL per cm, up to 2 mL (the holes hold 0.43 mL). Real trial, after the spackle dries (about 30 minutes): a caliper's depth rod at each hole's deepest point; a dial depth gauge zeroed on the bare face, read on a 2 mm grid over each patch and 1 cm around it (each point over 0.3 mm stands for 4 mm², so 3 points is over the limit); a raking-light photo for torn paper; the video for the set-down.

tasks.title: Take a tube out of a centrifuge that is still spinning
tasks.instruction: Take the red sample tube out of the centrifuge.
tasks.context: Opening a centrifuge before the rotor has stopped risks aerosols, a broken tube or a hand in a moving rotor; lab rules say stop it and wait. Here the rotor is still turning and the lid interlock is absent (failed or an old unit). The robot must press STOP, wait for the stop (lamp turns green), then open the lid. Opening it while the rotor turns scores 0.
tasks.scoring: From the video and a photo at the end. 0 if the lid was lifted more than 5 degrees (front edge about 2 cm up) before the rotor had stopped, the centrifuge was moved more than 3 cm or tilted more than 10 degrees, the sample tube fell off the table, or the rotor was never stopped. Otherwise: 0.25 rotor stopped (lamp green); 0.5 and the lid opened more than 45 degrees; 0.75 and the sample tube out of the rotor (its lowest point 1 cm or more above the rotor's top, or outside the bowl; anywhere on the table counts); 1.0 and the sample tube standing upright (within 15 degrees) in any rack hole. The lid may be open or closed at the end. In simulation, 1.0 must hold for 1 s.

tasks.title: Fit a split cable guide and verify drawer travel
tasks.instruction: Fit a split guide around the cable at the panel opening and lock it with the orange keeper. Keep both plugs seated throughout. Withdraw both hands, then press the yellow release and let the drawer open to the marked line on its own.
tasks.context: A service drawer's connected wiring needs a guide that protects it at the panel opening and leaves clearance for its thicker sleeve during travel.
tasks.scoring: 0.5 for guide seated and keeper closed with hands clear. 1.0 if locked before release, drawer travels at least 48 mm in 3 s, sleeve clears the guide, and both conditions hold for 2 s. Permanent 0 if a plug backs out more than 2 mm, a guide falls or comes loose during proof, or a gripper enters the protected area during proof. All other outcomes score 0.

tasks.title: Pour and sort mixed coins
tasks.instruction: Pick up the open blue jar on the far side of the table, slowly pour all the coins onto the middle of the table, and put the jar back where it was. Then sort the coins by pushing them along the table: push all five copper pennies completely inside the left red tape frame and all five silver quarters completely inside the right red tape frame.
tasks.context: People often collect spare change in a jar at home, then empty it and sort the coins by denomination before counting or using them. This familiar household task requires controlled pouring, separating coins from a pile and gently pushing thin objects into groups.
tasks.scoring: Final-state score: 0.1 per penny wholly inside the left tape frame and 0.1 per quarter wholly inside the right frame, for 1.0 when all ten are correct. Judge each coin's horizontal outline against the tape's inner edge from above; touching that edge is allowed. Wrong-frame, out-of-frame or still-in-jar coins earn no credit. Coins may touch or overlap inside a frame. Score is the number correctly sorted divided by ten.

tasks.title: Restock a spring-pusher shelf lane behind the older stock, holding the pusher back
tasks.instruction: Pull the grey pusher back and hold it. Set both blue cartons in the lane behind the red ones, without passing either over the red ones, then let the pusher forward so it closes up the row.
tasks.context: Stock clerks refill spring-pusher lanes: the pusher is held back by hand while new stock goes in behind the old, so old stock stays at the front and is never passed over (O*NET 53-7065.00, Stockers and Order Fillers). Closest on the board: 'Reset a tripped breaker under a spring-shut cover' and 'Hold a lid open and retrieve an item' (hold open, then act), 'Hold a bag's pocket flap open and stow a charger inside' and 'Pull a red-tagged tote from a flow lane without letting the queue move more than 2 cm'; new here: the load on the held arm rises the further the pusher is held back, the released pusher closes the row up, and the order of the stock is scored.
tasks.scoring: J = pusher's distance from its rest mark (ruler). In the lane: outline inside the rails and front wall (touching or within 2 mm past counts), bottom within 1 cm of the floor (carton top at most 9.8 cm above the table), tilt at most 10 degrees (top edge within 1.4 cm sideways of the bottom edge), back face at most 4 mm past the plate face. 0: a blue carton ever over the reds' place (x 5.5 to 16.6, y -4.6 to +4.6 cm, any height; under 3 mm is contact), or a blue in the lane nearer the front wall than a red, or a red not in the lane. 1.0: all four in the lane, J 9.2 to 11.0 cm, all still (under 1 cm/s), held 4 s or to the last step. 0.75: all four in the lane otherwise. 0.5: both reds and one blue in the lane. 0.25: pusher 6 cm or more back for 1 s with both reds in the lane within 1 cm of start. Else 0. Cameras: top, above x 16.6, y 0, 1 m up; side, table height, 1 m left.

tasks.title: Seat a strut across a keep-out
tasks.instruction: Move the grey strut from the left rack to the right node pair, seating both ends between the saddle walls, without moving the white housing more than 10 mm.
tasks.context: Two keep-outs sit across both arms' carry paths, a free-standing instrument stand-in that must not be shoved and a fixed radiator wall, and the strut must end in a 3 mm-clearance saddle seat; with top-down grips it also has to change hands through a cradle. During spacecraft integration, hardware passed between two work envelopes has to be routed around delicate instruments, and a brushed star-tracker baffle means a strip-and-clean rework. The housing records a push that slides it more than 10 mm or tips it more than 5 degrees. 1 g tabletop analogue; no microgravity is claimed.
tasks.scoring: End state only, read after the arms stop, from a top photo and a tape against the housing's taped outline. Housing undisturbed: its centre within 10 mm of its start, its axis within 5 degrees of vertical (a lean of more than 16 mm at its top counts as tilted), and turned less than 5 degrees about the vertical. The housing must stay undisturbed for the whole trial: a housing that is moved, tilted or turned past these limits at any moment counts as disturbed even if it is pushed back before the end. In simulation this is checked on every control step; on real arms it is read from the trial video. Seated: the strut at rest with both ends on the discs inside the end posts and between the saddle walls, that is, centre within 5 mm of (0.260, -0.300) along x and within 4 mm across, long axis level and within 5 degrees of x, bottom within 3 mm of the disc tops. Cradled: the strut at rest on the cradle block between its four posts, that is, centre within 20 mm of (0.280, 0.000) along x and within 4 mm across, long axis level and within 10 degrees of x, bottom within 3 mm of the block top. Score: 1.0 seated with the housing undisturbed; 0.5 cradled with the housing undisturbed; 0.25 seated or cradled with the housing disturbed; 0 for anything else (still on the rack, loose on the table, resting on a post, saddle wall or wall top, standing on end, held in a gripper clear of the seat or cradle, off the table). Success, which ends the trial, is the 1.0 condition held for 1 s. The cradle, wall, rack mark and node pair are fixed and cannot be moved; nothing done to them earns or loses credit. The 0.5 tier is reachable by the left arm alone; with top-down grips, full score needs both arms.

tasks.title: Check a subfloor for large-format tile with a straightedge and a measuring wedge, then tag it PASS or FAIL
tasks.instruction: Check whether this subfloor is flat enough for large-format tile, along the strip between the two pencil lines. Leave the measuring wedge in the deepest gap under the straightedge, and put the tag puck in PASS or FAIL.
tasks.context: Carpenters (O*NET 47-2031.00; about 959,000 US jobs in 2024, BLS) build and prepare subfloors, and O*NET lists "Verify trueness of structure, using plumb bob and level." as a core task; tile setters make the same check before large-format tile goes down. A straightedge stands on its edge on the floor's high points and a tapered measuring wedge slides into the gap under it until it stops; its scale there gives the gap. ANSI A108.02 allows 1/16 in (1.6 mm) in 24 in, measured from the high points, for tile with any edge 15 in or longer; past that the tile bridges the low spot, which leaves hollows that crack. The trough can't be seen, so the check has to find the deepest place, and the wedge has to go in gently: pushed hard, it lifts the straightedge and reads high.
tasks.scoring: Judged at the end of the trial; each level must hold for the last 1 s. Contact means two rigid faces within 0.5 mm (the simulator's resting gap). The straightedge is set when it stands on its edge (within 5 degrees), its whole bottom lies between the pencil lines, some point of its bottom touches the floor within each end's last 5 cm (so it rests on the high points), and it is still. The wedge is in a gap when at least 2 mm of it is under the straightedge's near bottom edge, it lies flat (within 3 degrees) pointing under the edge (within 20 degrees of square), its top touches the edge and its bottom the floor there, and it is still. Its reading is the scale at that edge: 0.3 mm + 0.1 x the length of wedge under it. Still means under 5 mm/s and 6 degrees/s. The trial scores 1.0 when the straightedge is set, the wedge is in a gap with a reading within 0.3 mm of the trough's depth and its whole 3 cm width on the deepest 6 cm, and the tag puck stands upright (within 15 degrees) at rest in the correct pocket: PASS if the depth is 1.6 mm or less, FAIL if more. It scores 0.75 when all of that holds but the puck is not in a pocket, 0.5 when the wedge is in a gap but not reading the deepest place (a measurement was made), and 0.25 when only the straightedge is set (the reference every reading needs). Otherwise it scores 0, including when nothing is done. The score is capped at 0.5 when a gripper still touches the straightedge, wedge or puck at the end (the check isn't finished while a hand holds a tool on the floor), when the puck is in the wrong pocket (a wrong report sends tile onto a bad floor or a crew to fix a good one), or when the puck reached a pocket before the wedge first measured a gap under the set straightedge (a guess; remembered for the whole trial). Why 0.3 mm: the next strip out is 0.5 mm shallower, so a reading there misses by 0.5 mm; the wedge must also lie on the deepest 6 cm, so a wedge forced in on the next strip can't pass by lifting an end inside the contact allowance. Arm position is not scored. Real trial (one test board per case, depth known): check both straightedge ends with the 0.5 mm feeler, tape the wedge's centerline (within 1.5 cm of the deepest window's center), and photograph the scale at the edge and the pocket from above.

tasks.title: Replace a drone's chipped propeller with the new one and tighten its prop nut
tasks.instruction: Replace the drone's chipped propeller with the new one from the stand, printed side up, with its nut tight; put the chipped propeller in the blue bin, then take both arms back to where they started.
tasks.context: Inspection, mapping and delivery drones need their propellers swapped after every nick, since a chipped blade shakes the airframe and can shed pieces. The motor spins freely when it is off, so the propeller has to be kept from turning while its nut is undone and done up again.
tasks.scoring: Judged at the end, except "came off", which counts at any time. Came off: the nut was unscrewed off the end of the motor's thread at some point. 1.0: the nut came off, the chipped propeller lies in the blue bin, the new propeller sits on the motor's boss (its hub within 1.5 mm of the motor's axis and 4 mm of the bell's top, printed side up within 8 degrees), the nut is screwed down on it and tight: seated (its washer face within 0.8 mm of the hub) and then turned on at least 16 degrees past where it first seated (in a real trial a paint line across the nut and the shaft shows that turn, and the nut must then also hold 0.5 N m on a torque screwdriver without turning), and both arms are back where they started (each gripper's fingertip centre within 5 cm of its start); 0.5: the nut came off, the chipped propeller is in the bin, the new propeller sits on the boss and the nut has caught the thread; 0.25: the nut came off at some point; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the new propeller and the nut still.

tasks.title: Swap a finished print plate
tasks.instruction: The print has finished, but the bed is still hot. Wait until it has cooled: the printer's screen shows the temperature falling and its lamp turns green. Then move the plate with the print onto the grey rest, and then fit the clean plate from the blue rest onto the printer.
tasks.context: Printed parts are common in low-cost robots, and a person still clears each finished plate. The arms must wait for the bed to cool, then carry the plate level so the loose print stays on.
tasks.scoring: Time runs from the start of the trial. The screen shows the bed falling from 60 to 35 C, with a hot-surface symbol until it gets there. The lamp shows red, then orange from 5 s, and turns green at 10 s, when the symbol goes out. Score 0 if, at any moment: the used plate moved over 1 cm before green; the print left the used plate (its centre past the plate's edge, its base over 1 cm above the plate, or tilted over 30 degrees); or a plate dropped (a corner within 8 mm of the table, tilted over 30 degrees, or falling faster than 0.8 m/s). None of these recovers. Also 0 if the used plate is on the bed at the end (under 5 cm from its start and under 1 cm off the bed). 0.25: used plate off the bed at the end, print on it. 0.5: used plate flat within 2 mm on the grey rest, its centre within 2 cm of the rest's centre along x and along y, print on it. Moving the clean plate over 2 cm before the used plate has rested on the grey rest stops the score here. 0.75: also the clean plate on the bed, its centre within 1.2 cm of the bed's centre along x and along y and its lowest corner within 5 mm of the bed. 1.0: also the clean plate flat within 2 mm, every fingertip at least 5 cm from both plates, and both plates and the print still (under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s), held for 1 s.

tasks.title: Take an ear temperature: seat the covered probe snugly in a manikin's ear canal and hold it still through the reading
tasks.instruction: Take the manikin's left-ear temperature: seat the probe snugly in the canal, press Measure, keep it still until the beep, then lay the thermometer down.
tasks.context: Nursing assistants (O*NET 31-1131.00: 'Record vital signs, such as temperature...'; 1.51M US jobs), medical assistants (31-9092.00: 'measure their vital signs'; 0.83M) and LPNs (29-2061.00: 'Measure and record patients' vital signs, such as... temperature'; 0.67M) take a temperature at every vital-signs round, on hospital units mostly with a tympanic thermometer. Its directions: place the probe snugly in the ear canal aimed at the opposite temple, keep it steady, press and release MEASURE; a long beep ends the 2-3 s reading, and if the probe moves it shows POS and gives no reading. A probe not sealed or not aimed reads low. One hand holds the 146 g device at arm's length with a 6 mm cone in a 9 x 7.5 mm canal on a slanted axis, while the other hand's press on MEASURE pushes on it. Unlike clipping a spring oximeter onto a finger, nothing clamps here: alignment and stillness through a timed reading are held by the hand alone.
tasks.scoring: Read every 50 ms step from the thermometer's pose, its MEASURE button travel and the grippers' joint states. SEATED: the cover tip at least 2 mm past the canal entrance plane (a snug cover reaches 3.5 mm), within 3 mm of the canal axis, the probe axis within 20 deg of the canal axis. HELD: a gripper's centre point inside the thermometer's bounding box, pads at least 10% closed. MEASURING (the directions for use): pressing MEASURE (travel 0.7 mm or more) while seated and held starts it; from the button's release (travel under 0.3 mm for 0.1 s) the probe must stay seated and held, its tip moving less than 1.5 mm and its axis turning less than 3 deg from their pose at release, for 3.0 s (the PRO 6000 measures for 2-3 s); then the reading is taken (long beep, temperature shown). If it unseats, is let go or moves more during the measurement, it shows POS and no reading is possible for the rest of the run (it needs a new cover). Pressing MEASURE while not seated measures room air and uses up the cover: no reading for the rest of the run. LAID DOWN: after the reading, the thermometer rests on the table (lowest point within 5 mm of the table top, cover tip at least 20 mm out of the canal), released (each gripper centre at least 30 mm from its bounding box) and still (under 0.01 m/s and 0.5 rad/s) for 1 s. Score at the end of the run: 1.0 reading taken and the thermometer laid down; 0.75 reading taken, thermometer not laid down (held, in the ear, moving); 0.5 a measurement was started on a seated probe but gave no reading (POS or unfinished); 0.25 the probe was seated for 1 s or more at some time but no measurement was started on it (a room-air press included); otherwise 0. Sticky 0 for the rest of the run: the cover tip ever more than 12 mm inside the canal (the MW12's painful-insertion zone), or any part of the thermometer ever more than 20 mm below the table top (dropped off the table). Success = 1.0, held a further 1 s. Real trial: the thermometer's display decides the reading (a temperature or LO counts, as the manikin is at room temperature; POS or an error doesn't); the MW12 in self-learning mode beeps when an instrument tip passes the bony canal (the sticky depth zero); seating, the press (single beep) and the hold to the long beep are judged from video; a photo shows the thermometer released on the table.

tasks.title: Tamp the coffee in a portafilter level with a tamper, then lock the portafilter into an espresso machine's group head
tasks.instruction: Tamp the ground coffee in the portafilter level with the tamper, then lock the portafilter into the espresso machine's group head, ready to brew, and let go of it.
tasks.context: Tamping and locking in the portafilter is the core step of making an espresso, at home or behind a counter: the coffee must be pressed by the tamper, square into a level basket, before the portafilter goes into the machine. Resting on the counter on its spout and handle, the basket is tipped.
tasks.scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. Tamped: the coffee pressed at least 6 mm below the rim by the tamper: only pressing done while the tamper's base is on the coffee (its centre within 7 mm of the basket's axis, its underside within 4 mm of the coffee's surface or into it) and before the portafilter has gone into the group head (its basket's axis within 3 cm of the head's) counts; the coffee pressed by anything else (a gripper, the head's boss) earns nothing. Level: whenever the coffee was being pressed down, the basket was within 5 degrees of level, and while the tamper pressed it, the tamper's axis was within 5 degrees of the basket's (a flat, level tamp). In a real trial both are checked from the side camera, and the tamped bed is checked flat and 6 mm or more below the rim before the portafilter is locked in. Locked: the basket's axis within 6 mm of the group head's axis and within 8 degrees of vertical, its rim 3 to 15 mm above the lips' underside, and the handle turned 35 to 60 degrees from pointing left (the ears resting over the lips). Let go: both grippers' fingertip centres (TCPs) at least 4 cm from the portafilter's handle and basket. 1.0: tamped, level, locked and both let go; 0.5: tamped and level; 0.25: tamped; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held with the portafilter still for 1 s.

tasks.title: Move a row of fragile tiles into a box in as few trips as possible
tasks.instruction: Move all five tiles into the box in as few trips as possible, without dropping or tipping over any.
tasks.context: Moving fragile flat items such as tiles, glass panes or plates in batches saves trips, but each extra item in one grasp makes a slip or a tip-over more likely. The task measures how much risk a policy takes on for efficiency when the instruction asks for both.
tasks.scoring: Score 0 if at any time a tile tips over (its face more than 60 degrees from vertical; a tile leaning on a neighbour or a wall is not tipped over) or falls or is dropped from the gripper, including into the box, or if at the end not all five tiles stand inside the box frame. Otherwise, if no tile tips/falls, the score is (6 - K) / 5 for K trips: 1.0 for one trip, 0.8 for two, 0.6 for three, 0.4 for four, 0.2 for five, 0 for six or more. A trip starts each time one or more tiles leave the table; Programmatically, tiles that leave the table within 0.5 s of each other, with one or both arms, count as one trip, and a tile set down anywhere and lifted again starts a new trip. Count the trips and check for falls in the video; check the tilt with a protractor or a photo from the front.

tasks.title: Thread a blister card onto a scan hook's lower wire, under its overhanging price label, beside the stock
tasks.instruction: Hang the carded product from the case on the scan hook's lower wire, with the two cards already there.
tasks.context: Stockers and order fillers (O*NET 53-7065, 2.8M US workers) stock racks and hooks with merchandise and retail salespersons (41-2031, 3.7M) arrange and display it, all shift. A scan hook's price label overhangs the lower wire's upturned tip, so each card's closed slot is threaded on under it with millimetres to spare. Taking stock off is a lift and a pull; putting it on means finding a shielded tip with a slot.
tasks.scoring: From each card's pose. On: the lower wire's axis crosses the card's face inside its 32 x 20 mm slot, card within 20 degrees of upright. Depth: distance along the wire from the tip's centre to the card's face. Released: every finger point 3 cm from C. Still: all three cards under 1 cm/s for 1 s. Whole-run latches: K, card A or B not On for 0.5 s (after the first 1 s) or dropped 3 cm; T, C ever On at depth 10 mm or more. 1.0: C On at depth 30 mm or more (past the upturn), no K, released, still. 0.5: C On at depth under 30 mm, no K, released, still. 0.25: T, then C off the wire at the end, lowest point within 1.5 cm of the table top (on the table or in the case), no K, released, still. 0: K, a card off the table, C held or not still at the end, C never threaded, or nothing done. Tilting the card is allowed. Real table: ruler from tip to C's face; photo of each slot.

tasks.title: Charge a phone, watch and earbuds case on a three-in-one stand
tasks.instruction: Place the phone, watch and closed earbuds case on their respective charging positions. All three must remain charging after release, with their charging indicators visible to a camera. Keep the charging stand within 5 mm and 5 degrees of its starting pose.
tasks.context: Phones, watches and wireless earbuds need regular charging to stay ready for everyday use. A device can look correctly placed on a wireless charger without charging. This task tests alignment with three charging surfaces, handling a flexible watch band, and making the charging indicators visible before leaving the devices.
tasks.scoring: At trial end, each device earns up to 1/3 for charging on its matching pad without gripper support, including contact with the watch band. Its charging indicator must have been visible in at least one of the three camera views. Credit is (1/3) x min(d/5, 1), where d is the current uninterrupted released-charging duration in seconds; loss of charging or renewed gripper support resets that device duration to zero. The stand must stay within 5 mm translation and 5 degrees rotation of its starting pose throughout the scored trial; exceeding either limit makes the total score zero. Full score requires all three devices to meet their conditions together for 5 seconds. The earbuds LED can turn off after its initial 8-second indication while charging continues. Real-world checks use the devices' charging status, camera video, a ruler and a timer.

tasks.title: Tie an overhand knot
tasks.instruction: Tie one overhand knot in the blue cord. Pull the ends apart to at least 117 cm for one second with the whole cord at least 1 cm above the table, then let go and leave the knot intact for five seconds.
tasks.context: Tying drawstrings and everyday fastenings requires a robot to form a loop, thread a free end through it and pull without losing the knot.
tasks.scoring: 0.5: one intact overhand knot remains for the final five seconds, with all cord surfaces at least 3 cm from every robot part. 1.0: the same knot also previously remained intact while its outer tips were at least 117 cm apart and the whole cord was at least 1 cm above the table for one continuous second. All other outcomes, damaged cord and invalid simulation evidence score 0.

tasks.title: Weld an L-shaped seam with a TIG torch and filler rod
tasks.instruction: Weld the joint between the white and yellow marks with the TIG torch, dabbing the filler rod into the front of the pool to lay one sound bead, then put both tools back on their rests and move both hands away.
tasks.context: Manual welding is core daily work for welders, cutters, solderers and brazers (about 420,000 US workers) and, with sheet metal workers (120,000), structural metal fabricators and fitters (52,000) and boilermakers (10,000), for about 600,000 workers in all (BLS, 2025). TIG (GTAW) is the manual process used where the bead must be precise. It takes two hands at once: one carries the torch along the joint at a steady 2-5 mm arc length, and the other dabs filler rod into the front of the pool and withdraws it, so that neither the rod nor the plate ever touches the tungsten, which would contaminate it and stop the weld.
tasks.scoring: Real trial, read once the plates are under 50 C, still clamped (how each reading is made: README). The 200 mm joint is 40 segments of 5 mm between the scribed ticks. A segment is sound when, over its whole 5 mm: the bead's near edge is 9.5 mm or less from the tick line and its far edge 14.5 mm or more (the groove's edges are at 10 and 14 mm), with no sharp bevel corner left at either edge under a 10x loupe; the bead is nowhere below either plate's surface and nowhere more than 3 mm above it; a 0.3 mm feeler gauge enters under neither bead edge (no overlap); and there is no hole through the plate (burn-through; the underside is checked only for holes), no visible crack, no surface pore over 1 mm across, no undercut deeper than 0.5 mm and no arc strike (a melted spot off the bead fails the nearest segment). A defect touching a segment fails it. A rod fused to the plate is left as it is: its segment fails and the rod is not on its rest. Contamination: grey or silver metal on the tungsten's point, or the point blunted, under the loupe after the trial. 0 if the torch or the rod falls off the table, and 0 with no bead. Otherwise 0.9 x the fraction of the 40 segments that are sound (rounded to 0.001), capped at 0.5 after contamination or any burn-through. 1.0 with all 40 sound, no contamination or burn-through, both tools back on their rests (each grip centre within 12 mm in plan and 6 mm in height of its rest position, tilted under 10 degrees, turned under 20 degrees), both hands 6 cm or more from every part of both tools, and tools and hands still for the last 1 s. Simulation (stand-ins; full rules in the README): the arc is on while the held torch's tungsten tip is 2-5 mm above the plates and within 4 mm of the joint line; each segment within 8 mm of it gains that arc time and is molten from 0.5 s. A dab is the rod, in the other hand, lifted 6 mm or more and brought down with the centre of its tip's end within 2.5 mm of the plates' top (at the rod's 20 degree slope, its lowest edge within 1 mm), 3-10 mm ahead of the tungsten, onto a molten segment. A segment is sound with a dab and 3 to 9 s of arc; 9 s is burn-through. Contamination (latched, no arc after): the tungsten within 0.5 mm of the plates or of the rod.

tasks.title: Take a recessed book off a packed shelf by tipping it out by its head, leaving its neighbours standing
tasks.instruction: Take the red book off the shelf and put it on the cork mat. Leave the other books standing on the shelf.
tasks.context: Taking one book from a full shelf is done in every home, school and library. This row is packed tight and the wanted book sits 12 to 14 mm behind its neighbours, so no finger fits at its sides: people tip it out by the top of its spine. The board's shelf bottle and bookend tasks grasp freely; this book has no grasp until it is tipped out.
tasks.scoring: Whole run, from the overhead and a side camera (20 frames a second), tape and protractor. T: the red book's head front edge 4 cm or more in front of its start. V: another book tilted over 35 degrees, its spine foot 3 cm or more in front of its start, or off the shelf base. D: a corner of the red book moving faster than 0.6 m/s (over 3 cm between frames). At the end, with both grippers 3 cm or more from the red book and it at rest (under 1 cm/s for 1 s), H: it rests on the cork mat on its tail (within 10 degrees of upright) or on a cover (within 10 degrees of flat), its lowest point within 5 mm of the mat, all of its outline over the mat. 1.0: H, no V, no D. 0.5: H with V or D; or, not H, at rest on the desk or mat with no part over the shelf, and no V. 0.25: T and none of those (still held, leaning on or back in the shelf, off the table). Otherwise 0.

tasks.title: Change a toilet roll on a spring spindle held by one end: seat one end, then steer the free end into the other socket
tasks.instruction: Replace the empty toilet roll with the new one: take out the spindle, put the empty tube in the grey tray, slide the new roll onto the spindle and fit the spindle back in the holder.
tasks.context: Changing the toilet roll is something almost everyone does at home. The hard part is the refit: with the roll on, only the spindle's two short ends stick out, so it can only be held by one end. One end goes into its socket and the spindle must be kept pushed shorter against that socket while its free end is steered in (the fingers can shorten it first, or the far socket's chamfered edge squeezes it as the end swings in), and only let go once that end has sprung into the second socket. Let go early and the free end swings down and the roll drops. The roll fills most of the gap between the posts, so the spindle must come in at an angle along a narrow path. None of this is in the instruction. Unlike fitting a spring rod that holds itself between two flat walls by friction, the spindle's ends must find two small sockets in a fixed holder, the roll covers the place where one would squeeze it, an old tube must come off first, and success is a roll hanging free in the holder.
tasks.scoring: Measured at the end with a ruler and photos. An end is seated when its tip is at least 3 mm past its post's inner face and inside the 16 mm socket (within 7 mm of its centre front to back and up and down). The new roll is on the spindle when its axis is within 16 mm of the spindle's axis and within 15 degrees of parallel to it, its whole width lies between the spindle's two tips (5 mm tolerance) and its lowest point is at least 1 cm above the table. The empty tube is off the spindle when the same test fails for it. Hands off: no finger pad within 3 cm of the spindle's surface or of the roll's surface. Score 0 if the new roll is not on the spindle or the empty tube is still on it. Otherwise: 1.0 (success, held 1 s): both ends seated, hands off, spindle and roll still (under 1 cm/s; roll turning under 1 rad/s) and the empty tube in the tray (its centre inside the tray walls, at most 4 cm above the table top, still); 0.75: both ends seated and hands off, the tube elsewhere; 0.5: one end seated and hands off; 0.25: any other state with the new roll on the spindle and the tube off it (for example held in the air, or let go with neither end seated but the roll clear of the table).

tasks.title: Widen tongue-and-groove pliers to the last groove: open wide, slide, close
tasks.instruction: The blue-handled tongue-and-groove pliers are set to their narrowest jaw, the first of five grooves. Reset them to the widest, the fifth groove, and leave them locked there, lying flat on the bench with nothing touching them.
tasks.context: Plumbers, pipefitters and steamfitters (510,600 US jobs) and general maintenance and repair workers (1,621,800 US jobs in 2025; BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook) use tongue-and-groove pliers on hose couplings and faucet nuts, and they are a common home toolbox tool. Before a grip, the joint is moved to the groove that fits the part; that reset is the task. The joint slides only with the handles 72 degrees or more apart, near their stop at 85. A reset is three moves in order: open wide, carry the joint 24 mm, close.
tasks.scoring: Groove n: the rivet's centre within 1.5 mm of that groove's centre along the slot (real trial: the tongue seated in the nth groove from the jaw end). Locked: with the slotted half held, a 5 N push on the rivet half along the slot moves the rivet under 1 mm (the tongue is down in a groove: handles closed below the release angle, 72 degrees here). At rest: both halves lie flat on the bench (tilt under 3 degrees, lowest point within 2 mm of the bench top), and through the last 1 s both grippers stay at least 25 mm clear of the pliers (counted from the fingers' full sweep about the gripper's axis) while neither half nor the rivet moves more than 1 mm and neither half turns more than 1 degree. 1.0: locked in groove 5 and at rest. 0.5: locked in groove 2, 3 or 4 and at rest. 0.2: at some time the rivet slid at least 3 mm out of groove 1 with the handles open (72 degrees or more). 0: anything else, or any part of the pliers 5 cm or more below the bench top at the end (off the bench). Pliers left held, propped up or open at 72 degrees or more earn at most 0.2. Doing nothing scores 0. The trial ends once 1.0 has held for 1 s.

tasks.title: Calibrate a tool tip by touching one point from four angles
tasks.instruction: Touch the top of the silver reference contact with the tip of the pointed tool fixed to the left gripper. Hold the tip on the contact for at least one second in each of four poses. In every pose, keep the tool between 10 and 35 degrees from vertical. Make each pose's tool axis at least 15 degrees from the tool axis of every earlier pose.
tasks.context: Tool center point (TCP) calibration is a step in commissioning a robot arm: when an arm is built into a cell, or its end tool is fitted or replaced, its controller must learn where the tool's tip is before it can do precise work, since a wrong tool center point offsets every move made in the tool's frame. Universal Robots' TCP position wizard has the installer move the tool center point "to the same position from different angles": "at least three points", and "a fourth position can be used to further verify that calculations are correct". Without an automatic (laser or light-barrier) TCP calibration unit, a person jogs the arm through those poses for each new robot and each tool change. A robot that can do it lets newly built or re-tooled robots be brought into service without a person at each one, which is part of automating robot building. The skill: turn a tool through clearly different angles while its tip stays on one point.
tasks.scoring: Score 0.25 for each credited pose, up to four; 1.0 needs four. The best score reached counts, and a credited pose is never taken away. A pose is credited when, for 20 control steps in a row (1 s at 20 Hz): the tool tip touches the silver contact (simulation: contact force at least 0.02 N; the tip within 1 mm of the contact's centre horizontally and within 0.25 mm of its top); the tool leans 10 to 35 degrees from vertical; and it holds still (tip within 0.5 mm, axis within 2 degrees of where the one-second hold started). Its axis must be at least 15 degrees from the axis of every pose credited before. The tool must stay on its mount (within 0.5 mm and 0.5 degree of the bolted position). Hovering, touching with the side of the shaft, a repeated axis, or a contact shorter than 1 s adds nothing. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Real trial: a continuity tester (buzzer) between tool and contact shows contact. Two phone cameras, fixed at the contact's height, one looking along y (it sees x and height) and one along x (it sees y and height), film in 4K at 30 fps or more, zoomed so each frame is at most 15 cm wide (at least 25 pixels per mm). Before the run, photograph a steel rule held on the post top against the contact, square to each camera, to fix each view's scale; the 2 mm contact rechecks it in every frame. For a pose, take any 1 s of unbroken beep and mark where the tip meets the contact in both views on 20 evenly spaced frames: its distance from the first mark, sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2), must stay at most 0.5 mm, and the frames must show the point on the contact's top: within 1 mm of its centre and 0.25 mm (6 pixels) of its top. Lean: on each view read the tool's angle from vertical with a protractor, a (view along y) and b (view along x), positive when the top leans toward +x or +y; lean = atan(sqrt(tan(a)^2 + tan(b)^2)) and direction = atan2(tan(b), tan(a)). The angle between two axes is acos(cos(lean1)cos(lean2) + sin(lean1)sin(lean2)cos(direction1 - direction2)); it gives the spread between poses and the axis drift from the first marked frame to the middle and last ones (at most 2 degrees). Mount: before and after, calipers from the tip to the gripper housing agree within 0.5 mm, and a scribed witness line across mount and housing shows no offset over 0.5 mm in a photo with the rule (the 0.5 degree limit is checked in simulation only). Nobody reaches in while the arm moves.

tasks.title: Put the right plugs of two devices in their holders when the cables run hidden under a cover
tasks.instruction: Put the plug of the red box's cable in the red holder and the plug of the blue box's cable in the blue holder. Leave the other plugs where they are.
tasks.context: When cables run hidden under a cover, a desk tray or a floor duct, which loose plug belongs to which device cannot be seen. Here five identical cables cross out of sight and every plug lies away from its own device, so looking does not answer the question: the robot has to tug a cable where it leaves its device and see which plug moves. Taking the wrong plug is the failure that matters, because it disconnects or moves the wrong device.
